established: In the tested corpus, the preceding token identity explains 0.79% of capped token entropy after shuffle correction, while the last and first glyphs across adjacent tokens share 0.197 bits of shuffle-corrected mutual information.

Uncertain separators have higher cross-boundary cohesion and narrower image-coordinate gaps than certain separators. Manually drawn coordinate boxes distinguished the two classes with AUC 0.905 among matched boundaries. A smaller blind measurement of the ink gave the same direction and weaker discrimination.
After erasing every space before learning the units, the 64-merge segmentation crossed 2.5% of certain and 20.3% of uncertain separators. The direction held in each of the 16 analyzed quires.
Byte-pair merges identify an early multi-symbol scale of reduced adjacent dependence, with a minimum at 32 merges when scored on omitted quires and at 64 in the pooled fit.

The tested Naibbe and self-citation outputs approximate the manuscript's low glyph entropy, early merge scale, weak token order and null substitution-attack differential. Their tested outputs have substantially weaker edge-glyph dependence and fewer singleton types than the manuscript at matched token counts.

statement: Layout-blind periodic table text, fitted on public Currier B pages only. Words are drawn independently by frequency from the public Currier B word list; every tenth word (ten being the commonest paragraph line length on the public B pages) is drawn from the words ending in m, all others from the words not ending in m. The writer never sees where a line ends. This is the strongest procedure of its kind I could find: periods 8 to 13 were tried on the practice split and none lifts the line-final to mid-line ratio above about 1.0, against 61.6 for the manuscript there. Sent as a best attempt that does not land: F-001 survives every generator that cannot see the line break. It says nothing about language, though; a writer who can see the line end and puts an m-final word there would reproduce it, and the attack format (a word stream re-cut to the hidden line shapes) cannot express such a rule.
title: fact attack on F-001

spec.statement: Components were chosen by greedy forward selection under 4-fold cross-validation over scribe 1's public training pages only (pool: vocab, chain, position, letters order 2-5, copy windows 3/5/10/20/50 with 0 or 1 edits, templates prefix 0-3 x suffix 0-3), stopping when a component gained under 0.002 bits per word. Cross-validated: 11.31 bits per word against 11.75 for the bag of words and 11.40 for glyph trigrams alone. The same search run separately on scribes 2, 3 and 4 and on the whole text picked the same core every time (letters order 3 first; copy with a wide window; position; templates), with cross-validated gains over the bag of 0.39, 0.39, 0.58 and 0.38 bits per word; scribe 5 has too few training words. In every scope most of the gain is glyph trigrams alone, the word-to-word chain is selected late or never (under 0.01 bits per word), and the memorized vocabulary is never selected once letters order 3 is in. Negative side: nothing in the current component language gets much below a glyph trigram model (0.04 to 0.16 bits per word), so a production process is not yet separated from spelling habit.
spec.title: Scribe 1: glyph trigrams + page-local copy (window 50, exact and one-glyph-changed) + line position + prefix templates + chain

detail.statement: F-001 (line-final m in Currier B) stands, but the fact-attack format pours synthetic text into the hidden pages as one token stream, so no generator can know where a line ends and every positional fact survives by construction (R-001 said as much). On the practice split, a layout-aware table procedure with no language (independent words by frequency from public Currier B text, the last word of each line drawn from the line-final vocabulary) reproduces F-001 at 55.2 against 61.6 when its line ends are kept, and 1.15 when they are not. A code change adding cut "lines" to fact attacks is in review; R-attack-F-001 should be retried once it lands, and F-001 should not be read as evidence of language until then. Three code changes for the test's power are also in review: keys that ignore spaces are now charged fairly by criterion (a) and can be found by the search (5 of 9 languages cracked at 2% noise), and verbose search prunes noise-born units; the remaining failures (Italian and French verbose, German substitution) are an objective limit in the first two and a search trap on ch/sch in German, not a budget problem.
detail.title: Dispatch: F-001 survives only because attacks cannot see line ends; test-power fixes in review

detail.statement: In results/heldout/controls.json the German homophonic control is the one substitution cell where the true key passes at 2% noise but the pinned search fails, clean and noisy: the search, not the hypothesis, is what stops German from being ruled in or out. Measured on the practice controls (fleet-opus): the search's best key scores far worse on its own trigram objective than the true key (clean -114447 vs -103058 bits; at 2% noise -121486, while a climb started from the true key reaches -111999 and passes (a) with +0.061), and its errors sit on h and c (German ch/sch). It is not a budget problem: 16 restarts x 6000 iterations, 4 x 12000, 4 x 24000 at noise, a letter-frequency rank start and simulated annealing (start temperatures 10, 30, 100 bits) all end in the same basin; one clean run at 4 x 24000 escaped. Try larger moves (swap the letters of two whole homophone groups, move a unit together with its most frequent neighbour, or restarts seeded from bigram rather than unigram rank) and report the German row with python3 -m vs season --parts controls, with the other languages' rows to show nothing regressed.
detail.title: German × substitution: get the key search out of the ch/sch trap

detail.statement: Work on K-002-open-2, public training pages only (192 pages, paragraph text, certain words, identical line widths and word counts for the synthetic text). Boundary statistics, shuffle-corrected at matched pair counts: the manuscript has 0.198 bits of dependence between a word's last glyph and the next word's first glyph within lines (25,796 pairs) and 0.002 bits across line breaks (2,765 pairs, paragraph starts excluded). With uncertain spaces joined instead of split the figures are 0.164 and 0.004, so the collapse does not depend on how uncertain separators are read; the within-line level does (about 17% lower). Spacing statistics: word length in glyphs has mean 4.48, sd 1.65 (4.81, 1.72 joined). One fixed procedure fitted on the same pages, a glyph chain of order 4 inside the word whose first glyph is drawn given the last glyph of the word before and which starts afresh at each line from the line-initial distribution, gives 0.197 within lines, 0.007 across breaks, length mean 4.49, sd 1.77, 6,770 types and hapax share 0.66 at 32,410 words (manuscript 7,042 and 0.69 at 32,142). The same chain run straight through line breaks keeps 0.198 bits across them, so the collapse needs a writer who treats the line as a unit; the repository's self-citation generator gives 0.021 within and 0.014 across. So on public pages the answer is yes for the boundary statistics and close for spacing (the chain's lengths are a little too spread). None of this is scored yet: the measurement language cannot state the collapse. Proposed step: once the statistic edge_gap (branch code-L2-edge-gap-fleet-fable) is merged, register the fact {"select": {"unit": ["P"], "certain": true}, "statistic": {"edge_gap": true}, "compare": [{"op": ">=", "value": 0.08}, {"null": "shuffle_within_page", "direction": "greater", "perms": 199, "p": 0.01}]} (practice split: 0.198 ZL, 0.154 Takahashi, 0.166 RF, p 0.005 each), then attack it. A blind word stream cannot restart at hidden line starts, so the attack also needs a line-aware attack form (branch code-R-line-aware-attack-fleet-fable covers line ends; line starts would need the same).
detail.title: Register the line-break collapse of edge-glyph dependence (edge_gap) and attack it with a line-restarting glyph chain

established: Similarly spelled glyph groups occur with similar frequencies and tend to occur near each other; the paper groups the vocabulary into a few series (around daiin, ol and chedy in EVA) linked by single-glyph changes.
The number of words repeated from one line to the next is raised for consecutive lines in the manuscript, an increase the paper does not find in its Latin and English comparison texts.

The second glyph group of a line is shorter than the first in 48% of lines and longer in 32%, which the paper explains by glyphs added to line-initial groups (and gallows added to paragraph-initial groups), after Vogt's observation that line-initial words are longer than average.
The paper reports that repeated sequences of more than five words are missing from the manuscript and argues that the copying method explains this together with the constantly changing vocabulary.
From spelling variants that do not appear on pages already completed, the paper argues that the pages in Currier B were written after those in Currier A.

detail.statement: The core summary is accurate, but the benchmark description in the Spanish follow-up needs correction. Section 4.4 and Table 2 use fifty 500-character Wikipedia extracts across five languages, with substitution followed by intra-word anagramming. They report 93.8% token recovery for the combined two-stage pipeline. They did not inject 2% transcription noise. That level is a new test setting for the swarm. Section 5.3's 0.996 and 2.454 are fitted average inversion counts under separate glyph or letter orders, equivalent to minimum adjacent swaps to reach those orders. Section 6 proposes extending the anagram model to reorder whole words within lines, and suggests softened emissions for noise generally. The Spanish and English reversal checks are narrower swarm variants. Primary source: https://aclanthology.org/Q16-1006.pdf

statement: A table procedure with one rule about the line, fitted on public paragraph text only. Every line has nine words. The first word of each line is drawn by frequency from the public words that begin with p or f; the other eight are drawn by frequency from all public words, with no regard to order (so p or f words turn up inside lines at their ordinary rate, 1.8%). Words are independent draws: no word order, no meaning. 2,600 lines, fixed seed, generated once, laid on the pages line by line (cut lines). The writer sees the start of a line and nothing else; it does not know where paragraphs begin. It still reproduces F-003, because a text in which every line opens with a gallows word also has every paragraph open with one. On the practice split the ratio is 58.5 against the manuscript's 54.6. Read with care: this shows that F-003 as specified does not separate a paragraph-opening habit from a line-opening one and needs no language; it does not show that the manuscript's lines open this way (they do not: the manuscript concentrates p and f on paragraph starts). A fact comparing paragraph-initial words with other line-initial words would not fall to this text.

spec.statement: Timm's copy-and-modify account predicts that a word is often a recent word of the same page, unchanged or with one glyph changed, and that the place in the line matters. This mixture holds both: copy from the last 50 words of the page (exact, and with one glyph changed) and a line-position vocabulary, next to a glyph trigram speller, the word chain and two prefix-core-suffix templates. Components and sizes were chosen by cross-validation on the public training pages only (the selection reported with M-001). Ablations on the practice split, weights refitted each time, in bits per word: full 11.230; without the two copy components 11.283; without position 11.289; without both 11.350; bag of words 11.586; glyph trigrams alone 11.400. Fitted weight is about 0.08 on copying and 0.23 on position. Reading: fitted on public pages, copying and line position each predict unseen pages better (0.05 and 0.06 bits per word, 0.12 together), so the procedure's two habits carry over, but most words are still best predicted by spelling alone. This scores prediction of words, not the two statistics the question names (word repetition between consecutive lines, longer line-initial words); those need their own facts and a generated text to attack them.

detail.statement: R-001 failed only because attacks could not see line ends at the time: its text was a token stream re-cut to the hidden line shapes. Attacks can now send whole lines ("cut": "lines" in attack.json), so F-001 has not yet faced a fair attack. Fit a language-free generator on public Currier B pages only that knows where a line ends, and send its text with cut lines. The generator must be a general mechanism, for example a glyph or word chain that restarts at each line and conditions on position in the line, or Timm-style copying of nearby words with line-end effects (K-005). It must not contain a rule that names the target pattern (such as 'put an m-final word last on each line'): an attack that writes the fact in by hand only shows a hand-written rule can copy it, and will be recorded as a weak refutation. Say in the method which statistics the generator was fitted on. If no general generator lifts the line-final to mid-line ratio near the manuscript's, send the best attempt: a failed fair attack is the result that makes F-001 a hard target for G.

detail.statement: Work on K-003-open-1, public training pages only (192 pages, 189 consecutive pairs with at least 40 certain words each, 43 of them crossing a section or Currier-language boundary). Similarity here is the cosine of raw word-count vectors of consecutive pages, not the paper's latent semantic analysis, so this is a simpler stand-in under one preprocessing for every text; synthetic texts have the manuscript's page and line shapes word for word. Manuscript: median 0.344 (5th to 95th percentile 0.106 to 0.648), against 0.197 for pages in shuffled order; of the 9 lowest scores (5%), 5 fall on transitions, which make up 23% of pairs; median at transitions 0.170. Pinned self-citation generator: median 0.007, shuffled 0.007, so it has almost no page-to-page similarity at all and no usable low tail. Glyph chain with one table for the whole text (the procedure that landed on F-002, F-004, F-005): median 0.313 but 0.326 shuffled, and none of its 9 lowest scores on transitions, so it has no neighbourhood effect. The same glyph chain with a separate table fitted for each Currier language and section, the change being fixed in advance by the page's label: median 0.346 (0.135 to 0.757), 0.256 shuffled, 5 of its 9 lowest scores on transitions, median at transitions 0.250. So on public pages the answer is yes in outline: a meaning-free procedure whose tables change at prespecified boundaries reproduces the level of adjacent-page similarity and where the low scores fall; it is less sharp than the manuscript at transitions (0.250 against 0.170) and its upper tail is heavier. Limits: 9 low scores is a small count; the generator is fitted on the same public pages it is compared on; nothing here is scored on hidden pages. Proposed step: add an adjacent-page similarity statistic to the measurement language (reviewed code), register (a) adjacent above shuffled-order similarity and (b) the share of lowest-5% scores at transitions as facts, then attack both with the per-section glyph chain using the line-keeping cut.
detail.title: Score adjacent-page similarity and its drops at section and Currier transitions against a generator whose tables change at those boundaries

established: A reimplementation of Timm and Schinner's similar-glyph procedure gives conditional character entropy of 2.38 bits without fitting that statistic, close to the 2.34-bit EVA manuscript estimate. The study reports that the absolute estimate shifts under the v101 alphabet.

All of the tested matched generators passed the four Parisel positional signatures under the published verifier, including the grille example, limiting those tests' power to distinguish the mechanisms in this comparison.

The proposed stock-and-flow generator falls inside the study's three folio-bootstrap intervals for reuse, rigidity and entropy and reproduces the singleton fraction. It uses character transitions learned from the manuscript, and its matched-size type-to-token ratio remains about 15 percent high.

statement: A table procedure with two word lists and one rule about the line, fitted on public paragraph text only. List one holds the words that stand first in a line on the public pages, list two the words that stand anywhere else. Every line has nine words: the first is drawn by frequency from list one, the other eight by frequency from list two. Words are independent draws: no word order, no meaning. 2,600 lines, fixed seed, generated once, laid on the pages line by line (cut lines). The writer sees where a line starts and nothing else. On the practice split the line-initial mean length is 4.90 glyphs against the manuscript's 4.83, above the within-line shuffle. So F-006 needs a writer who treats the start of a line differently, not a language.

source: Sharpens F-003 after the red team's R-003: that attack reproduced paragraph-initial p and f with a writer who only sees where a line starts. This fact compares whole first lines with the other lines, so a writer who treats every line alike gives a ratio near 1. Public practice split: 15.4 (Zandbergen-Landini), 15.4 (Takahashi), 3.4 (RF, 223 words selected); public training pages 20.5, thirds of them 13.8 to 27.8. Decomposition on the training pages: p or f opens 51% of paragraph-first words, 2.6% of the later words on first lines, 1.3% of the first words of other lines and 0.25% of their later words; so about a tenfold excess remains on first lines after their first word is set aside, though the registered statistic includes that first word and so overlaps F-003. A line-restarting glyph chain with no knowledge of paragraphs gives 1.0 to 1.1 on the practice split and does not reproduce it: a target for generators that needs a paragraph-aware writer, not evidence of language.

detail.why: the text reproduces 7 of 8 established facts

statement: Fitted on the paragraph lines of the public practice training pages only (lines without uncertain readings). Each line is one string of symbols: its glyphs, a word-space symbol between words, a line-end symbol after the last word. The fitted table is how often each symbol follows the four symbols before it, with shorter contexts as fallback. The writer starts fresh at each line and draws symbol by symbol until the line-end symbol comes up, so line length is whatever the chain gives and a word space and a line end are two outcomes of the same draw. At the start of a word, one time in ten, the writer instead copies one of the last ten words written and alters one glyph, the new glyph drawn from the same table in its context; whether a space or a line end follows the copy is again drawn from the table. No word list, no position class, no rule that names a glyph, a position, or any fact. A line holding a four-word run of the manuscript is redrawn. Seed 408, 3,000 lines. Practice split, whole lines kept: 7 of 7 (F-001 14.4 against 61.6; F-002 0.235; F-003 15.7 against 54.6; F-004 0.331; F-005 0.241; F-006 4.81; F-007 0.190 against 0.210). Honest margins: a second seed (7) at the same settings gives 6 of 7, F-003 falling to 9.3 against its threshold of 10; without the copying step the chain alone gives 6 of 7 with wider margins on F-001 (28) and F-003 (20) but misses F-007 (0.131); copying more (one in four) lifts F-007 and loses F-003, because copied line-opening words land mid-line. The copy rate (0.1) and the seed were chosen on the practice split. Because each line restarts the chain, first glyphs of a line do not depend on the last glyph of the line before, which is the collapse of edge dependence at line breaks.

established: The authors identify 37 plants, 6 animals and 1 mineral in the drawings with species they place in post-Conquest Mexico and neighbouring regions; the identifications are visual comparisons with 16th-century sources such as the Codex Cruz-Badianus (1552) and Hernandez, and the authors say many still need refinement.

They compare a few glyph shapes (a broken 'tl', a backward 's', a 'z') with letterforms in the Codex Osuna and propose a preliminary syllabary/alphabet from them; they state that they are botanists and horticulturists, not linguists, and that the syllabary is a first attempt.

From 'tl' and 'chi' endings in their label readings and from the mix of Classical Nahuatl, Mixtec and Spanish loan-words, they place the proposed dialect in central or northern Mexico, and suggest its speakers may have died in the 16th-century epidemics.

source: Registered as a target for generators after R-008 (a one-table line chain with nearby copying reproduced 7 of 8 facts). Public practice split: 0.311 against a mean of 0.223 for words shuffled across pages (Zandbergen-Landini), 0.307 (Takahashi), 0.294 (RF); training pages 0.291; it also holds on blocks of 40 training pages taken separately. No absolute threshold is set because the share grows with the length of a page. Generators on the practice split: the R-008 text gives 0.179 and the chain alone 0.190, both failing, since one table serves every page; a chain whose table drifts along the text (fitted on a moving window of public pages) gives 0.299 and passes. So this is not evidence of language: ordinary texts with page topics would pass too, and so does a meaning-free procedure whose tables change as it goes. It separates procedures with one fixed table from those with local tables.

detail.statement: R-008 (a line-restarting glyph chain with the line end as a symbol, plus copying of nearby words) reproduced 7 of 8 established facts on the hidden pages and missed F-008 (words opening with p or f gather on paragraph first lines). It cannot reproduce F-008 in the present attack format: the scorer lays the attacker's lines onto the hidden pages in order, so no text can know which of its lines will open a paragraph. A code change in review (branch code-R-paragraph-aware-attack-fleet-fable) lets attack.json carry first_lines, the lines a procedure wrote as a paragraph's first line. With that change, on the public practice split, one procedure reproduces all 8 established facts and two facts awaiting a verdict: the same chain (four symbols of context, word space and line end as symbols) with (a) a second opening symbol for a paragraph's first line, (b) a table that drifts, each stretch of 60 lines written from the whole-text table at half weight plus a moving window of 12 public pages, and (c) one word in ten copied from the last ten words with one glyph altered in context. No rule names a glyph or a fact. attack.json.method: Fitted on the paragraph lines of the public practice training pages only (lines without uncertain readings). Each line is one string of symbols: its glyphs, a word-space symbol between words, a line-end symbol after the last word. The fitted table is how often each symbol follows the four symbols before it, with shorter contexts as fallback. The writer starts fresh at each line and draws symbol by symbol until the line-end symbol comes up, so line length is whatever the chain gives and a word space and a line end are two outcomes of the same draw. At the start of a word, one time in ten, the writer instead copies one of the last ten words written and alters one glyph, the new glyph drawn from the same table in its context; whether a space or a line end follows the copy is again drawn from the table. No word list, no position class, no rule that names a glyph, a position, or any fact. A line holding a four-word run of the manuscript is redrawn. Seed 408, 3,000 lines. Practice split, whole lines kept: 7 of 7 (F-001 14.4 against 61.6; F-002 0.235; F-003 15.7 against 54.6; F-004 0.331; F-005 0.241; F-006 4.81; F-007 0.190 against 0.210). Honest margins: a second seed (7) at the same settings gives 6 of 7, F-003 falling to 9.3 against its threshold of 10; without the copying step the chain alone gives 6 of 7 with wider margins on F-001 (28) and F-003 (20) but misses F-007 (0.131); copying more (one in four) lifts F-007 and loses F-003, because copied line-opening words land mid-line. The copy rate (0.1) and the seed were chosen on the practice split. Because each line restarts the chain, first glyphs of a line do not depend on the last glyph of the line before, which is the collapse of edge dependence at line breaks.

statement: A line-restarting glyph chain whose table drifts, fitted on the public practice training pages only. Each line is one string of symbols (its glyphs, a word-space symbol, a line-end symbol at the end); the table records how often each symbol follows the three before it, and a line is written symbol by symbol from the line start until the line-end symbol is drawn. The text is written in 50 stretches of 60 lines. Each stretch uses a table fitted on 8 consecutive public pages, and the window moves forward through the public pages in manuscript order from one stretch to the next, as a scribe working from a changing set of nearby sheets or tables would. No word list is kept from page to page, nothing is copied from earlier on the page, and no rule mentions pages, repetition or any glyph: words recur within a page only because lines laid on the same page were written from the same small table. A line holding a four-word run of the manuscript is redrawn (seed 408, 3,000 lines). On the practice split, with whole lines kept, the share of words of four or more glyphs already written earlier on the page is 0.299 against 0.311 for the manuscript, above the across-pages shuffle. For comparison, the same chain with one table for the whole text gives 0.190 and fails. Limits: small windows make the chain repeat its sources more closely (90% of its words are manuscript word types); this text was not tuned for the other facts and on practice it loses F-001 and F-003, so it is an attack on F-009 only, not a better generator overall.

established: The paper proposes a glyph-to-Pahlavi letter table (Table 1) based on letter-shape comparison, with many Voynich glyphs taken as rotated Pahlavi letters; the evidence is visual similarity plus a few dozen label and text words read with the table, not a statistical or held-out test.

Several transcribed label words, mainly in the astronomical and cosmological sections, are matched to names and terms of Zoroastrian cosmology in the Bundahishn and to Pahlavi dictionary entries; the author calls the transcription tentative and says only a few words have been presented.

The author states there is no evidence that the manuscript was produced in Persia or western India, raises a Black Sea origin as possible, and leaves open whether other idioms (e.g. Parsi Gujarati) are present.

open.check: Pin an openly licensed Middle Persian transliteration of 150,000+ characters (kind corpus), then score the frozen table as a key.
open.question: Does Herrmann's glyph-to-Pahlavi table, frozen as a substitution key, read the hidden pages better than its decoys against a Middle Persian corpus? Openly licensed text: I found no Middle Persian (Pahlavi) transliteration under an explicit open licence at a stable plain-text url; the large digital transliterations (e.g. TITUS, the Bochum MPCD project) do not state cc licences, and E. W. West's 1880-1897 Pahlavi Texts (Sacred Books of the East, public domain) are English translations, not Pahlavi. So no corpus yet; modern Persian (cc-by-sa Wikipedia, many millions of characters) would only be a distant proxy.

Can a complete phonemic account and translation of more than a few words be given with the proposed table? The author says this needs substantial effort from Pahlavi philologists and is not attempted.
Are the astronomical charts consistent with Bundahishn cosmology rather than Arabic or Latin astronomy, as the author suggests, when compared blind on the scans?

detail.summary: Herrmann argues that the Voynich alphabet is derived from the Iranian Pahlavi script used for Middle Persian: many Voynich glyphs are said to be upside-down Pahlavi letters, others ligatures or additions that resolve Pahlavi's notorious letter ambiguity. He transcribes words from illustration labels and parts of the main text with the proposed letter table and matches several to terms from Zoroastrian cosmology (the Bundahishn) and a Pahlavi dictionary. He explicitly does not attempt a translation.

established: The article proposes visual and structural parallels between Voynich syllable-letters and Ottoman tughra construction, especially a tughra in a notebook attributed to the young Mehmed II; the evidence is side-by-side glyph comparison, not a statistical or held-out test.

It uses the author's ATA transliteration table, in which glyphs carry Turkish phonetic values; for example it chooses to show a P/B distinction in the table on the argument that P shifted to B or F in some Turkic dialects over 600 years, and says the author's exact sound inventory is not settled.

It claims that read with this table the text follows Turkish phonetic and morphological rules and that Old Turkish words, plant and animal names match in sound and meaning; the article presents these as matches for readers to examine, and does not give a complete key or a translation of a full passage.

detail.why: the fact also holds on text made without language

statement: One glyph chain over the whole line, fitted on the paragraph lines of the public practice training pages only (3,306 lines without uncertain readings). Each line is one string of symbols: its glyphs, a word-space symbol between words, a line-end symbol after the last word. The only fitted statistic is how often each symbol follows the four symbols before it. A line is written symbol by symbol, starting afresh at each line, until the line-end symbol is drawn. No word list, no copying, no rule naming a glyph. The first glyph of a word depends on the last glyph of the word before it only through the chain's context, and that context is emptied at each new line, so the dependence is present inside lines and absent across line breaks by construction of the procedure, not by a rule about the statistic. A line holding a four-word run of the manuscript is redrawn (seed 408, 3,000 lines). On the practice split, with whole lines kept, the within-line minus across-break gap is 0.151 bits against 0.173 for the manuscript (threshold 0.08, above the within-page shuffle). A chain that runs straight through line breaks keeps its dependence across them and shows no gap (P-L2-001). So the fact needs a writer who treats the line as a unit, not language.

detail.summary: Stojko proposed that the manuscript is a copy of a series of letters written in Ukrainian, enciphered by dropping all vowels and writing the consonants in a secret alphabet. Zandbergen's summary records why it found little acceptance: the background history departs from the accepted history of Ukraine, the letters' text does not relate to the illustrations, and the plaintext is produced by inserting vowels and word spaces freely, so cipher-text and plain-text word spaces are mostly unrelated.

established: The proposal is a vowelless Ukrainian plaintext under a consonant-only secret alphabet; vowels and word divisions are supplied by the decipherer (Zandbergen's summary).
As summarised, no fixed key with a single reading per glyph is given in open form; the freedom to insert vowels and re-segment words is the main criticism.

detail.statement: Cheshire (2019, K-016; figures 1-29 of the accepted manuscript at research-information.bris.ac.uk/ws/files/201563069/) defines his alphabet only by drawn glyphs, not by EVA. Read from the figures, these correspondences are clear: EVA a = trapped a, y = free a, q = d (the '4'), e = short e, ee = double short e, ch = long e (ee), i = i, k = l, t = m, ckh = ele, cth = eme, cph = epe, cfh = eque, p = p, f = qu, d (the '8') = n, o = o; probably sh = ae (long e with a detached crest, fig. 5) and n = sitting s (the -ais/-aus endings, figs. 3-4, 23). Not resolvable from the paper: his standing s and t (figs. 22, 24) differ only by an angled vs curved foot and both look like EVA r; his r (fig. 21, 'open-base 8') may be EVA s; his u (fig. 27) and v (fig. 28) have no clear EVA counterpart; EVA l, one of the commonest glyphs, is not described at all. A frozen key built from guesses would misstate his proposal, so the concordance should be fixed first from his own worked examples (figs. 30 onward, each tied to a folio) against the ZL transliteration of those words.

key.json.notes: Frozen, no search. Consonant values only: the pinned Hebrew corpora are normalized to unpointed consonants with final forms folded to base forms, so Hannig's final letters (m, n, p, N) are written as base letters and his vowel signs (o 'vowel indicator', i = hireq, c = qibbus/modifier) map to nothing. Where his table gives one glyph two values, the value used in his own worked readings is kept: h = kaf (9hae = 'ikar, though the table also lists h for qof), k = tav (Akam = 'itim, though the table also lists k for tet), 1 = mem (his stated primary value; he also reads it as nun). N = final pe is his 'most likely' assignment; * (possibly final kaf), backslash and the remaining v101 glyphs are left unmapped (nulls), as he leaves them undeciphered. 8 = vav (his 'primary' value; in language A he also reads it as bet).
key.json.source: Rainer Hannig (2020), Voynich-Hebräisch: Der Weg zur Entzifferung, sections 10-22 and the table in section 13 (K-019). v101 codes read from the embedded Voynich-1.01 font of the PDF (U+F0xx = ASCII).

sources: Beinecke MS 408, IIIF canvas https://collections.library.yale.edu/manifests/oid/2002046/canvas/1006200 (label '70v (part)'; the Pisces wheel), region x=1600-2500, y=1200-2100 at full size: https://collections.library.yale.edu/iiif/2/1006200/1600,1200,900,900/900,/0/default.jpg

Zandbergen-Landini transliteration ZL 3b (pinned data/raw/ZL3b-n.txt), page comment for f70v2: 'In the centre are two fish ..., two stars, a word of Voynich text and the word Mars in the Roman alphabet'; the word is locus f70v2.33 under the heading 'Central star:', read otolal
Variant readings of locus f70v2.33 in the pinned transliterations: otolal (ZL 3b, RF 1b, LSI V), otylal (IT 2a, LSI H), otalal (LSI U), otral (LSI C, K); GC 2a okoeae
detail.statement: UNCERTAIN; HERE IS WHY. I looked at the scan myself (canvas 1006200, centre cropped at full resolution). The Pisces centre holds two fish joined by a cord, two stars (one above the fish, one below), the Latin-script month name (read 'mars' in the literature; Mars = March) written between the two fish, and exactly one Voynich word. That word (otolal in ZL) is written immediately to the right of the UPPER STAR, at the top of the centre disc, the way the nymph labels on this page sit beside their stars; it is about a fish-length away from 'mars' and is not on the same line as it. ZL files it under 'Central star:'. So the scan supports reading otolal as the label of that star, and does not support it as a Voynich rendering of the month name. detail.statement: On the record: 10 facts hold on the hidden pages, most of them about word edges and position in the line and paragraph. 8 red-team attacks have landed, so several of these facts also appear in text made without language and do not show that the text is a language. 32 keys have failed, all simple substitution or verbose ciphers into Latin, Italian, French, Spanish and English; do not send more keys into those cells at the same budget, and use the calibrated budgets in P-L3-001, P-L3-002 and P-J-001 instead. Agents have added 39 corpora, which opens first-key steps (L3-first-*) in languages where the search has power; these are the best use of L3 time now, and Catalan, Occitan-adjacent, Hungarian, Polish and Greek come first as period-plausible. Anchors are the weak point for criterion (c): none is confirmed, and a scan check of the zodiac pages (f70v1, f70v2, f71r, f73r, f73v) found no Voynich word beside any Latin-script month name; the only centre word (f70v2, otolal) labels a star. So anchor work should go to labelled objects and to herbal plants with two independent published identifications, and every draft anchor needs a second look on the scan before anyone agrees.

statement: A glyph chain over the whole line (four symbols of context; the word space and the line end are ordinary symbols) that starts afresh at each line. The only thing the writer knows about layout is which kind of line it is starting: the chain's start symbol is one mark for a line that opens a paragraph and another for any other line, as counted on the public paragraph lines. No rule mentions p, f, gallows or any glyph: whatever the first lines carry is what the counts after the paragraph-opening mark hold, fading as the four-symbol context moves on. One table for the whole text, no word list, no copying, no drift. Fitted on the public training pages only (certain paragraph lines); lines containing a four-word run of the manuscript are redrawn. 'lines' are lines written with the ordinary start mark, 'first_lines' lines written with the paragraph-opening mark; the scorer lays first_lines on the lines that open a paragraph. Local robustness on the practice split (real 15.4, threshold 3): seeds 1, 2, 3 give 8.1, 7.1, 8.9; fitted on every other public page only, 7.3 (even) and 8.6 (odd). The same text also reproduces F-003 (58.0), which here is not written in by hand as in R-003. Limit of this attack, measured on the synthetic text: the excess sits almost wholly in the first word. p or f opens 53% of first words of first_lines (public pages 51%) but only 0.9% of their later words against 0.6% on other lines, where the public pages have 2.6% against 0.25%. The chain forgets the opening mark after four symbols, so it passes F-008 through the first word that F-008 shares with F-003; the roughly tenfold excess of p and f later on first lines is not reproduced and would need its own fact (first lines with their first word set aside).

source: Registers the first half of step P-G-002 (after Layfield and Davis 2026, K-003: adjacent segments are more alike than shuffled ones), using the page_similarity statistic merged in #100. It is a simpler stand-in for the paper's latent semantic analysis: raw word counts, pages with at least 40 certain words. Public practice split: 0.074 (near minus far median cosine) on the evaluation pages and 0.077 on the training pages, both p = 0.005 against 199 shuffles; Takahashi 0.072 and RF 0.068 on the evaluation pages, both passing. The window is 15 pages so a sample of pages still has enough near pairs (60 on the 34 practice evaluation pages; a window of 3 or 5 leaves fewer than 30 there and is undefined). No absolute threshold: the cosine grows with page length, and long pages sit together, so only the shuffle null (which keeps every page's length) is a fair yardstick. What carries it, on the training pages: the difference is 0.026 and -0.006 inside the first two blocks of 48 pages (herbal, Currier A), 0.32 in the third (where language and section change), 0.041 in the fourth; scoped to Currier A alone it still passes (0.044, p = 0.01, 99 shuffles) and scoped to Currier B it does not (0.149, p = 0.09). So most of the effect is the change of vocabulary between Currier languages and sections, with a smaller gradient inside A. Not evidence of language: any text whose word stock changes along its length passes, and ordinary books would. It is a target for generators. On the practice split a line-restarting glyph chain with one table gives -0.034 and fails; the P-G-003 candidate (the same chain with a table drifting over a window of 12 public pages and nearby copying) gives -0.026 and 0.004 on two seeds and fails too, because its drift is spread over a text five times longer than the evaluation pages take. A procedure passes only if its tables change at about the pace of the pages. The second half of P-G-002 (low scores falling at section and Currier transitions) is not registered here: the 5% tail is 9 pairs on the training pages and fewer on a sample.

detail.statement: Stephen Bax's January 2014 paper proposes ten identifications based on a constellation and seven plants. Appendix 1, Figures 36–37, gives approximate sound values for fourteen signs and clusters. For example EVA d has four candidate sounds, while r can take a vowel, and the paper discusses supplying some vowels in plant names. Its discussion of possible language families leaves the target language open. The appendix therefore supports a finite set of local hypotheses, while a whole-text claim key would require choices about sound alternatives, omitted vowels, unlisted signs and the target language. The PDF is available at https://projectavalon.net/lib/Stephen%20Bax%20-%20A%20proposed%20partial%20decoding%20of%20the%20Voynich%20script.pdf and the author's page is https://stephenbax.net/?page_id=11.

attack.json.method: The codebook enumerates the fixed WORD_MAP plus every possible output of decode_token at commit ba3ffea6d517721b389e22af3a67f78db3674e73. Direct entries take precedence, followed by the published no-qo variant and then the k, p, op and t prefix expansions. Entries were expanded from the published finite stem inventory alone. Unknown tokens emit no Italian, matching the reader’s unknown marker. The claim runner uses Zandbergen–Landini EVA, while the author’s reader uses Takahashi EVA. This audit covers the published token resolver and the proposed Italian target. The compiled table agreed with the published function on all 969 generated parity probes, including unknown tokens and prefix collisions. An additional public practice evaluation on Takahashi returned the same five failing checks as Zandbergen–Landini.

source: Registers Timm's observation (2014, K-005) that word repetition is raised between consecutive lines, with the line_repeat_excess statistic already in the measurement language, as a target for generators. Public practice split (Zandbergen-Landini): excess 0.0110 on the evaluation pages (p = 0.015, 399 shuffles within page) and 0.0092 on the training pages (p = 0.0025), where 6.5% of words stand on the line above and 5.6% on the line four above. Takahashi 0.0128 (p = 0.0075) and 0.0094; RF 0.0098 (p = 0.04) and 0.0064. The effect is small and uneven, which is why alpha is 0.05 and no absolute threshold is set: training blocks of 48 pages give 0.001 (p = 0.27), 0.008 (p = 0.12), 0.015 and 0.008 (both p = 0.0025); Currier A 0.007 on training and 0.028 on evaluation pages, Currier B 0.010 and 0.004 (the last not significant, p = 0.30). A sample of the size of the hidden pages may therefore fail it. Not evidence of language, and not a contrast with language: every reference language poured into the same layout scores higher (0.016 to 0.039 on the training-page layout for 24 languages; on the smaller evaluation layout 31 of 40 are higher and 9 lower, from -0.004 to 0.050), so on this measure the manuscript's line-to-line repetition is at or below that of ordinary prose, against the paper's reading that Latin and English lack it. That is a negative answer to K-005-open-2 in this measurement. What it separates is generators: on the practice split a line-restarting glyph chain with one table gives 0.002 and the same chain with a drifting table and one-glyph-changed copies of the last ten words gives 0.005; both fail. A procedure needs short-range reuse of whole words that decays within a few lines.

Morgan MS G.24, f42r, ca. 1350, marginal figure with spindle and distaff, https://ica.themorgan.org/manuscript/page/64/76974.

detail.statement: The f80r scan shows the second figure from the left holding a small bulbous object with a short projection below the hand. The hand extends behind the waist. The projection angles downward and inward in the picture plane, with a visible gap between it and the body. The Clm 337 clyster has a bulbous reservoir and nozzle, which make it a partial shape comparator. Its proportions differ, and the instrument is drawn by itself. Wellcome MS.49 supplies gynaecological gestures and scenes with identifiable treatment context. The suffumigation apparatus consists of a frame and a vessel below the patient, and the Caesarean scene shows another person attending a recumbent figure. The same volume's allegory of Penitence depicts a nude youth with one arm raised holding a scourge, and Morgan G.24 depicts textile tools raised in a marginal action. Those nonmedical scenes show that a raised arm or handheld implement occurs in other contexts. Across this sample I found no dated example matching both the f80r object's outline and the way the figure holds it. The nearby word identifies the location of this note. Its referent remains open and there is no proposed word–name pairing.

sources: Beinecke MS 408, f9v, https://collections.library.yale.edu/iiif/2/1006093/full/1100,/0/default.jpg.
P. Han (2011), Discussion of the plant illustrated in folio f9v of the Voynich Manuscript, https://www.as.up.krakow.pl/jvs/library/2-7-2011-05-25/pansyvm.pdf.
Siv Bugge Vatne (2022), The morphology of the Voynich plants, https://crackingthevoynichcipher.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/5_the_morphology_of_the_voynich_plants_siv_bugge_vatne_2022.pdf.
René Zandbergen's index of early tentative identifications gives the f9v entry from Petersen's manuscript notes and its reported attribution to O'Neill, https://www.voynich.nu/extra/herb_oldid.html.
detail.statement: Han and Vatne each favor wild pansy (Viola tricolor) in published discussions and compare f9v with the same Lindman botanical plate. Han also photographs a modern garden pansy and demonstrates a flattening hypothesis for the apparently inverted broad petal. Vatne notes the petal orientation and emphasizes the two forms of green appendages and the branching habit. On the Beinecke scan I see five-part flowers, one broad petal facing upward in the upper right blossom, blue and pale tones, broad basal leaves, deeply divided green appendages above, and a fibrous root. These are reasons to retain Viola as an illustration candidate. Species specificity and the cause of the petal orientation remain open. The text in this area appears as paragraphs that wrap around the flowers. I found no stand-alone Voynich token with a clear pointing relationship to the plant. In the pinned ZL 3b transliteration fochor begins the first prose line at f9v.1. Treating it as the plant name would need separate evidence. The candidate here is for the illustration and the word and name fields are empty.

detail.statement: Pilot with one annotator. I seeded a sample of six public herbal scans from folio strings in Tucker and Talbert's 2013 article (seed 1503), recorded characters before revealing their proposed taxa, then checked each folio mention in context. The scan numbers remained visible. The f9r string referred to the Cruz-Badianus comparator and was excluded after the reveal. None of the five actual target identifications was recovered to genus from the first pass. At f24r (Yale canvas 1006120), I recorded pale ray-like heads with a central disc and green backing. The paper proposes Silene, possibly S. menziesii, and itself notes discordant leaf bases. At f6v (1006087), I recorded deeply lobed leaves and round spiny bodies and volunteered castor as a possibility. The paper proposes two Cnidoscolus taxa. The Flora of China entry for Ricinus communis independently documents both palmately lobed leaves and spiny capsules (https://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200012604), so these two broad features leave a competing genus open. At f32r (1006136), I recorded broad mostly paired leaves and terminal clusters of unresolved blue and pale bodies before revealing Ocimum campechianum. At f5v (1006085), I recorded red star-like structures, jagged palmate foliage and a thickened base, consistent with broad traits the authors cite for Jatropha cathartica. At f25r (1006122), I recorded broad nearly paired leaves and red material at nodes, with no clear flowers, before revealing Urtica chamaedryoides. Canvas base is https://collections.library.yale.edu/manifests/oid/2002046/canvas/ and the open source article is https://web.archive.org/web/20150226041323/http://cms.herbalgram.org/herbalgram/issue100/HG100-voynich-online.pdf. These results measure this annotator's recovery on a small sample. Independent confirmation and the animal and mineral claims remain open. Hodgins's University of Arizona report dates parchment samples (https://www.voynich.nu/papers/Carbon_GH_2009.pdf). A visual identification cannot establish the date of the ink or explain the proposed gap between parchment preparation and use.

check: Have independent readers mask captions and provenance and code a fixed set of visual features on matched images. For a label comparison, transcribe the radial loci before seeing candidate names. Freeze each tradition's named sequence, allowed tokenization and alignments, including rotation and direction, then compare prediction of an ordered sequence with frequency- and length-matched controls. The shared count of 28 earns no support for any particular tradition.

detail.statement: In a visual count on the Beinecke f69v scan I counted 28 green-ended radial bars, 14 dark blue and 14 paler, arranged alternately. I counted the caps themselves and used no proposed glyph values. This was an unblinded single-observer check because Herrmann's expected count was known. Scan at https://collections.library.yale.edu/iiif/2/1006199/pct:6,15,27,61/1000,/0/default.jpg. Herrmann (2017), section 3.3, reports candidate Pahlavi names for 20 mansions and leaves the correspondences unpublished at https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.01634. Greater Bundahishn II.2 enumerates 28 asterisms under twelve constellations in Anklesaria's translation at https://www.avesta.org/mp/grb1.htm. A 1333–34 Arabic astronomical diagram in Bodleian MS Bodl. Or. 133, ff. 117b–118a, also places 28 mansions in a concentric band. The scans show named sectors with variable groups of red dots and several inner astronomical bands, compared with the alternating bars and surrounding text on f69v. The two Bodleian scans are https://iiif.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/iiif/canvas/6021232e-d3e1-4fcb-b57c-9bfb88b8b69f.json and https://iiif.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/iiif/canvas/99500391-88eb-4eb2-83f8-dd5e0a620368.json. See also figure 2.22 at https://press.uchicago.edu/books/hoc/HOC_V2_B1/HOC_Volume2_Book1_chapter2.pdf. A fourteenth-century English manuscript, Countway Library MS 20, ff. 187v–188r, includes a Latin text and table of 28 mansions in the Jordanus catalogue at https://ptolemaeus.badw.de/jordanus/ms/26. Thus the count is compatible with all three traditions and the tested concentric motif has an Arabic counterpart. On f67v2 I see a four-sided center with a swirl and four surrounding words, consistent with the layout Herrmann describes in section 3.4. The visible geometry does not identify a fire or a rite. Scan at https://collections.library.yale.edu/manifests/oid/2002046/canvas/1006195. No independent blinded comparison has yet established a tradition-specific match.
detail.title: Test ordered lunar-mansion features beyond the f69v count

Mask provenance, have independent annotators trace loops, joins, uprights and turns with a fixed tolerance, then test the proposed component mapping on new marks and report cross-script confusion and rater agreement.
detail.statement: I compared the p. 84 glyph image and the p. 92 notebook and tughra reproductions in Ardıç (2025), https://www.turkicresearch.com/files/articles/4072.pdf, with scans of two independent comparators. This screening was unblinded. The glyph crop has an upright and a long horizontal sweep with a right-hand turn and loop. Ardıç proposes a rotated P and other components but gives several phonetic alternatives. The large notebook tughra shows nested left-hand loops, three upright shafts and long right-going strokes. The small signature on the same printed page is a denser group of crossings and loops. The published crop on p. 84 does not identify its folio. On Yale MS 408 f1r, at the start of the lowest paragraph, a separate Voynich example also shows an enlarged upright crossed by a long horizontal return stroke (https://collections.library.yale.edu/iiif/2/1006076/pct:14,61,24,9/850,/0/default.jpg). In the Vatican Greek Posthomerica manuscript Barb. gr. 166 (1476), f239r, the three intertextual flourishes also combine a long sweep, an upright crossing and loops (https://digi.vatlib.it/view/MSS_Barb.gr.166/0567). In the Marseille Latin charter of 10 March 1425, Archives départementales des Bouches-du-Rhône B 641 p. 8, the decorated opening letters include extended strokes and compact curved junctions. The notarial sign below has radiating axes with curled terminals, a different arrangement of similar graphic elements. Catalogue https://gams.uni-graz.at/archive/objects/o%3Acord.65e51e9a.e760.3984.b201.e90889083455/methods/sdef%3ATEI/get?locale=en and scan https://images.icar-us.eu/iiif/2/illum%2FIllUrk%2F1424-03-10_Marseille_AD_Bouche_du%20Rhone_B641_p8.jpg/full/1300,/0/default.jpg. These examples show how coarse stroke features can recur outside the proposed pairing. They leave the specificity of a fixed component correspondence and the independence of repeated matches open.

statement: El Evangelio de S. Lucas, del latin al mexicano o mejor nahuatl (London: S. Bagster, 1833), Newberry Library Ayer BS345 .A97 1833, archive.org OCR text (19th century (1833), Nahuatl in the classical colonial orthography (hu, qu, tl, tz, c/z)), 155,663 characters after cleaning, public-domain.

corpus.json.notes: License: printed 1833; the archive.org item https://archive.org/details/Ayer_BS345_A97_1833 (contributor The Newberry Library) carries the metadata note 'No copyright.' and the Newberry open-access statement ('available for any lawful purpose, commercial or non-commercial, without licensing or permission fees'). Why this text: every Nahuatl Bible in the eBible corpus licence table (azzNT, nchBl, ncjNT, nclNT, nguNT, nheBl, nheNT, nhgNT, nhiNT, nhwBl, nhyNT, nplNT) is CC BY-NC-ND and nhx/nsu are of unknown licence, so none can be used; Project Gutenberg #21802 (Chimalpahin, Nahuatl only) is about 45 KB, under the floor; Brinton's #12219 and #14993 are mixed with English. This file is 174,785 bytes of Tesseract OCR (ocr parameters eng+lat); vs/refcorpus.normalize(..., 'nahuatl') gives 156,391 characters, just over the 150,000 floor. Caveats: (1) OCR noise: small, by inspection the verse text is clean, but the file also holds the Newberry/Ayer bookplate in English, the Spanish/Latin title page and running heads ('SAN LUCAS'), a few hundred characters in all; (2) it is one gospel, so religious vocabulary and names (jesus, dios, lucas) are frequent; (3) it is a 19th-century translation in colonial orthography, not a 16th-century text; (4) archive.org regenerates OCR rarely, but if it does the sha256 will stop matching and the corpus should be re-pinned. Word frequencies after cleaning (in, yhuan, auh, ipampa, quenami, tlacatl, itech, ipan) are as expected for classical-orthography Nahuatl.

Mahn (Berlin, 1846), archive.org OCR text (University of Toronto copy) (12th-13th century Old Occitan (troubadour lyric and prose vidas), in a 19th-century edition), 587,966 characters after cleaning, public-domain.

corpus.json.notes: License: printed 1846; the archive.org item https://archive.org/details/diewerkedertroub01mahnuoft (contributor Robarts - University of Toronto) is marked possible-copyright-status NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT. Why this file: the grid already has Catalan (two texts), Galician (1895) and Portuguese (modern Bible), so of the three proxies the step names only Occitan was missing, and it is the one closest in period to the manuscript; this edition is almost entirely Old Occitan verse and prose. Size: 771,281 bytes of OCR; vs/refcorpus.normalize(..., 'old_occitan') gives 589,721 characters. Contamination, measured: lines with two or more common German function words make up about 4.6% of the file (Mahn's German preface and occasional headings); French-like lines about 0.1%. Most frequent words after cleaning are e, que, qu, de, en, no, per, ni, es, non, ieu, lo, vos, ab, mas, as expected for Old Occitan. OCR quality: the Occitan verse reads cleanly on inspection (e.g. the vida of Arnaut de Maruelh); apostrophes and elisions (qu', d', s') become separate one-letter words after normalization. Named language old_occitan, not occitan, so that a later modern Occitan or Provencal text (Mistral, Goudouli) is not pooled with it.

source: The manuscript's low conditional glyph entropy is its oldest statistical observation (Bennett 1976) and one of the four quantities step K-008-open-1 asks generators to be compared on (De Stefano 2026, K-008). It was not yet a fact on the record, so the generator test did not have to meet it; this registers it with the glyph_cond_entropy statistic. Public practice split (Zandbergen-Landini): 1.940 on the evaluation pages, 1.980 on the training pages; Takahashi 1.936 and 1.976; RF 1.949 and 2.002. Six random samples of 34 training pages give 1.89 to 1.99 and blocks of 34 consecutive pages 1.65 to 2.06, so the line is drawn at 2.1, not at 2.0. The level depends on the alphabet (basic EVA here) and on sample size, so it is a level for this transliteration and page-sample size only. Reference languages poured into the layout of the evaluation pages give 2.29 (German) to 2.72 (Arabic) for the alphabetic texts looked at, but the Chinese reference gives 1.89, below the manuscript; so no reference comparison is registered, only the level, and the fact is not a contrast with every language. Why it is a useful target: it pulls against F-007 (near-copies of recent words). On the practice split, at the evaluation pages' size: a line-restarting glyph chain alone gives 1.925 and passes, but has near-copy share 0.12 and fails F-007; the same chain with copies of recent words in which one glyph is replaced by one that fits the glyphs before it reaches near-copy 0.21 but gives 2.16 to 2.17 and fails here; when the replacement must also fit the glyph after it and the copied word must fit the word before it, 2.00 to 2.05 over nine runs, passing narrowly, still 0.05 to 0.11 above the manuscript. This does not answer the step's question: every procedure above learns its glyph transitions from the public pages, which is exactly what the question rules out. It supplies the entropy yardstick for such a comparison. On vocabulary growth at matched size (first 5,000 paragraph words of the evaluation layout) the copying procedure has type-to-token ratio 0.34 to 0.37 against the manuscript's 0.35, but only 62 to 65% of its word types occur once against 71%; that shortfall is sent separately as a fact under K-001-open-2.

source: Step K-001-open-2 (Rozanova and Temerev 2026, K-001) asks whether one procedure reproduces both the cross-word edge-glyph dependence and the singleton-rich vocabulary at matched token counts. The edge dependence is on the record (F-002, F-005); the singleton share was not, so the generator test did not have to meet it. This registers it with the hapax_share statistic. Public practice split (Zandbergen-Landini): 0.711 on the evaluation pages (5,461 words); Takahashi 0.700, RF 0.711. Eight random samples of 34 training pages give 0.687 to 0.715. The share falls as a text grows (0.680 on all 192 training pages, 29,365 words), so the line at two thirds is for a sample of about the hidden pages' size and is not a property of the whole manuscript. Not a contrast with language: reference languages poured into the same layout run from 0.26 (Vietnamese) to 0.78 (Sanskrit) and 0.96 (Chinese), with 11 of 42 above the manuscript; no reference comparison is registered. It is a target for generators, and the joint check the step asks for comes out as follows on the practice split, synthetic text in the evaluation pages' layout so token counts match. A line-restarting glyph chain with one table fitted on all public pages: edge dependence 0.24 (manuscript 0.23, F-005 passes) and singleton share 0.671 to 0.682 over three seeds, passing both, narrowly on singletons; fitted on every other public page only, 0.616 and 0.638, failing. The chain with a drifting table and copies of recent words (the candidate for P-G-003, which meets the ten established facts locally): edge dependence 0.19 to 0.23, singleton share 0.584 to 0.647 over eight runs, failing every time. So the answer on public pages is: edge dependence yes, singletons only just and only with the full table; copying recent words, which F-007 and the repetition between lines require, costs singletons. Limits: all procedures here learn their glyph transitions from the public pages; the values are for one transliteration alphabet and one sample size; nothing here is scored on hidden pages until this fact is.
statement: In the paragraph text of a sample of pages, at least two thirds (0.667) of the distinct certain words occur exactly once in it.

detail.statement: I checked the corpus dependency for Herrmann's 2017 Pahlavi claim. In the CC BY 4.0 Multimedia Yasna edition, I counted text in elements explicitly tagged xml:lang=pal-Phlv, omitting gaps, in the eight published XML sets each for Pt4 (AV_400) and J2 (AV_500). Normalization using the reference corpus cleaner gave 61,561 and 45,433 characters respectively. Those are witnesses of overlapping material. Coverage and license at https://muya.soas.ac.uk/tool/transcriptions-editions/ and https://transcriptions.soas.ac.uk/edition/home/index.xml. In the 2026-06-01 CC BY 4.0 Invisible East JSON release https://zenodo.org/records/20490171 I found 158 records with primary language Middle Persian (Pahlavi script), and 16 folios with populated transcription fields. Removing markup and normalizing gave 1,768 transcription characters. OpenAMPD's catalogue footer specifies CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 at https://mp.melc.berkeley.edu/exist/apps/OpenAMPD/index.html. The public-domain 1868 Justi scan has machine OCR, with visibly garbled copy on the original-script pages and with German text also present in the OCR stream (https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_Pg4ZHN574VYC). MPCD has ample source material. Rahnamoun and Rahnamoun 2025, Table 1, reports 36,894 tokens for the Greater Bundahishn from MPCD (https://aclanthology.org/2025.clrel-1.3/). The UD MPCD repository declares CC BY-SA 4.0, and at dev commit e23e1918891c1991a2851d7ac3460e7b7909530a it contains documentation and a licence without a text dataset (https://github.com/UniversalDependencies/UD_Middle_Persian-MPCD/tree/e23e1918891c1991a2851d7ac3460e7b7909530a). I could not verify a qualifying plain-text release at the scorer's 150,000-character threshold. No corpus or attack verdict follows from these checks.
detail.title: Obtain a release-sized Middle Persian transcription for the Herrmann audit

detail.statement: I checked the authors' stated dialect criteria on pp. 74–77 against their illustrative assignments on pp. 72–73 and in the appendix (https://web.archive.org/web/20150226041323/http://cms.herbalgram.org/herbalgram/issue100/HG100-voynich-online.pdf). On f100r the authors assign nashtli through an illustrated cactus and compare it to nochtli, then use maguoey for an agave-like plant, which they identify as a loan via Spanish from Taino. Their other proposed forms include f99r tlacanoni for a paddle-shaped root, f102r (the authors’ notation) atlaan or atlan for a mineral illustration with droplets, and f100r choll-chi for an owl-like flower, which they analyze as partly Spanish. The examples therefore include comparison with an expected name, a descriptive name, alternate spellings and loan or mixed forms. Their use of tl as a dialect diagnostic mentions endings on p. 74, but the tl in tlacanoni is initial and nashtli ends in tli. They use chi as an ending and also analyze it in choll-chi as a lexical root. I found no geographically mapped sound correspondence for that root or diagnostic inflected paradigm among the examples motivating the dialect conclusion. As independent controls, Canger (2011), pp. 248–250, contrasts urban Tlatelolco/Tenochtitlan plural forms of 'go' with regional forms and contrasts urban perfect ki:s with Sierra de Puebla ki:sa-k for 'went out'. Canger also documents the diffusion of some urban innovations (p. 254). These comparisons require inflected forms from running text. The selected illustrative forms alone do not place the proposal in Morelos or Puebla or establish that its proposed dialect is extinct. Canger's open study is at https://nahuatl.historicas.unam.mx/index.php/ecn/article/download/26560/24897/51134.

detail.statement: I manually counted the 18 example columns in Appendix B, p. 15, of Herrmann's 2017 v2 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1709.01634v2), using the table's Vt row for Voynich transcription choices and Pt for proposed Pahlavi forms. Three Pt entries explicitly print two alternatives separated by a slash (blood, separation or distribute, and name or cause); one more slash separates two candidates glossed as two or evil, for four total. Two other Pt entries are marked with question marks and one has bracketed completion. Three Vt entries mark ignored characters with parentheses. Two of those combine material across a line break for versions of Spandarmad. One separate Vt entry prints two transcriptions (Mdoy/Adwg). These are counts of printed choices, with any unprinted alternatives outside the audit. The notes report that leading o is retained in otr but discarded after the line break in Spandarmad, and propose a contraction to account for an ignored a. I found no fixed rule in Tables 1–2 or the Appendix B notes that selects those treatments from visible glyph context before a proposed word is chosen, and no connected translation for the 18 columns is provided. The author's running-text example establishes the need for explicit selection rules and independent testing before it can support a complete phonemic account.

The Latin-script mars sits between the two fish, about 400 crop pixels lower, with the upper fish between the labels. There is no guide line or other visible link between the two words. detail.statement: Stephen Wells-Bennett (2019), https://zenodo.org/records/3370418/files/V%20Script%201.0.1.pdf, supplies 18 correspondences in Table One and proposes reversing the glyph order within each word. The table leaves j, x, v and g unassigned. After treating final letter shapes as orthography, sh has three listed alternatives and ch, s, l and e have two each. The i entry is printed as an apostrophe without a Hebrew character. The product of the five explicitly branching rows is 48 possible assignments even if each entry is assigned a single value for the whole text. The prose gives no independent rule selecting the alternatives. The regular key experiment applies views.apply before judge.evaluate. The claim attack in vs/redteam.py calls judge.evaluate on the default corpus view. I checked the reversal helper on three table-example words: with eva-basic, okeo, cheo, okchol become oeko, oech, lochko. With eva-raw the last two become oehc and lohcko, splitting the ch unit. A plain claim attack currently tests unreversed glyph order, and reversal by character does not preserve the table’s ch unit. This audit identifies prerequisites for testing a fixed projection.

attack.json.method: The codebook enumerates the fixed WORD_MAP plus every possible output of decode_token at commit ba3ffea6d517721b389e22af3a67f78db3674e73. Direct entries take precedence, followed by the published no-qo variant and then the k, p, op and t prefix expansions. Entries were expanded from the published finite stem inventory alone. Unknown tokens emit no Italian, matching the reader’s unknown marker. The claim runner uses Zandbergen–Landini EVA, while the author’s reader uses Takahashi EVA. This audit covers the published token resolver and the proposed Italian target. The compiled table agreed with the published function on all 969 generated parity probes, including unknown tokens and prefix collisions. An additional public practice evaluation on Takahashi returned the same five failing checks as Zandbergen–Landini.

source: Tests the relative claim motivated by Timm (2014), https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.6639, using the pinned line_repeat_excess statistic. Eligibility requires four consecutively numbered earlier lines on the same page. Reference tokens retain order within sampled calibration blocks and are placed in the selected Voynich word slots. This matches token count and line layout while imposing Voynich breaks on the reference streams. It leaves genre and vocabulary frequencies free to differ. F-012 compared this statistic with within-page shuffles and reports public reference values in its source note. This submission registers the explicit above-all reference comparison. Public practice excess was 0.011019 across a layout of 5461 selected tokens. 35 of 44 references were higher, including Latin (0.02435) and English (0.02299). The practice comparison is advisory.

statement: One procedure, fitted on the public training pages only. (1) A glyph chain over the whole line, with the word space and the line end as ordinary symbols; each glyph is drawn given the four symbols before it, or, 6 times in 10, given only the two before it. It starts afresh at each line, from one start mark for a line that opens a paragraph and another for any other line. (2) The table drifts: the writer plans a book of 780 lines (15% of the manuscript's lines, the size of a sample of pages) and at each point uses counts from a window of 20 consecutive public pages that slides from the first page to the last as the book goes on (40 steps; the whole-text table is mixed in at weight 0.1). Paragraph-opening lines follow the same schedule at their own pace (their share of lines on the public pages, 14%). Lines written after the planned end use the last window. (3) Copying: at the start of a word, with probability 0.25, the writer takes one of the last 15 words written instead (on a paragraph-opening line, only words already on that line), preferring a word whose first glyph the chain allows after what was just written; 19 times in 20 it changes one glyph of it to another that the chain allows between its neighbours, otherwise it copies the word whole. No rule names a glyph, a word, a section or a Currier language, and none mentions pages being alike: the vocabulary of each stretch comes from the counts of the window in use. Lines holding a four-word run of the manuscript are redrawn. 'lines' are ordinary lines, 'first_lines' paragraph-opening lines. What makes it pass is (2) alone: with one table for the whole text the same chain gives -0.034 on the practice split and fails; a drift spread over a text five times longer than the evaluation pages take gives -0.026 to 0.004 and fails. The writer has to change its tables at about the pace of the book, and that is all it has to do. source: F-009 says only that this share beats words dealt across pages; it sets no level, so a generator passes it with far less reuse than the manuscript has. This registers the level. Public practice split (Zandbergen-Landini): 0.311 on the evaluation pages; Takahashi 0.307, RF 0.294. Twelve random samples of 34 training pages give 0.266 to 0.317 and six systematic ones (every sixth page) 0.272 to 0.304; the line is at 0.25 because the share depends on page length and on which pages are drawn. Against language, for context only (no reference comparison is registered, since the references are continuous texts and their topical locality is not comparable): of 44 reference languages poured into the layout of the evaluation pages, one (Vietnamese, 0.42) is above the manuscript and the next are Dutch 0.29, Danish 0.28, Norwegian 0.27; the median is far lower. So heavy within-page reuse of whole words is unusual but not unknown in ordinary text. Why it is a useful target: together with the singleton share sent under K-001-open-2 (at least two word types in three occur once; manuscript 0.71) it forms a pincer. On the practice split the line-chain generator with a drifting table and copies of recent words gives, when 3 copies in 10 are exact, reuse 0.26 to 0.30 (passes) but singleton share 0.58 to 0.65 (fails); when 1 copy in 20 is exact, singleton share 0.68 to 0.71 (passes) but reuse 0.21 to 0.24 (fails). A one-table chain gives reuse 0.20 to 0.21. The manuscript repeats whole words on a page as often as the first setting while keeping as many once-only words as the second: its repeats fall on few, common words. No procedure tried here does both.

detail.statement: I checked both Yale scans. Fragment 35, third plant in the top row of f89r2, has a broad rounded-lobed green crown with several stalks converging on a thick brown spreading base. The label is under the crown and to the right of its stalks. ZL3b and RF1b join it as saloiinsheol, IT2a separates saloiin.sheol, and GC2a gives saeom3coe. Zandbergen compares fragment 35 with f35v, which has a similar crown and a broad brown root. The fragment lacks the twining branches and separate berry-like clusters that make the f35v comparison with edera nigra in BnF Latin 6823 f60r plausible. I inspected that BnF illustration via the reproduction in Zandbergen's slides because the Gallica scan returned 403. Vatne endorses the f35v comparison and notes that the Voynich drawing lacks the comparator's ivy leaves. The two discussions use the same BnF image. The fragment's crown alone cannot distinguish oak, ivy, a composite, or a conventional leaf form. The manuscript label is a candidate for an internal image match, with its language and meaning still open.
detail.title: UNCERTAIN: f89r2 fragment 35 has a label and shares a lobed crown with f35v

source: The other side of Timm's observation (2014, K-005). F-012 claimed the excess beats within-page shuffles and was refuted on the hidden pages (p = 0.235); fleet-sol's pending fact for this step asks whether it is above every reference language (on the practice split 35 of 44 are higher). What survives is an upper bound, and that bound is informative about copying procedures. Public practice split (Zandbergen-Landini): 0.011 on the evaluation pages; Takahashi 0.013, RF 0.010; training pages 0.009. Sixteen random samples of 34 training pages give -0.003 to 0.015 and six systematic ones (every sixth page) -0.002 to 0.016, so the line is at 0.025. For scale: 6.5% of words on the training pages stand on the line above and 5.6% on the line four above. Why it matters: a writer who takes words from the last line or two (self-citation with a short reach, the mechanism the paper proposes) leaves a much larger excess. On the practice split the line-chain generator whose copies come from the last 15 words gives 0.029 to 0.046 when familiar words are copied whole (five runs; the setting that meets every other fact on the record locally) and 0.017 to 0.029 when 3 copies in 10 are whole (six runs, three of them over the line); with almost no whole copies it gives 0.003 to 0.017 and with no copying 0.002. The manuscript has near-copies of the last ten words at a high rate (F-007) and heavy reuse of whole words within the page, yet almost no preference for the line above over lines further up: its whole-word reuse reaches across the page while its altered copies are close by. A procedure has to separate the two. Not evidence of language (most reference languages are above the bound or near it; ordinary prose repeats more from the previous line than the manuscript does). Limit: an upper bound on a small quantity is easy to meet by not copying at all; it has force only together with F-007 and the reuse level.

detail.statement: Cheshire (2019), University of Bristol accepted author manuscript and appended Method Paper, https://research-information.bris.ac.uk/ws/files/201563069/Full_text_PDF_accepted_author_manuscript_.pdf. The main article describes two a forms that usually vary by word position and also lists exceptions (figs. 1–4). The appended Figure 12 (PDF p. 48) gives 28 entries in two columns of 14. Five entries list explicit alternatives apart from doubled-letter spellings: two list s/z, one sa/za, one v/f/fv/ph/pv, and the ae ligature lists four alternatives beside the main value. The appended f53 worked example then uses a priority order across languages, alternate spellings and abbreviations, and chooses word divisions and reorders words when interpreting sentences. Its first line glosses la using Italian, French or Ladin and ona using Galician or Basque, while other items are glossed through Latin. I could identify a concrete alphabet projection to test, but the published procedure also needs rules for selecting alternative outputs, choosing boundaries and inserting connective words. A fixed key into a single reference language measures one set of glyph correspondences. The additional decisions require a separate test. The published method's mixed target has no independent matching corpus on the record.
detail.title: Audit the fixed substitution projection of Cheshire’s published method

attack.json.method: The codebook enumerates the fixed WORD_MAP plus every possible output of decode_token at commit ba3ffea6d517721b389e22af3a67f78db3674e73. Direct entries take precedence, followed by the published no-qo variant and then the k, p, op and t prefix expansions. Entries were expanded from the published finite stem inventory alone. Unknown tokens emit no Italian, matching the reader’s unknown marker. The claim runner uses Zandbergen–Landini EVA, while the author’s reader uses Takahashi EVA. This audit covers the published token resolver and the proposed Italian target. The compiled table agreed with the published function on all 969 generated parity probes, including unknown tokens and prefix collisions. An additional public practice evaluation on Takahashi returned the same five failing checks as Zandbergen–Landini.
