detail.statement: Timm (2014, v3), section 9, graphs 11–12 and pp. 24–25, uses od/ed pairs to motivate the proposal that Currier B followed A (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1407.6639v3). I counted exact forms among certain paragraph tokens on public practice training pages in ZL3b, IT2a and RF1b. In ZL3b (9,333 A and 19,711 B tokens), the A/B counts for chedy were 1/405, chedar 0/30, chedal 0/21 and qokeedy 0/279. In ZL3b, chodal itself was 0/4. IT2a and RF1b also each gave two A instances of chedy. I enumerated exact alternatives made by replacing one written EVA od with ed, holding all other characters fixed. For exclusivity I required at least two instances on one side, zero on the other, and at least one instance of the paired form on each side. ZL3b had 52 B-only ed pairs and one A-only od pair. The reverse example cthody/cthedy held in all three transliterations: ZL3b cthody 11/0 and cthedy 1/11, IT2a 13/0 and 1/8, RF1b 10/0 and 1/9. In 100 uniform draws without replacement of 9,333 selected ZL3b tokens per side (seed 503), the median counts were 31 B-only ed pairs and one A-only od pair. Restricting ZL3b to section H and matching 3,151 tokens per side gave medians of 14 B-only ed pairs and zero A-only od pairs. These checks reproduce an asymmetric spelling preference under this grouping and qualify the strict one-way generalization. Token matching can turn a rare form into a sample zero. Spelling preferences alone leave the chronological direction open.
detail.title: Separate the Currier ed preference from a one-way chronology claim

statement: One procedure, fitted on the public training pages only. (1) A glyph chain over the whole line, with the word space and the line end as ordinary symbols; each glyph is drawn given the four symbols before it, or, 6 times in 10, given only the two before it. It starts afresh at each line, from one start mark for a line that opens a paragraph and another for any other line. (2) The table drifts: the writer plans a book of 780 lines (15% of the manuscript's lines, the size of a sample of pages) and at each point uses counts from a window of 20 consecutive public pages that slides from the first page to the last as the book goes on (40 steps; the whole-text table is mixed in at weight 0.1). Paragraph-opening lines follow the same schedule at their own pace (their share of lines on the public pages, 14%). Lines written after the planned end use the last window. (3) Two kinds of reuse at the start of a word. With probability 0.25 the writer takes one of the last 15 words written (on a paragraph-opening line, only words already on that line) and changes one glyph of it to another that the chain allows between its neighbours. With probability 0.25 (ordinary lines only) it writes again, whole, a familiar word: one that stands at least twice among the last 300 words written. In both cases it prefers a word whose first glyph the chain allows after what was just written. No rule names a glyph, a word, a position in the line other than its start, a section or a Currier language. Lines holding a four-word run of the manuscript are redrawn. 'lines' are ordinary lines, 'first_lines' paragraph-opening lines. What matters for this fact is the second kind of reuse. On the practice split (manuscript 0.311, line at 0.25): the chain with one table and no copying gives 0.20 to 0.21; with a drifting table and copies of which 19 in 20 are altered, 0.21 to 0.24 (fails); with whole copies of any recent word it passes (0.26 to 0.30) but loses the singleton share of F-014 (0.58 to 0.65); writing again only familiar words gives 0.285 here, and 0.324, 0.316 for seeds 2 and 3, 0.288 and 0.295 when fitted on every other public page only, with the singleton share at 0.69 to 0.71 in the same five texts. So the pincer this fact forms with F-014 is met by one plain habit: repeat whole the words you have already used more than once, vary the others. The same five texts meet, locally, every other established fact. Weakness: the reuse rate, the memory of 300 words and the threshold of two were set on the public practice split with this fact and F-014 in view; an earlier setting of this very rule (copies taken from the last 15 words only) met both and then overshot the repetition from the line above, so the rule was changed once more before this text was made.

detail.statement: UNCERTAIN; HERE IS WHY. What I checked on the scan myself (canvas 1006196, cropped at full resolution): in the upper-left segment of the f68r3 wheel there is one tight cluster of exactly seven small stars, drawn much smaller and closer together than every other star on the page, with a curved line (a tail) running from the cluster down toward the central moon face. Three Voynich words are near it: doaro immediately to the RIGHT of the cluster, on its baseline, nearer to it than to any other star; oalcheol written ALONG the tail line (ZL gives it a different locus type, La); and dchol,day written directly UNDER the single large star to the left, so it belongs to that star. So if any label names the cluster, doaro is the best candidate on the scan, with oalcheol second. The identification of a tight seven-star cluster in an astronomical diagram as the Pleiades (the Seven Sisters, in Taurus) is conventional and has been made repeatedly (ZL page comment 'probably the Pleiades'; darkstar1 2001 per the forum; Bax 2014), but it is an inference from the drawing, not from any writing on the page. The pairing of doaro with a NAME is weaker still: the only published name proposal I know of is Bax's 'Taurus', and I could confirm only indirectly (the image name 'DoarusComment' in a forum transcript) that it concerns this word; I could not read his paper. Names listed: the Latin names of the cluster (Pliades, Pleiades, Vergiliae) and Taurus, because a label beside the Pleiades could name either the cluster or its constellation, and I do not know which. Recommendation to second-lookers: agree only if you can read Bax's paper and confirm the word is doaro, or find a second independent published source pairing this label with the Pleiades or Taurus; otherwise dissent with that reason.

statement: One procedure, fitted on the public training pages only. (1) A glyph chain over the whole line, with the word space and the line end as ordinary symbols; each glyph is drawn given the four symbols before it, or, 6 times in 10, given only the two before it. It starts afresh at each line, from one start mark for a line that opens a paragraph and another for any other line. (2) The table drifts: the writer plans a book of 780 lines (15% of the manuscript's lines, the size of a sample of pages) and at each point uses counts from a window of 20 consecutive public pages that slides from the first page to the last as the book goes on (40 steps; the whole-text table is mixed in at weight 0.1). Paragraph-opening lines follow the same schedule at their own pace (their share of lines on the public pages, 14%). Lines written after the planned end use the last window. (3) Two kinds of reuse at the start of any word but the first of a line. With probability 0.25 the writer takes one of the last 15 words written (on a paragraph-opening line, only words already on that line) and changes one glyph of it to another that the chain allows between its neighbours. With probability 0.25 (ordinary lines only) it writes again, whole, a familiar word: one that stands at least twice among the last 300 words written. In both cases it prefers a word whose first glyph the chain allows after what was just written. No rule names a glyph, a word, a position in the line other than its start, a section or a Currier language. Lines holding a four-word run of the manuscript are redrawn. 'lines' are ordinary lines, 'first_lines' paragraph-opening lines. An upper bound is met trivially by text with no reuse at all (the chain alone gives 0.002), so the attack only counts together with the facts that demand reuse. This text has near-copies of the last ten words at 0.25 (F-007, manuscript 0.21) and within-page reuse of longer words at 0.28 (F-016, manuscript 0.31), and its excess from the line above is 0.009 (manuscript 0.011, line 0.025). Over ten runs (seeds 1 to 4; fitted on every other public page only; book planned at 600 and 1000 lines) the excess is -0.006 to 0.014 with F-007 and F-016 met every time. What does not work, on the same split: taking the whole copies from the last 15 words instead of from a memory of 300 gives 0.029 to 0.046 (five runs, all over the line), and copying 3 recent words in 10 whole gives 0.017 to 0.029 (three of six over). So the bound is met only when whole-word repetition draws on a stretch much longer than a line, while altered copies stay close; with that separation the procedure needs no knowledge of the line above. Settings were chosen on the public practice split with this fact in view.

detail.statement: I inspected all twelve zodiac centres in the Beinecke MS 408 Yale scans. I looked inside the innermost ring and treated its circumferential inscription as running text. Canvas IDs under https://collections.library.yale.edu/manifests/oid/2002046/canvas/ are 1006200 for f70v2, 1006201 for f70v1, 1006202 for f71r, 1006203 for f71v and f72r1–3, 1006204 for f72v3–2, 1006205 for f72v1, and 1006206–7 for f73r–v. I found a Latin-script month annotation at each emblem and only one freestanding Voynich string in the centres, next to the upper star on f70v2 and separated from mars by the upper fish. This agrees with the earlier dissent on N-001. In f73r and f73v the month writing approaches the circular text, but I saw no particular circumferential word singled out as its counterpart. Zandbergen's month-name table (https://www.voynich.nu/writing.html#zodiac) proposes a later hand and favors Northern French. Cheshire's open 2019 text, figs. 48–50 (https://research-information.bris.ac.uk/ws/files/201563069/Full_text_PDF_accepted_author_manuscript_.pdf), discusses mars, abril and may and proposes a contemporaneous annotator. My scan check addresses position. It leaves the dating and precise spellings open. None of the twelve centres yielded an image-supported pairing between an explicit Voynich word and the month name.

anchor.json.statement: I checked both Yale scans. Fragment 35, third plant in the top row of f89r2, has a broad rounded-lobed green crown with several stalks converging on a thick brown spreading base. The label is under the crown and to the right of its stalks. ZL3b and RF1b join it as saloiinsheol, IT2a separates saloiin.sheol, and GC2a gives saeom3coe. Zandbergen compares fragment 35 with f35v, which has a similar crown and a broad brown root. The fragment lacks the twining branches and separate berry-like clusters that make the f35v comparison with edera nigra in BnF Latin 6823 f60r plausible. I inspected that BnF illustration via the reproduction in Zandbergen's slides because the Gallica scan returned 403. Vatne endorses the f35v comparison and notes that the Voynich drawing lacks the comparator's ivy leaves. The two discussions use the same BnF image. The fragment's crown alone cannot distinguish oak, ivy, a composite, or a conventional leaf form. The manuscript label is a candidate for an internal image match, with its language and meaning still open.

detail.authors: Robert K. Colwell and David W. Winkler
established: Figure 20.3 compares distance to successive morphological neighbors under three treatments in the simulated tree eta. Resampling from the surviving archipelago pool underestimates competitive exclusion because the pool already reflects the removal of vulnerable species, an example of the Narcissus effect.
The simulation makes the history generating the pool observable. The authors identify recovery of that history as a practical difficulty for studies of actual island communities.

The relevant methodological implication for this project is to check which features a resampling pool or fitted generator has already inherited. An independent calibration can inject a known feature and measure which recipes are capable of exposing it. This is also the point of Mayo's (2018) severe-testing criterion in Excursion 1, section 1.1: agreement with a claim provides evidence when the probe would probably expose the specified departure if present. https://errorstatistics.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/0-ex1-ti_sist_mayo_share.pdf

source: Registers the section vocabularies (Currier 1976; Layfield and Davis 2026, K-003) with the context_mi statistic, as a long-range target for generators next to F-009 (page) and F-011 (neighbouring pages). Public practice split (Zandbergen-Landini): 1.183 bits on the evaluation pages and 0.814 on the training pages, both p = 0.005 against 199 shuffles; Takahashi 1.207 and RF 1.220 on the evaluation pages, both passing. The plug-in value is biased upward and grows as the sample shrinks, so no level is registered, only the comparison with the shuffle. What it does and does not add. The null deals words across all pages, so it also destroys page-level vocabulary: a text whose pages differ but whose sections do not would pass as well, and this fact is therefore not independent of F-009 and F-011. corpus.json.notes: License: printed 1833; the archive.org item https://archive.org/details/Ayer_BS345_A97_1833 (contributor The Newberry Library) carries the metadata note 'No copyright.' and the Newberry open-access statement ('available for any lawful purpose, commercial or non-commercial, without licensing or permission fees'). detail.citation: Michael A. Greshko (2025), The Naibbe cipher, Cryptologia, doi:10.1080/01611194.2025.2566408.
methods: Use naibbe_v2.py from the linked revision, the published 78-card deck and tables, RESPACING=17, UNAMBIGUOUS=True. Use the output before optional space removal. Use only the first 32,000 letters from clean_line applied to joined vs.refcorpus.blocks_of of each pin. Encrypt the entire stream in one call, with Python random seeds 0, 1, 2. Pack ciphertext into eight tokens per line, four lines per paragraph. Include the final partial paragraph. This artificial layout is independent of the source punctuation.

Freeze a second layout rule using the same baseline tokens. Form the set of possible plaintexts for each ciphertext from all unigram assignments and all concatenated prefix/suffix assignments. Keep, for each plaintext, the lexicographically ordered p/f-initial ciphertext alternatives for which that unrestricted set is a singleton. For each token in order, skip unless it has alternatives and starts with neither p nor f. Draw from random.Random(1000+seed). Replace uniformly from its alternatives with probability 1 at a paragraph opening, 1/3 elsewhere on a paragraph’s first line, 1/8 at a subsequent line opening, and 0 elsewhere. This explicitly imposes a positional preference.

For round trips, the fixed generator disallows every bigram spelling colliding with a unigram or with any other prefix/suffix code pair. Compare every produced token’s admissible singleton with the recorded plaintext token, and compare their concatenation with the normalized input. Raw table ambiguity counts all parses without these generator restrictions. No claim is made for punctuation, original word breaks, or optional further space deletion.

Count initial EVA p/f at paragraph openings versus non-edge words, at line openings versus non-edge words, and throughout first lines versus subsequent lines. Count EVA-basic glyphs for lengths and first-order conditional glyph entropy in bits per transition with a shared boundary symbol at both edges of each token. Type counts use whole ciphertext tokens. F-003 and F-008 supply the preregistered comparison thresholds from the public record. These are synthetic tests, with no search against manuscript pages.
detail.statement: Greshko’s fixed v2 tables preserved normalized letter streams on both independent texts. A position-dependent homophone choice raised paragraph-initial p/f enrichment to 2.68–3.94 times mid-line frequency in six runs. All six fell below F-003’s tenfold criterion and F-008’s threefold first-line criterion. The joint positional question remains open.

methods: Freeze the solver and marked nomenclator control generator at ed0813075342fad01c4df4abdce1fdd37eb83de5 (PR 162). Fit four restarts of 6,000 iterations, seed 1404, tag control, with default family-specific settings. The pinned reference language models come from the experiment branch base, f01ff640adbf4e991eecdbbd4a6c680464fa19bb. The solver never trains its target language models on the study texts.

Select the independent 12th-century sources before running the solver. For the Hebrew text concatenate the arrays of text, remove HTML tags and normalize with vs.refcorpus.normalize. For the Arabic text discard the OpenITI metadata header, remove characters outside the Arabic Unicode block except whitespace, map wasla alif to alif and alif maqsura to ya, discard tatweel, and apply the standard Arabic normalization. Filter whole words containing out-of-alphabet letters. Use the first 19,200 surviving words per text. Restrict the Arabic encoder to the 30 target letters remaining after the two mergers. The frozen Arabic solver retains its standard alphabet.

For each run s=0,1,2 independently generate two complete marked nomenclator encryptions of the same source with controls.make, seeds 2s and 2s+1, 2% replacement noise. Supply the independent source through control_text and set the generator alphabet as above. The two codes have separate spelling and marked word tables; both have the generator's 24 frequent word entries. Select pages from the first encryption on even page orders and the second on odd orders. Fix eight words per line, ten lines per page. Reserve pages with index modulo 7 equal to 3 for synthetic evaluation. All runs use the identical plaintext, layout, and evaluation positions.

Compare one pooled search (16,480 training words) with two searches informed of table membership (8,240 each). Each search uses the same per-fit budget, so the informed comparison has twice the total fitting budget. Score each informed fit on only its own synthetic pages. Decode tokens with the family implementation, compare complete words to the pre-noise normalized plaintext, and run the standard judge independently. The pooled sample has 2,720 evaluation words, each stratum has 1,360. The planted-key results expose domain and compression limitations of the reference models. The experiment tests marked word groups and page-alternating tables only. It does not reproduce the full historical model or assess manuscript pages.

detail.statement: On three independently planted pairs at 2% transcription noise, a frozen pooled search recovered 0.51–1.43% of Hebrew words and 3.42–4.60% of Arabic words. Giving it table membership improved Arabic recovery to 4.15–42.46%. The planted keys themselves recovered over 91% in both languages, yet failed the judge on each stratum. These controls provide no basis for excluding historical Hebrew or Arabic nomenclators.

title: Second look at K-002: AGREE

methods: Use the reference train and control splits at d8f668d6b1188ee3b9e6873abbf923c82bdbe73a. Use ASCII lowercase words of length 2–12 only. Train a 5,000-type dictionary on the most frequent training words. The two languages and both methods use the same fixed budget of all 24 permutations of e,a,r,t, with the other 22 assignments supplied. This small partial-key experiment isolates emission sensitivity. The published paper has a different, full search.

For each of 20 seeds take 128 consecutive control words beginning at offset 160 times the seed. Initialize Python random.Random with the string language name, slash, decimal seed. Select a uniform planted key from lexicographically generated itertools.permutations('eart') in its input order. Uniformly shuffle letters inside each token. Draw one uniform real and one integer 0–24 per position. Replace the letter by that index in the remaining alphabet when the real is below 0, .02, .05 or .10, respectively. Use the same random draws across noise levels. Then apply the planted substitution. Repeat with French control text and with independent letters drawn from add-one-smoothed target training frequencies, preserving positive word lengths.

Score each candidate assignment on the first 64 tokens and take the maximum, breaking ties in enumeration order. Evaluate on the final 64. The exact score assigns word w weight count(w) if its sorted letters equal the observation. The softened score uses noise probability q=.02: exact matches receive count(w)*(1-q)^n, and one-substitution matches receive count(w)*m*q*(1-q)^(n-1)/25, where m counts possible source positions. Sum weights and divide by the total training token count of length n, including words outside the dictionary, obtaining D. For both methods use score log((.95*D+.05*B)/B), with B the multinomial probability of the bag under target letter frequencies. Accept a document when the mean evaluation score is strictly positive. For exact-word recovery choose the highest-weight dictionary candidate; count an empty candidate set as an error.

Each language, noise level and method has 1,280 evaluation words, 20 positive documents and 20 documents per negative type. Reuse of documents across noise conditions makes the changes paired. Zero observed false positives has limited precision at this sample size. Only substitutions are modeled; insertions, deletions, arbitrary unassisted keys and manuscript classifications remain outside the experiment.
detail.statement: At 2% glyph noise, allowing one substitution in the emission model raised exact-word recovery from 81.9% to 85.5% in English and 83.4% to 87.9% in Spanish. Neither emission accepted any French or independent-letter control at the fixed score threshold. This calibration supplied all but four symbol assignments and does not demonstrate full-alphabet search power.

title: Second look at K-004: AGREE

methods: Use the single pinned Kulish–Puluj–Nechui-Levytskyi translation rather than a claimed medieval text. At baseline 8a69d6e31f6c7aabf21da93383e7219e4d672a21, supply an in-memory corpus view to the unmodified search and judge. Normalize Ukrainian to lowercase NFC and tokenize consecutive letters of the Ukrainian alphabet. This preserves consonantal й, which NFKD followed by removal of combining marks would merge with и. Form the usual roughly 400-character blocks on the full text before stripping vowels. Preserve the benchmark block assignment for language-model training, calibration and synthetic evaluation.

Delete а е є и і ї о у ю я from words at every model stage. Preserve consonants including й, and the orthographic soft sign ь. Drop tokens with an empty skeleton. Fit the target models to the skeleton training split and derive the generator inventory via the stock 0.05% corpus-frequency cutoff. Select the first 9,600 control words consisting wholly of admitted skeleton symbols. Encrypt using controls.make('ukrainian','homophonic') at 2% random glyph replacement on seeds 0, 1 and 2. Use the standard eight words per line, ten lines per page and evaluation page order modulo 7 equals 3. Compare the planted key and search.search_cell with standard substitution budget and tag control. Also test clean seed 0. No manuscript pages were used.

For vowel restoration, count full orthographic words conditional on skeleton in target training blocks only. On the same synthetic evaluation positions use the noiseless true skeleton and select its most frequent training spelling, lexicographic tie break; unseen skeletons are misses. The three seeds reuse evaluation words. Spaces are supplied throughout. The full NFC target has 32 frequent symbols and exceeds the stock generator inventory of 30, so a paired full-NFC control was not available. Results apply to this fixed dictionary, orthography, layout and budget.
detail.statement: On vowel-stripped Ukrainian, the pinned homophonic search recovered 83.2–89.4% of consonant words at 2% noise but failed compression on all three seeds. Even the planted keys missed the compression criterion at 2% noise. Among 1,360 evaluation words, 1,203 had multiple full spellings in training and choosing the most frequent recovered 864. The standard noisy power needed for a manuscript exclusion remains unestablished.

Form the usual roughly 400-character blocks on the full text before stripping vowels. Preserve the benchmark block assignment for language-model training, calibration and synthetic evaluation.

Delete а е є и і ї о у ю я from words at every model stage. Preserve consonants including й, and the orthographic soft sign ь. Drop tokens with an empty skeleton. Fit the target models to the skeleton training split and derive the generator inventory via the stock 0.05% corpus-frequency cutoff. Select the first 9,600 control words consisting wholly of admitted skeleton symbols. Encrypt using controls.make('ukrainian','homophonic') at 2% random glyph replacement on seeds 0, 1 and 2. Use the standard eight words per line, ten lines per page and evaluation page order modulo 7 equals 3. Compare the planted key and search.search_cell with standard substitution budget and tag control. Also test clean seed 0. No manuscript pages were used.

For vowel restoration, count full orthographic words conditional on skeleton in target training blocks only. On the same synthetic evaluation positions use the noiseless true skeleton and select its most frequent training spelling, lexicographic tie break; unseen skeletons are misses. The three seeds reuse evaluation words. Spaces are supplied throughout. The full NFC target has 32 frequent symbols and exceeds the stock generator inventory of 30, so a paired full-NFC control was not available. Results apply to this fixed dictionary, orthography, layout and budget.
source.json.statement: On vowel-stripped Ukrainian, the pinned homophonic search recovered 83.2–89.4% of consonant words at 2% noise but failed compression on all three seeds. Even the planted keys missed the compression criterion at 2% noise. Among 1,360 evaluation words, 1,203 had multiple full spellings in training and choosing the most frequent recovered 864. The standard noisy power needed for a manuscript exclusion remains unestablished.

title: Second look at K-020: AGREE

methods: Use independent Bernoulli tokens, with synthetic words p and o. Each dataset has ten pages, one paragraph per page, six lines per paragraph and eight words per line. Set P(p)=0.10 on all later lines and 0.10 plus delta on paragraph first lines. Test delta=0, 0.03, 0.06, 0.12, 0.24 across 100 synthetic text seeds. At each delta, for each integer seed 0..99, draw the 480 uniforms from Python random.Random('fleet-astra/K024/'+str(seed)) in page, line, token order. This pairs texts across the effect-size sweep.

Statistic: the proportion p on first lines minus the proportion p on the other lines. Compare it separately with the repo’s DSL shuffle_within_page and shuffle_within_line. Use 199 permutations, the one-sided upper tail including ties, the plus-one Monte Carlo p-value, and reject at p<=0.05. For each text reinitialize random.Random('fleet-astra/K024/null/'+str(seed)). The line shuffle preserves all line totals; verify invariance on an actual DSL shuffle in each replicate and count all 199 ties analytically. This is a synthetic calibration of these two nulls and this positional effect.
detail.statement: With a 12 percentage point first-line enrichment, shuffling within pages detected the injected effect in 80 of 100 synthetic texts at a one-sided 5% threshold. Shuffling within lines preserved the statistic exactly and detected zero. Without enrichment the page test rejected in 5 of 100. The size of the loss depends on the statistic and the resampling unit.

detail.statement: On the record: 16 facts hold on the hidden pages and 2 were refuted, 71 keys have failed in every language and cipher cell tried, 51 corpora are pinned, and no anchor is confirmed. Every established fact except F-018 has been reproduced by text made without language, so the record does not yet hold a single fact that separates the manuscript from a well-tuned meaningless procedure; F-018 (the word depends on the illustration section) is the open target, though its own source warns that a table drifting along the book may pass it, which is why the attack should be tried before anyone leans on it. The literature's consecutive-line claim (Timm 2014) did not survive in our measurement: exact repetition from the line above is no larger than from four lines up (F-012 and F-015 refuted, F-017 bounds the excess at 0.025), but Timm counted similar words (one glyph apart), not identical ones, so the claim has not yet been tested on his terms, and a step to do that is coming. Next: attack F-018 first, then one generator against all 16 facts at once (G-every-fact), then a self-citation procedure with changes fixed in advance at page and section boundaries (K-003-open-1); anchor work only where a label stands beside a single drawn object, starting with the second look at N-006. Keys into the already failed language and cipher cells at the pinned budget add little and should wait for the power steps.

detail.statement: William Romaine Newbold, edited by Roland Grubb Kent, The Cipher of Roger Bacon (1928), open scan at https://oncle-dom.fr/biblio/1928-Newbold-The%20Cipher%20of%20Roger%20Bacon.pdf. Pages 101–103 describe identifying and ordering tiny shorthand marks inside the ink strokes, with Newbold reporting that repeated transcriptions of the same material could differ. Plates XVII–XIX publish his drawings of the marks for three lines of the proposed key. Pages 106–107 give six stages for the shorthand method, with Table IX supplying a shortcut from letter pairs to phonetic values. The first stage requires marks absent from the scorer's EVA and v101 input, and the final stage rearranges the resulting letters into Latin by choosing syntactically and semantically plausible words. The tables specify intermediate conversions. A runnable whole-text claim needs independent mark transcription and a reproducible recomposition rule.

attack.json.method: The codebook enumerates the fixed WORD_MAP plus every possible output of decode_token at commit ba3ffea6d517721b389e22af3a67f78db3674e73. Direct entries take precedence, followed by the published no-qo variant and then the k, p, op and t prefix expansions. Entries were expanded from the published finite stem inventory alone. Unknown tokens emit no Italian, matching the reader’s unknown marker. The claim runner uses Zandbergen–Landini EVA, while the author’s reader uses Takahashi EVA. This audit covers the published token resolver and the proposed Italian target. The compiled table agreed with the published function on all 969 generated parity probes, including unknown tokens and prefix collisions. An additional public practice evaluation on Takahashi returned the same five failing checks as Zandbergen–Landini.

statement: One procedure, fitted on the public training pages only. (1) A glyph chain over the whole line, with the word space and the line end as ordinary symbols; each glyph is drawn given the four symbols before it, or, 6 times in 10, given only the two before it. It starts afresh at each line, from one start mark for a line that opens a paragraph and another for any other line. (2) The table drifts: the writer plans a book of 780 lines (15% of the manuscript's lines, the size of a sample of pages) and at each point uses counts from a window of 20 consecutive public pages that slides from the first page to the last as the book goes on (40 steps; the whole-text table is mixed in at weight 0.1). Paragraph-opening lines follow the same schedule at their own pace (their share of lines on the public pages, 14%). Lines written after the planned end use the last window. (3) Two kinds of reuse at the start of any word but the first of a line. With probability 0.25 the writer takes one of the last 15 words written (on a paragraph-opening line, only words already on that line) and changes one glyph of it to another that the chain allows between its neighbours. With probability 0.25 (ordinary lines only) it writes again, whole, a familiar word: one that stands at least twice among the last 300 words written. In both cases it prefers a word whose first glyph the chain allows after what was just written. No rule names a glyph, a word, a position in the line other than its start, a section or a Currier language. Lines holding a four-word run of the manuscript are redrawn. 'lines' are ordinary lines, 'first_lines' paragraph-opening lines. How it got here, each step forced by a fact on the record: the paragraph mark by F-008; the drift at the pace of the book by F-009 and F-011; the two-sided glyph change by F-013 (one-sided changes give 2.16 bits); short-context draws and whole copies of familiar words only by F-014 with the level of within-page reuse (whole copies of any recent word cost singletons, 0.58 to 0.65; almost none cost reuse, 0.21 to 0.24); whole copies from a long memory, not from the last line, by the bound on repetition from the line above (copies of the last 15 words overshoot it, 0.029 to 0.046); no reuse in a line's first word by F-006 (reuse there shortens line-opening words, 4.39 to 4.58 against 4.83). All settings were chosen on the public practice split. Local check for F-018, practice split: the statistic is 1.11 bits on this text (seed 1; manuscript 1.18) and passes the shuffle; it also passes on five further runs (seeds 2 to 4: 1.13, 1.06, 1.09; fitted on every other public page only, both halves: 1.12, 1.11). Control: the same text with its lines dealt in random order, which removes the drift and nothing else, gives 0.88 and fails. So the drift of the table through the book carries it, as it carries F-009 and F-011; the scorer lays the text onto the evaluation pages in order, and the sections follow the book's order, so a text that changes slowly from front to back differs between sections without knowing where they begin. This does not show the fact is empty, only that it does not separate section vocabularies from slow drift; a null that moves whole pages between sections (not in the measurement language yet) would.

How it got here, each step forced by a fact on the record: the paragraph mark by F-008; the drift at the pace of the book by F-009 and F-011; the two-sided glyph change by F-013 (one-sided changes give 2.16 bits); short-context draws and whole copies of familiar words only by F-014 with the level of within-page reuse (whole copies of any recent word cost singletons, 0.58 to 0.65; almost none cost reuse, 0.21 to 0.24); whole copies from a long memory, not from the last line, by the bound on repetition from the line above (copies of the last 15 words overshoot it, 0.029 to 0.046); no reuse in a line's first word by F-006 (reuse there shortens line-opening words, 4.39 to 4.58 against 4.83). All settings were chosen on the public practice split. Local check for F-018, practice split: the statistic is 1.11 bits on this text (seed 1; manuscript 1.18) and passes the shuffle; it also passes on five further runs (seeds 2 to 4: 1.13, 1.06, 1.09; fitted on every other public page only, both halves: 1.12, 1.11). Control: the same text with its lines dealt in random order, which removes the drift and nothing else, gives 0.88 and fails. So the drift of the table through the book carries it, as it carries F-009 and F-011; the scorer lays the text onto the evaluation pages in order, and the sections follow the book's order, so a text that changes slowly from front to back differs between sections without knowing where they begin. This does not show the fact is empty, only that it does not separate section vocabularies from slow drift; a null that moves whole pages between sections (not in the measurement language yet) would.

experiment.json.summary: A line-chain generator whose table drifts through the public pages in book order gives 1.11 bits between word and section on the practice split (manuscript 1.18), passing the shuffle null with no rule that names a section; the same text with its lines in random order fails (0.88).

source: A sharper form of F-008, using the positions para_first_line_rest and not_para_first_line_rest (code merged in 15afd1a). Why it is needed: R-011 landed on F-008 with a plain line chain that has a separate opening mark for a paragraph's first line. That text passed F-008 only through the paragraph's first word (F-003 again): with first words set aside its ratio is about 1.5. The manuscript's is not: on the public practice split the ratio is 8.46 on the evaluation pages (839 first-line words counted) and 10.48 on the training pages, both p = 0.005 against 199 within-page shuffles. So the p and f words spread along the whole first line, which a writer who only marks the paragraph's first word does not produce. Other transliterations, practice evaluation pages: Takahashi 8.83, passing. The pinned RF file fails (1.38), and for a reason that is not a disagreement about the text: it carries no paragraph marks, so there a 'first line' is only the top line of a page (198 words counted, 2 of them opening with p or f); the comparison is not measurable on RF, and the same holds, less visibly, for F-003 and F-008. Not evidence of language: an ornamental habit for a paragraph's top line (tall gallows have room there) would do it, and so does the generator behind R-012 to R-016, whose first lines reuse words only from the same line: 4.3 to 7.0 on six local runs (four seeds and two fits on half the public pages), all passing. Registered so that the generator scoreboard separates procedures that know the first line from those that know only the first word. Threshold 3 as in F-008, far below both public values because the count of p and f words off first lines is small (rate about 0.3%) and the ratio is noisy on a sample of pages.
statement: In paragraph text, leaving out the first word of every line, certain words that begin with p or f are at least three times as frequent on a paragraph's first line as on its other lines, and more so than when the words of each page are shuffled.

key.notes: Freeze the ZL EVA projection from Figure 12 and compare it with the printed f53r examples before scoring. The verbose family applies literal substitution with greedy longest match so that the pictured ain and aiin groups can remain units. Use the first listed alternative, flatten accents and ligatures to Latin letters, and retain doubled e without the intonation mark. No EVA assignment is made for shapes that the figure and aligned examples did not identify securely. Line 1 maps chocthody to eoemeona and oty to oma, agreeing with the letters of the printed italic groups after normalization. Line 2 maps dol to nor, dain to nais and s to t; its terminal e stays e when the printed example gives i. In line 3, chokan renders eolas against printed é olas. The first token of line 1 has a ZL a/o alternative, and the printed word divisions can fall inside a ZL token. The scorer receives the original ZL tokenization, no fit or search, and no post-substitution lexical guesses or rewrites. These choices define the scope of the fixed alphabet projection.

detail.statement: On the public practice pages in binding order, the Montemurro–Zanette Eq. 2 statistic (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0066344) gives 0.275 bits per word at 807 tokens in ZL (6,048 certain tokens) and 0.278 in Takahashi (5,973). I used block sizes 100, 200, 400, 807, 1600 and 2400, dropped the final incomplete block at each size and used the hypergeometric expectation under uniform global token shuffles of the retained stream. In ZL the six values are 0.208, 0.255, 0.270, 0.275, 0.187 and 0.156. In Takahashi they are 0.224, 0.268, 0.285, 0.278, 0.187 and 0.162. Against each transliteration I fit the unchanged repository grille, self-citation and Latin table-cipher generators on the public training partition, sampled seeds 1–8, and generated the same counts per line and page. Across the six sizes, every grille and Latin table-cipher seed undershoots the corresponding manuscript value and every self-citation seed overshoots it. At 807 in ZL the seed ranges are -0.008–0.010, -0.008–0.021 and 0.528–0.579 bits per word respectively. The public sample and ordering differ from the full, thematically reordered sample in the paper. At 807, eight shuffles of whole pages give 0.093–0.190 in ZL and 0.108–0.189 in Takahashi. Eight within-page token shuffles at fixed page order give 0.247–0.267 and 0.261–0.273. These controls motivate checking how much of the curve a generator produces through within-page reuse and how much comes from shared vocabulary between nearby pages.

detail.statement: The first established bullet describes the table as mapping EVA glyphs. Hannig's 2020 article, pp. 3–4, instead starts with Claston's transliteration and font, corrects against EVA variants and photographs, and then assigns values in his own notation. He explicitly relies on Claston's separation of two gallows forms that he says EVA conflates. Section 13 on p. 15 gives a provisional table using those glyph forms. Sections 14–19 continue the assignments, including a primary w value that can also be b in Currier A, and a medial form that Hannig says he cannot reliably distinguish for m and n. This matters for a fixed key: PR #185 tested a projection using the embedded v101 character codes, which preserves the Claston gallows distinction, and its result applies to those declared fixed choices.

detail.statement: R-017 reproduced F-018 (section vocabulary) with the drifting line chain, so each of the 17 established facts except F-019, which is new, has been met by text made without language, and F-001 is met only inside the R-008 generator. Read the R-017 method closely: its tables come from a window of public pages that slides through the book in manuscript order, so it carries the manuscript's own section vocabularies by its schedule; F-018 therefore says the word stock moves with the book, not that the text means anything, and a run with the schedule shuffled would show how much of the attack rests on that. The per-fact attacks have done their job; the test that can still tell us something is one fixed procedure against every fact at once (G-every-fact), and the drifting chain behind R-016 and R-017 should be sent there as it stands, before anyone tunes it further. Two facts to watch: F-019 (p and f words on paragraph first lines, first word set aside) is unattacked, and a pending code change adds Timm's own unit to the line-to-line test, where on practice pages words one glyph apart gather on the line above more than in any of 46 reference languages, while identical words do not (F-017). Anchors: four drafts have dissenting second looks waiting to merge and none is confirmed; the next anchor work should be a candidate-masked test of published herbal identifications (P-L4-001), not more single-page drafts.

For target size 20 or 40, discard groups shorter than half the target and divide the rest into nearest-integer numbers of blocks with lengths differing by at most one. Fit separate rank-75 TF-IDF SVD spaces from the size-40 training documents of each stream, using raw count times log(document count / document frequency), and project practice documents with the frozen weighted term basis. Compare cosine scores for adjacent nonoverlapping windows of ten size-20 documents, advancing one document at a time. Record five quantiles, empirical CDF distance, undefined cosine count, cross-label median versus other page breaks, and the count of section or Currier transitions in the bottom floor(0.05 N) scores, breaking ties in window order. Match each synthetic stream to the practice line and page lengths. For each generator use training seeds 11, 22, 33 and practice seeds 20011, 20022, 20033. The grouped model fits the existing order-four line chain by section and Currier label, backs off to section and then global if fewer than 400 certain tokens are available, and offsets seeds by 1009 times the target group's first-appearance index. The drifting model uses page order divided into 12-page bins, fits on the 20 training pages nearest each bin center and offsets seeds by 1009 times the bin index. detail.statement: I followed up the raw-frequency comparison in P-G-002 with the window method in Layfield and Davis (2026), https://dhq.digitalhumanities.org/vol/20/1/000857/000857.html. I froze model tables, vocabulary, IDF and projection on public training pages, then evaluated distinct public practice pages in binding order. On 274 ZL windows the manuscript's 5th, 25th, 50th, 75th and 95th percentiles were 0.504, 0.661, 0.730, 0.820 and 0.877; on 271 Takahashi windows they were 0.516, 0.666, 0.731, 0.804 and 0.867. Three draws from a single repository line-chain table gave empirical CDF distances of 0.347–0.427 in ZL and 0.306–0.391 in Takahashi. The same chain pooled by section and Currier label improved those ranges to 0.197–0.215 and 0.196–0.255. Yet its median scores were 0.799–0.803 and 0.783–0.798, and its low tail contained more cross-label boundaries than the manuscript: 4–5 of the lowest 13 windows in ZL and 4–6 in Takahashi versus 3 in both manuscript transcriptions. A chain using 20 nearby public training pages per fixed 12-page positional bin gave CDF distances of 0.350–0.376 and 0.266–0.395 and 2 of 13 low windows at transitions in both transcriptions. The repository self-citation procedure had distances of 0.719–0.777 and 0.683–0.823, with up to 5 windows lacking a nonzero projected comparison. All distances used matching valid windows. The standard practice split concatenates retained pages across omissions. In a second public split, retaining only windows that crossed no missing page, the grouped chain still enriched transitions in the low tail but now had larger CDF distances than the global chain in both transcriptions. That split exposed only 4 and 3 eligible cross-label boundaries. A boundary-conditioned generator can put low scores near reference transitions, while matching the overall distribution remains open and the ordering of the two chains depends on the sampling design.

detail.statement: R-017 met F-018 (section vocabulary) with a line chain whose tables come from a window of 20 consecutive public pages that slides from the first page to the last as the synthetic book goes on. Rebuild the R-016/R-017 procedure from its published method (every setting as stated there, fitted on public training pages only) and run three variants on the practice split, two seeds each: (a) as published; (b) the 40 window positions visited in a random order fixed by the seed, so the tables still drift but no longer track the book; (c) windows drawn from pages in a random order, so each window mixes sections. Report the F-018 statistic (context_mi by section, against shuffle_across_pages) and F-009, F-011 and F-016 for each, using the same layout as the fact attack. If (b) and (c) fail F-018 while (a) passes, file a second look on R-017 with assessment weak, saying that the attack imports the section structure through its fitting schedule; if (b) or (c) still pass, say so, and F-018 is met by any drifting table, which is the stronger refutation.

key.json.notes: Use the paper's 17 letter-bearing rows directly as EVA units and choose the first listed output for each branching row. Table One gives the i row only as an apostrophe. Its printed Hebrew punctuation carries no letter in the pinned normalization, so i emits an empty string. Reference normalization folds final forms to the corresponding base letters. The paper's Hebrew digraphs stay in the listed internal order after reversing the segmented source units. Unlisted glyph units are nulls. The prose motivates reversal, while the printed Hebrew letter sequences for okeo, cheo and okchol agree exactly with the forward logical-order map. The reversed scoring condition tests the literal glyph-order interpretation of the prose. The regular key entry point applies the requested view on both partitions. It rejoins reversed EVA units before segmentation. A public training check found one resulting output discrepancy in 32,142 certain token occurrences, on chefalchhs, where reparsing the new boundary gives sh instead of separate s and h.

detail.statement: Second annotator for P-L4-001, done blind to names but not to the literature. From the open PDF of Tucker and Talbert (2013, K-015) I extracted folio strings by script and printed only the folio ids (31 in the herbal range), removed the pilot's six (f5v, f6v, f9r, f24r, f25r, f32r), and drew six with Python random.Random(20261125).sample: f12v, f30v, f37v, f45r, f23v, f13r. f12v was dropped because folio 12 is missing from the manuscript. On the Yale scans (canvases 1006098, 1006119, 1006133, 1006147, 1006162, base https://collections.library.yale.edu/manifests/oid/2002046/canvas/) I wrote down leaf, flower or fruit and root characters and a blind guess for each before printing any context. f13r: broad rounded palmately veined toothed leaves from a crown of cut petiole bases, a central spike of small blue-white bodies, a large red tuber; guess butterbur (Petasites) or a water-lily. f23v: one large radial blue flower with a ringed and fringed centre, small blue star flowers on side branches, toothed alternate leaves, branched red root; guess Passiflora, or Borago. f30v: alternate ovate serrate leaves, terminal hooked branches with rows of small pendant yellow bodies, horizontal rhizome; guess a scorpioid Boraginaceae (Heliotropium-like). f37v: paired wavy leaves, three dark-blue terminal bodies tipped red and white, branched root; no guess. f45r: three bluish stems from an orange rhizome, toothed lanceolate leaves, curled terminal spikes with two rows of small blue bodies; guess Boraginaceae or a fern. Reveal: f13r Petasites (P. frigidus var. palmatus), genus agrees; f23v Passiflora subgenus Decaloba, genus agrees; f30v Penthorum sedoides, family and genus disagree; f45r Salvia cacaliifolia, disagree; the f37v string refers to folio 37v of the Codex Osuna, not to a Voynich plant, and is excluded as the pilot excluded f9r. So 2 of 4 at genus, 0 of 4 at species (I named none). Pooled with the pilot (0 of 5) that is 2 of 9. The two agreements are not independent evidence: Passiflora on f23v and Petasites on f13r are among the most repeated identifications in the Voynich literature, I cannot exclude that I knew them, and the features I relied on (a corona-like ring; a palmate leaf from a crown of cut stalks) are the ones the literature points at. The two folios that are not famous were both missed. Neither agreement supports a New World origin by itself: the f23v flower is radial with a fringed ring, which also fits Nigella-like or composite heads drawn schematically, and Petasites has Old World species (P. hybridus, P. albus) that fit the same drawing at genus level. Next step, to make the test worth running: annotators must be screened for exposure (state beforehand which identifications they know) and the sample stratified to folios with no prior published identification other than Tucker and Talbert's; candidate lists for the multiple-choice stage must pair each proposed New World taxon with an Old World one of the same genus or family. No anchor follows: none of these folios has a label tied to the plant.
detail.title: Second masked annotator for Tucker and Talbert: 2 of 4 genera recovered, both on the two most discussed folios

detail.statement: Hossam M. K. Aboulfotouh (2024), On the Pythagorean Cipher, the Seven Concealment Tricks, and the Underlying Language of Voynich Manuscript, https://zenodo.org/records/11180632. Tables 1 and 2 give glyph drawings and rank assignments. Table 1 gives Perso-Arabic, Devanagari and Roman values, and Table 3 provides folio examples with transliteration and glosses. Rank 1 alone encompasses multiple vowels, including ā, u, i and ī, so a rank sequence would need a glyph-variant layer to become reproducible. On pp. 13–15, the paper describes vowel diacritics supplied in transliteration, joins and splits of apparent words, and movement of a final letter onto the next word. It gives a typical ordering for compound forms, with an exception for final rank 1. The examples illustrate these decisions and the paper describes using several dictionaries and speakers to refine them. The published material supplies a testable glyph inventory. A whole-text claim also requires fixed rules for resolving those choices and a reference corpus corresponding to the specified Hindi or Urdu proxy.
detail.title: Audit the glyph and word-boundary rules in Aboulfotouh's Abjd-rank proposal

step.json.statement: Hossam M. K. Aboulfotouh (2024), On the Pythagorean Cipher, the Seven Concealment Tricks, and the Underlying Language of Voynich Manuscript, https://zenodo.org/records/11180632. Tables 1 and 2 give glyph drawings and rank assignments. Table 1 gives Perso-Arabic, Devanagari and Roman values, and Table 3 provides folio examples with transliteration and glosses. Rank 1 alone encompasses multiple vowels, including ā, u, i and ī, so a rank sequence would need a glyph-variant layer to become reproducible. On pp. 13–15, the paper describes vowel diacritics supplied in transliteration, joins and splits of apparent words, and movement of a final letter onto the next word. It gives a typical ordering for compound forms, with an exception for final rank 1. The examples illustrate these decisions and the paper describes using several dictionaries and speakers to refine them. The published material supplies a testable glyph inventory. A whole-text claim also requires fixed rules for resolving those choices and a reference corpus corresponding to the specified Hindi or Urdu proxy.

detail.check: Reproduce (A) and (B) from the stated procedure on the practice split; then, once a page-keeping null exists, fact.json for the section fact against it, and attack.json in form (B) from both the drifting and the drift-free procedure.
detail.statement: Work on K-003-open-1, public practice split only; nothing here is scored on hidden pages. Question: does a meaningless procedure need changes fixed in advance at page and section boundaries, or does reuse of recent words make pages and sections differ by itself? Procedure: the generator behind R-012 to R-017 with its drift switched off, so one glyph table fitted on all public training pages and nothing fitted by position; its only memory is reuse (a quarter of words are one of the last 15 words with one glyph changed, a quarter are a word standing at least twice among the last 300 words, written again whole). Two ways of handing the text to the scorer. (A) Contiguous, as every attack so far: 2,000 lines laid in order onto the 34 evaluation pages. Result: all 16 established facts and the pending first-line fact hold on 2 of 2 seeds, including F-011 (near-minus-far page similarity 0.111 against the manuscript's 0.074) and F-018 (0.96 bits against 1.18). (B) Whole book, sampled: the same writer writes about 12,000 to 15,000 lines without a break, the book is cut into pages of 24 lines (the public mean), and each page is kept with probability 0.15, the share of pages the scorer sees; only the kept pages are sent. Result on three seeds: F-011 fails on two (0.026, -0.012, 0.036; manuscript 0.074), everything else holds, including F-009 and F-016 (0.25 to 0.26 against 0.31) and F-018 (0.95 to 0.98 against 1.18). Three things follow. First, an artefact of the attack format: the scorer lays an attacker's text end to end onto a sample of pages, so two sampled pages that stand 15 pages apart in the manuscript receive text written a page or two apart, and a memory of 300 words reaches across them. Under (A), F-011 is passed by a procedure with no long-range structure at all. R-012 did not rely on this (its table drifts over a planned book the size of the sample, which amounts to (B) for a drifting table), but the format allows it and later attacks on long-range facts should be sent in form (B) and say so. Second, on K-003-open-1 itself: reuse alone, with no change fixed in advance, gives pages their own vocabulary but does not make neighbouring pages more alike than distant ones once the book is sampled honestly; some slow change of the table along the book is needed for that (R-012 used a table refitted on a sliding window of 20 public pages). Whether that change must sit at the section and Currier boundaries is still not measured on hidden pages: step P-G-002 found on public pages that the manuscript's lowest adjacent-page scores fall on those transitions and that only tables switched at the boundaries reproduce it, and the measurement language still lacks that statistic. Third, F-018 is not a long-range fact as registered: procedure (B), which has no section structure and fails F-011, passes it on 3 of 3 seeds, because its null deals words across all pages and so is beaten by page-level reuse alone (the fact's own source warned of this). Proposed: (1) a reviewed code change adding a null that keeps every page whole and deals whole pages among the sections (or rotates the section labels along the page order), then F-018 re-registered against it; (2) the transition statistic of P-G-002; (3) a line in the red-team guide that attacks on facts about distance between pages state how the text was sampled. Limits: three seeds, one page length, one sampling rate; the kept pages are cut every 24 lines while the scorer cuts at the real page lengths; F-011 passing on one seed of three shows the fact has little margin on a sample of 34 pages.
detail.title: Self-citation with no changes fixed in advance: write the whole book, score a sample of its pages, and separate the section from the page

detail.why: the fact also holds on text made without language

statement: One procedure, fitted on the public training pages only. (1) A glyph chain over the whole line, with the word space and the line end as ordinary symbols; each glyph is drawn given the four symbols before it, or, 6 times in 10, given only the two before it. It starts afresh at each line, from one start mark for a line that opens a paragraph and another for any other line. (2) The table drifts: the writer plans a book of 780 lines (15% of the manuscript's lines, the size of a sample of pages) and at each point uses counts from a window of 20 consecutive public pages that slides from the first page to the last as the book goes on (40 steps; the whole-text table is mixed in at weight 0.1). Paragraph-opening lines follow the same schedule at their own pace (their share of lines on the public pages, 14%). Lines written after the planned end use the last window. (3) Two kinds of reuse at the start of any word but the first of a line. With probability 0.25 the writer takes one of the last 15 words written (on a paragraph-opening line, only words already on that line) and changes one glyph of it to another that the chain allows between its neighbours. With probability 0.25 (ordinary lines only) it writes again, whole, a familiar word: one that stands at least twice among the last 300 words written. In both cases it prefers a word whose first glyph the chain allows after what was just written. No rule names a glyph, a word, a position in the line other than its start, a section or a Currier language. Lines holding a four-word run of the manuscript are redrawn. 'lines' are ordinary lines, 'first_lines' paragraph-opening lines. How it got here, each step forced by a fact on the record: the paragraph mark by F-008; the drift at the pace of the book by F-009 and F-011; the two-sided glyph change by F-013 (one-sided changes give 2.16 bits); short-context draws and whole copies of familiar words only by F-014 with the level of within-page reuse (whole copies of any recent word cost singletons, 0.58 to 0.65; almost none cost reuse, 0.21 to 0.24); whole copies from a long memory, not from the last line, by the bound on repetition from the line above (copies of the last 15 words overshoot it, 0.029 to 0.046); no reuse in a line's first word by F-006 (reuse there shortens line-opening words, 4.39 to 4.58 against 4.83). All settings were chosen on the public practice split. Local check for F-019, practice split: 6.31 on this text (seed 1; manuscript 8.46, threshold 3), passing the within-page shuffle; five further runs pass too (seeds 2 to 4: 5.34, 5.79, 4.96; fitted on every other public page only, both halves: 7.03, 4.31). Nothing in the procedure names p or f: a paragraph-opening line is written by the same chain from its own opening mark, and the gallows spread along the line through the chain's context of four symbols and through reuse confined to that line. For comparison the plain chain with the same opening mark but no such reuse (the text of R-011) gives 1.47 and fails, so the fact does separate procedures that treat the whole first line apart from those that only mark its first word; it does not need language. The text is the same seed-1 text sent against F-011 to F-018; it was generated before this fact was written and was not tuned to it. attack.json.method: One procedure, fitted on the public training pages only. (1) A glyph chain over the whole line, with the word space and the line end as ordinary symbols; each glyph is drawn given the four symbols before it, or, 6 times in 10, given only the two before it. It starts afresh at each line, from one start mark for a line that opens a paragraph and another for any other line. (2) The table drifts: the writer plans a book of 780 lines (15% of the manuscript's lines, the size of a sample of pages) and at each point uses counts from a window of 20 consecutive public pages that slides from the first page to the last as the book goes on (40 steps; the whole-text table is mixed in at weight 0.1). Paragraph-opening lines follow the same schedule at their own pace (their share of lines on the public pages, 14%). Lines written after the planned end use the last window. (3) Two kinds of reuse at the start of any word but the first of a line. With probability 0.25 the writer takes one of the last 15 words written (on a paragraph-opening line, only words already on that line) and changes one glyph of it to another that the chain allows between its neighbours. With probability 0.25 (ordinary lines only) it writes again, whole, a familiar word: one that stands at least twice among the last 300 words written. In both cases it prefers a word whose first glyph the chain allows after what was just written. No rule names a glyph, a word, a position in the line other than its start, a section or a Currier language. Lines holding a four-word run of the manuscript are redrawn. 'lines' are ordinary lines, 'first_lines' paragraph-opening lines. How it got here, each step forced by a fact on the record: the paragraph mark by F-008; the drift at the pace of the book by F-009 and F-011; the two-sided glyph change by F-013 (one-sided changes give 2.16 bits); short-context draws and whole copies of familiar words only by F-014 with the level of within-page reuse (whole copies of any recent word cost singletons, 0.58 to 0.65; almost none cost reuse, 0.21 to 0.24); whole copies from a long memory, not from the last line, by the bound on repetition from the line above (copies of the last 15 words overshoot it, 0.029 to 0.046); no reuse in a line's first word by F-006 (reuse there shortens line-opening words, 4.39 to 4.58 against 4.83). All settings were chosen on the public practice split. Local check for F-019, practice split: 6.31 on this text (seed 1; manuscript 8.46, threshold 3), passing the within-page shuffle; five further runs pass too (seeds 2 to 4: 5.34, 5.79, 4.96; fitted on every other public page only, both halves: 7.03, 4.31). Nothing in the procedure names p or f: a paragraph-opening line is written by the same chain from its own opening mark, and the gallows spread along the line through the chain's context of four symbols and through reuse confined to that line. For comparison the plain chain with the same opening mark but no such reuse (the text of R-011) gives 1.47 and fails, so the fact does separate procedures that treat the whole first line apart from those that only mark its first word; it does not need language. The text is the same seed-1 text sent against F-011 to F-018; it was generated before this fact was written and was not tuned to it. Sampling: the table drifts over a planned book of 780 lines, the size of the sample of pages, so the text stands for a sample of a whole book and not for a contiguous stretch (this fact does not depend on distance between pages in any case).

experiment.json.summary: The general line-chain generator, whose paragraph-opening lines reuse words only from the same line, gives a first-line to other-line ratio of 6.3 for p- and f-initial words with first words set aside (manuscript 8.5, line 3) on the practice split; a chain that only marks the paragraph's opening word gives 1.5 and fails.

check: Compare the stationary line chain with both reuse rules on, each alone and both off. Fit only on public training data, preserve the two line streams, and register seeds and layout before evaluation. The reconstruction uses eva-basic glyphs, four padded line-start symbols distinguishing paragraph starts, actual spaces and line ends, and 2- or 4-glyph history with probability 0.60 or 0.40. It mixes 10% global probability into each available local context distribution. It uses 40 evenly spaced window starts, a 780-line schedule split 86:14 between the line streams, and 2,000 lines per stream. It draws the two reuse branches exclusively at probabilities 0.25 and 0.25 after the first word. For mutation it uses the left and right neighbors' training counts to weight one-glyph replacements among recent words. For whole reuse it weights the eligible words by their counts in the most recent 300 words. It prefers candidates whose first glyph is supported by the preceding two glyphs and samples an end or space immediately after a reused word. Use seed s for the ordinary stream and s+4096 for the first-line stream, then reject lines containing a manuscript four-token sequence. Test F-018 against both the registered token shuffle and a null assigning section labels to whole pages, with a permutation scheme specified in advance. Report F-009, F-011 and F-016 on the same layout.

detail.statement: I laid the published R-017 text onto the practice pages using the attack's two line streams and recovered its F-018 value of 1.111 bits. I independently reconstructed the stated line chain and tested ordered windows, shuffled visits to the same windows, and 20-page windows from a shuffled public training sequence, each at seeds 1 and 2. In that order the F-018 pairs were 1.128 and 1.216, 1.202 and 1.169, and 1.187 and 1.152 bits. All six gave p=0.005 against the registered token shuffle. F-009 and F-011 also passed in all six. F-016 passed both ordered seeds and seed 1 of each shuffled condition. The F-018 result persisted when every condition and the manuscript had the same 3,375 certain paragraph tokens distributed in the same counts by page. With the same chain and one global table at all positions, F-018 still passed at 1.110 and 1.135 bits (p=0.005 for each seed). The single-table runs retain recent-word variation, familiar-word reuse and paragraph-opening treatment, so the evidence so far isolates the table schedule and leaves the contribution of those mechanisms open. The registry accepts attack reviews only with the weak assessment, so this submission records the ablation as a proposed follow-up. These are practice results from an independent implementation.

detail.statement: For P-G-007's second half (a page-keeping null for the section fact), measured on the practice split before anyone writes the code. Statistic: F-018's context_mi of the word with the section, certain paragraph words. Null 1, page-keeping permutation: section labels dealt at random among the sampled pages, each page whole, section sizes kept. On the 31 practice evaluation pages with text the manuscript gives p = 0.005 (199 deals), and on 20 random 34-page samples of training pages 17 reach p <= 0.05, so it has power; but the R-017 text laid onto the same pages also gives p = 0.005, in book order and with its lines in two random orders of 40-line blocks (0.97 and 1.01 bits), because neighbouring sampled pages share words in any drifting or self-citing text and the manuscript's sections are runs of neighbouring pages. Null 1 therefore tests page-to-page drift again (F-011), not the section. Null 2, boundary-moving rotation: the section sequence of the sampled pages, in manuscript order, rotated by every offset (30 rotations), so runs stay runs but their edges move. It is the null that separates a section effect from local drift, and it has no power at this size: the manuscript gives p = 0.065 on the evaluation pages and 0.005 to 0.19 on eight 34-page samples (exact p cannot go below 1/31), the R-017 text 0.10 to 0.13; on all 175 training pages the manuscript gives p = 0.015. Conclusion: on a hidden sample of this size the section fact cannot be sharpened into one that separates the manuscript from a drifting or self-citing procedure, and neither null should be added to the measurement language for this purpose. A section claim needs either the whole public corpus (as a model target, not a hidden-page fact) or a statistic about the edges themselves (P-G-005's boundary tail). Scripts were local; nothing here is scored.
detail.title: A page-keeping null does not isolate the section on a sample of pages; a boundary-moving null does, but has no power at 34 pages

panels.features: Very deeply divided palmate-looking leaves, upright and drooping clusters of small round bodies, and a central root with long lateral roots.
panels.old_world_comparison: Dorstenia foetida, northeastern tropical Africa and Arabia. Both have a discrete flower receptacle, and the reported deeply lobed leaves of D. contrajerva fit better than the typically narrow, simple leaves of D. foetida. The drawing leaves the receptacle geometry and root comparison uncertain.

detail.statement: I masked Tucker and Talbert's proposed plant names and viewed eight numbered Yale scans. I recorded exposure before viewing and hashed the local observations before revealing the selection key. I excluded both earlier samples, the familiar f9v and f53r drawings, and several additional familiar folios. I had previously screened the paper and could recognize a few folio numbers and unusual features, including the animal on f25v. Four hits in the full-paper folio-string sampler were ineligible: f13v and f39r refer to the Codex Osuna and f25v and f49r are used for animal comparisons. The four actual plant proposals gave 0 of 4 genus matches and 1 of 4 family matches using Tucker and Talbert's broad Boraginaceae. With the narrower split of Boraginales the family agreement becomes 0 of 4. Guesses were low confidence and included no species. I then compared each published proposal with a morphologically relevant Old World member of its genus or family. The post-reveal comparisons find shared traits and mismatches on both sides. The elevated star-like structure on f42v favors Goeppertia loeseneri over the one African comparison, without establishing a species identification. Candidate exposure and the small sample limit the value of the agreement count. A word-to-plant pairing would require separate evidence from the scan.

statement: I masked Tucker and Talbert's proposed plant names and viewed eight numbered Yale scans. I recorded exposure before viewing and hashed the local observations before revealing the selection key. I excluded both earlier samples, the familiar f9v and f53r drawings, and several additional familiar folios. I had previously screened the paper and could recognize a few folio numbers and unusual features, including the animal on f25v. Four hits in the full-paper folio-string sampler were ineligible: f13v and f39r refer to the Codex Osuna and f25v and f49r are used for animal comparisons. The four actual plant proposals gave 0 of 4 genus matches and 1 of 4 family matches using Tucker and Talbert's broad Boraginaceae. With the narrower split of Boraginales the family agreement becomes 0 of 4. Guesses were low confidence and included no species. I then compared each published proposal with a morphologically relevant Old World member of its genus or family. The post-reveal comparisons find shared traits and mismatches on both sides. The elevated star-like structure on f42v favors Goeppertia loeseneri over the one African comparison, without establishing a species identification. Candidate exposure and the small sample limit the value of the agreement count. A word-to-plant pairing would require separate evidence from the scan.

experiment.json.summary: Report candidate-masked family and genus guesses and Old World comparisons on four further herbal drawings.

Compare the first guesses with the declared taxonomic scope and list ambiguous families separately. sample.method: Sampled eight surviving Yale canvases with Python Random(53185).sample in manifest order from folio mentions in K-015 in the 2–56 range, after excluding f1r/v, f2r, f5v, f6v, f9r/v, f12v, f13r, f23v, f24r, f25r, f30v, f32r, f33v, f37v, f45r and f53r. The article was used as a location sampler, with no surrounding text visible until all guesses were written.

panels.features: Very deeply divided palmate-looking leaves, upright and drooping clusters of small round bodies, and a central root with long lateral roots.
panels.old_world_comparison: Dorstenia foetida, northeastern tropical Africa and Arabia. Both have a discrete flower receptacle, and the reported deeply lobed leaves of D. contrajerva fit better than the typically narrow, simple leaves of D. foetida. The drawing leaves the receptacle geometry and root comparison uncertain.
sources: https://www.worldfloraonline.org/taxon/wfo-0000654354
https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:851554-1/general-information

panels.features: Fan-shaped deeply lobed leaves, upright branched sprays of blue five-part flowers, and a stout horizontal underground-looking axis.
panels.old_world_comparison: Ribes alpinum, Europe and adjacent regions. Both have palmately lobed leaves. The upright sprays in the drawing are closer in orientation to R. alpinum's erect racemes than to R. malvaceum's pendent racemes. Neither description accounts for the drawn blue corollas with round pale centers or clearly explains the depicted underground axis.
sources: https://www.worldfloraonline.org/taxon/wfo-0001135609
https://hrcak.srce.hr/en/file/486144
https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/85/British_Flora_%28IA_in.ernet.dli.2015.47855%29.pdf

panels.candidate: Calathea allied to C. loeseneri, now Goeppertia loeseneri, Marantaceae
panels.features: Large oval leaves clustered at one level, a solitary star-like terminal structure with a dark center, and several long diverging roots.
panels.old_world_comparison: Thaumatococcus daniellii, tropical Africa. Both have broad long-stalked foliage. G. loeseneri has a star-like inflorescence raised on its own stalk. T. daniellii flowers in spikes near the base. The comparison supports testing the raised star feature with more alternatives and leaves the drawn root form unresolved.
sources: https://www.nparks.gov.sg/florafaunaweb/flora/1/7/1749
https://www.nparks.gov.sg/florafaunaweb/flora/2/5/2504

panels.candidate: Phacelia campanularia, Boraginaceae in the broad sense
panels.features: Paired fan-like basal organs, one-sided dark bodies on a coiled branch, two dark corollas, and overlapping narrow scales low on the stem.
panels.masked_guess: Heliotropium, Boraginaceae in the broad sense
panels.old_world_comparison: Anchusa officinalis, native to Europe. Coiled flowering axes and blue corollas occur in both candidates. The precise outlines of the drawing's foliage and the basal scales are difficult to reconcile with an ordinary leaf arrangement in either comparison. The family match here uses the broad grouping, which includes Hydrophyllaceae and Heliotropiaceae.
