picture.json.statement: Annotated blind from the Beinecke scan only (canvas 1006209, '75v'). Upper drawing: a patterned tube descends from the top margin into a long blue scalloped vessel with two radiating bursts; ten two-line label tags hang from the vessel, each on a thin line that ends on the head of one of ten bare-breasted female figures standing in a long green trough (left four face right, the fifth faces the viewer, the right five face left). Lower drawing: a blue pool of two joined basins holding about 19 nude female figures, fed by a blue tube down the left margin and drained by a blue tube to the bottom edge. Label assignment: the label line ids f75v.18-.37 come in ten @/+ pairs, and there are ten tags; I assign tag i (counted left to right on the scan) to lines f75v.(16+2i) and .(17+2i), giving the first line id as 'label'. This assumes the transcription numbers the tags left to right; I did not read any words to check it. The seven short labels around the pool (f75v.50-.56 by line structure: three on one level, then four stacked) do not point at single figures and are left unassigned. Lines f75v.2-.11 marked as labels sit level with the top paragraph lines and are not tied to any drawn object here.

detail.authors: Claire L. Bowern and Daniel E. Gaskell

data.detail: The public companion matrix contains 814 transformed rows across 37 underlying source labels and 22 named transformations. The figures and Methods refer to the paper's own comparison counts.

established: Section 2 and Table 1 distinguish reversible additions or substitutions from transformations that remove information. The panel includes a Crema-inspired reversal with nulls, alternatives replacing letters with bigraphs, and reductions of vowels or consonants.

Figures 1–3 and Section 4 report that some transformations approach particular manuscript features. For instance, vowel removal in an Uzbek example comes close on some position summaries and remains far away on entropy. The distances vary across Latin sources under the same transformation, and manuscript renderings are closer to each other than the comparison items shown in Figure 2.

The exploratory comparison uses 200-word excerpts at 100 iterations and a common feature family. The discussion records that no tested transformation matches the feature set throughout, and treats altered-text comparisons as evidence that several word-level statistics can coexist with known-source text.

open.check: Freeze reversible addB and the unambiguous suffix-addition rules from Table 1. Use known texts and report held-apart entropy in bits per output symbol and bits per source symbol at context lengths zero through eight. Keep word and line breaks unchanged. Match output alphabet and expansion rate in independent random-padding, deterministic-padding and substitution controls. Verify exact inversion and compare across disjoint source works before drawing a conclusion.
open.question: Does the fall in measured character entropy under reversible symbol expansion persist when normalized by the length of the original source, and does it remain unusual against matched padding and substitution controls?

detail.summary: The open companion to K-012 applies 22 orthographic transformations to known texts and compares 42 released features. It includes reversible encipherment and deliberately lossy symbol conflation. The authors compare z-scored Euclidean distances and document how results depend on the underlying language and source text.

detail.statement: Pharmaceutical-style page in four rows, each starting with a tall red two-section jar with a green lid at the left margin and writing on it. Row 1: 12 separate roots or root-like parts (one a cluster of six open tubes, one a long segmented root with many leg-like rootlets). Row 2: 7 parts (a figure-eight twist, an arch, a bulb with a V-shaped sprout, a stack of coils, a root with a fan of spikes, a small tuft, a large root with tendrils). Row 3: 7 parts (crossed speckled legs, a dark red dripping bulb, a tailed root, a stack of bands, an S-shaped hairy rhizome, a curled banded part, a broom-like fibre mass under one large green leaf); the third jar stands on three short curled feet. Row 4: one whole plant, a long segmented orange root with a thin stem branching to about eight arrow- or heart-shaped green leaves and two hanging dark red clusters. The transcription's container lines f99r.1, 19, 32, 45 are given to the four jars, since each is written on its jar; the single part line of row 4 (f99r.46) goes to the row-4 plant. Rows 1-3 have 12, 8 and 8 part labels (f99r.2-14 with one two-line label, 20-27, 33-40) for 12, 7 and 7 parts. Labels sit next to the stalks, but whether each belongs to the part on its left or its right could not be settled from the scan alone, so those parts carry their row's block as label_group and label null.

detail.statement: I looked at all twelve inner disks on the Yale scans myself, at 800 by 800 canvas pixels or better, marking everything written inside each disk and, separately, the ring of text around it. Seven of the twelve I had already described blind for the picture steps before reading this step (f70v2, f72v1, f72v2, f72v3, f73r and f73v as submitted annotations, f72r3 as an unsubmitted draft); the other five (f70v1, f71r, f71v, f72r1, f72r2) I looked at for this step, knowing its claim. Per centre, emblem as drawn, then writing inside the disk. f70v2, two fish: a Latin-script word between the fish; one Voynich word standing free to the right of the upper star, which is tethered to the upper fish; a second star below with no label. f70v1, a horned animal with a dark green wash eating from a green bush: a Latin-script word under the belly; nothing in Voynich script inside the disk, and no text ring hugging this disk. f71r, a pale horned animal eating a green plant: a Latin-script word on the body; a Voynich text ring around the disk; no freestanding Voynich word. f71v, a pale red horned animal at a basket of green: Latin-script word under the belly; text ring; none freestanding. f72r1, a dark red horned animal at a basket of green: the same arrangement; none freestanding. f72r2, a man in green and a woman in blue clasping hands: Latin-script word between them at knee height; text ring; none freestanding. f72r3, two crayfish-like animals: Latin-script word under the lower one; text ring; none freestanding. f72v3, a four-legged animal with a curled tail: Latin-script word beneath; text ring; none freestanding. f72v2, a clothed figure holding a star: Latin-script word beside the figure; text ring; the star inside the disk has no label. f72v1, a balance: Latin-script word beneath; text ring; none freestanding. f73r, a dark green animal with a looped tail and a tethered star above it: Latin-script word beneath, touching the text ring; the star has no label. f73v, a clothed figure with a crossbow: Latin-script word at the feet, close to the text ring; none freestanding. Result: I find the same single freestanding Voynich string as the step, on f70v2, beside the upper star and separated from the Latin-script word by the upper fish, with no line joining the two. Two things the step does not say and the scans show: the other two centre stars (the lower one on f70v2 and the one on f73r) and the star held on f72v2 carry no label at all, so the f70v2 label looks like an ordinary star label that happens to sit inside the disk, not a caption for the emblem; and on f70v1 the disk has no text ring of its own, so there the Latin-script word is the only writing near the emblem. I did not read or compare the spellings of the Latin-script words and take no view on their date or language. Limits: I knew the step's claim for five of the twelve; and where the Latin-script word touches the ring text (f73r, f73v) I judged by eye that no ring word is set apart for it, which a second reviewer could dispute.

detail.statement: What I checked, from line ids and unit codes only (no words read, no candidate mansion names consulted): in ZL3b, RF1b, IT2a and GC2a, f69v consists of 3 circular text lines followed by exactly 28 radial lines, f69v.4 to f69v.31 (unit R). So the 28-fold division is also recorded by four independent transcribers as 28 text sectors, not only as the 28 bars counted visually (P-L4-002, and fleet-blue's second count). This still earns no support for any tradition: 28 is the common lunar-mansion count. The ordered test the step asks for splits into three sub-steps, to be taken in order by different seats. (A) [DONE here] Freeze the Voynich sequence: export f69v.4-.31 from all four transliterations with their ids, establish on the scan where f69v.4 sits and in which direction the numbering runs, and commit that file BEFORE any seat on (B) or (C) looks at named sequences. (B) Masked visual coding: two readers who have not seen candidate traditions code a fixed feature list on f69v and on each comparator image with captions and provenance masked: number of sectors; colour alternation (yes/no, period); marks per sector (count of dots or stars); text per sector (yes/no); number of concentric bands; position of any distinguished sector. Agreement between the two readers is reported before any comparison. (C) Ordered comparison, pre-registered: for each tradition (Bundahishn II.2, an Arabic manzil list, the Latin list of Countway MS 20), freeze the 28 names in its own order, one transliteration rule into EVA-like letters, and one similarity score per sector (e.g. normalised edit similarity of the first two glyphs). The statistic is the best mean similarity over all 56 alignments (28 rotations x 2 directions). Controls: the same maximum computed for 1,000 lists of 28 names drawn from the same tradition's vocabulary matched for length and letter frequency, and for the Voynich sequence shuffled within itself. A tradition passes only if its maximum exceeds the 99th percentile of both controls; report every tradition, including those that fail. Sub-step (A), done in this experiment by a seat that has not consulted any mansion-name list: ZL3b annotates each radial line with a clock position; f69v.4 is at 09:30 and the positions increase clockwise through 00:00 to f69v.31 at 08:45, so the numbering runs clockwise from roughly nine-thirty. Transliterations agree on most lines; differences are noted in place (e.g. f69v.4 okeey/okchy, f69v.8 ytory/ytary, f69v.15 oteeys/okeeys). (B) and (C) should take this sequence as fixed.

detail.check: On the public pages: for every page with at least three label words and thirty other words, the share of label words (three or more glyphs, certain) found in the page's own non-label text, against label sets dealt among pages of the same section; then the same own-page against other-page comparison for a held-out paragraph line. The claim fails if the label ratio clearly exceeds the ordinary-word ratio once words are matched for length and frequency more finely than five bins, or if a second transliteration gives a label effect at p below 0.01.
detail.statement: The third statistic proposed in P-L4-013 (a label word recurs in its own page's running text more than in other pages') needs no picture annotation, so I measured it now on the public practice pages only (226 pages; nothing from the hidden pages). Selection: the 46 public pages with at least three label words and at least thirty words of other text (15 pharmaceutical, 12 zodiac, 10 biological, 5 astronomical, 3 cosmological, 1 text), 886 label words of three or more glyphs with no uncertain reading. Statistic: the share of label words that occur somewhere in the non-label text of their own page. Null: the same share after the label sets are dealt to other pages of the same section, 999 deals. Result, exact word: 0.096 on the own page against a null mean of 0.085 (95th percentile 0.097), p = 0.079. Allowing one glyph of difference: 0.366 against 0.335 (95th percentile 0.361), p = 0.030 on 199 deals. By section, exact word, no section is significant on its own: astronomical 0.036 against 0.042, biological 0.200 against 0.190, cosmological 0.174 against 0.108, pharmaceutical 0.068 against 0.066, zodiac 0.091 against 0.074 (p from 0.11 to 0.75). So there is at most a weak page effect for labels, a ratio of about 1.13 to 1. The comparison that matters: ordinary words show a page effect at least as strong as labels do. Holding out the last paragraph line of every public page with six or more paragraph lines (925 words), 0.351 of its words occur in the rest of their own page, against 0.267 in the rest of another page of the same section, a ratio of about 1.32 to 1. Matched for frequency (five bins of how often a word occurs in the public running text, ordinary words reweighted to the labels' mix; the other-page rate here is the average over all other pages of the section, so the label figures differ slightly from the deal above), the ratios are 1.21 for labels (0.096 against 0.080) and 1.35 for ordinary words (0.144 against 0.107). Bin by bin the picture is mixed: among fairly common words (11 to 40 occurrences) labels have the higher ratio, 0.198 against 0.110 where ordinary words have 0.199 against 0.134; among the commonest (over 40) labels show almost none, 0.378 against 0.367 where ordinary words have 0.681 against 0.512. Half of the label words (448 of 886) occur at most once anywhere in the public running text and so can hardly recur on their page at all. This is the page-vocabulary effect already on the record (F-009), and meaningless procedures with a local memory reproduce it. Consequence for P-L4-013: statistic (3) as worded measures page vocabulary, not reference. A procedure that writes labels with the same memory it uses for the text would pass it at least as well as the manuscript does, and the manuscript's own labels pass it only marginally. It should not be registered as a fact meant to separate language from meaningless text unless it is redefined against that baseline, for example as the excess of the label recurrence ratio over the ratio for ordinary words of the same length and frequency on the same pages, where on the public pages the manuscript's labels do not rise above ordinary words. Statistics (1) and (2) are not touched by this; they need agreed annotations, which do not exist yet. Limits: one transliteration (ZL), public pages only, the frequency match is coarse (five bins) and does not match word length, the bin-by-bin counts are small (65 to 448 labels per bin), and the section deal keeps page sizes with the text, not with the labels. Addendum: a first look at statistic (2), with object kinds that need no annotation. The transliteration's own locus types separate labels written on a container from labels beside a detached plant part, and twelve public pharmaceutical pages carry both (36 container labels, 141 plant-part labels, labels with an uncertain reading left out). If labels named their objects, labels of the two kinds might differ in form on the same page. Eight features of form were compared, each against the two tags shuffled within the page (2000 shuffles, two-sided): glyphs per label 6.9 against 6.1 (p = 0.07), words per label 1.00 against 1.09 (p = 0.10), first glyph o 0.53 against 0.57 (p = 0.70), opening ok or ot 0.39 against 0.37 (p = 0.84), final y 0.50 against 0.44 (p = 0.59), final l or r 0.08 against 0.23 (p = 0.05), a pedestalled gallows 0.03 against 0.03 (p = 1.0), first glyph d or s 0.14 against 0.19 (p = 0.44). The smallest of eight p values is 0.05, which is what eight unrelated comparisons give by chance about one time in three; nothing here survives the number of comparisons. So on the public pages a label's form does not tell a jar from a root. That is a null on a small sample (36 container labels), chosen features and one transliteration, not evidence of no meaning: names of containers and of plants need not differ in their first or last glyph. It does mean statistic (2) should be registered with the features fixed in advance and with the expectation, on this evidence, that it may well fail for the manuscript itself. Second addendum, the nearest thing the transliteration alone offers to the proposal's 'labels share roots with the text about the same object'. On the pharmaceutical pages each row opens with a jar and is followed by the plant parts drawn beside it; if a jar's label named a preparation and the parts' labels its ingredients, or the reverse, a jar's label might resemble the labels of its own row more than those of another row. Nine public pages have two or more such rows with clean readings (28 rows, 130 plant-part labels). Similarity is one minus edit distance over the longer length; null: the jars' labels dealt among the rows of their own page (3000 deals). Jar against all labels of its row: 0.244 against 0.253 under the null (p = 0.72). Jar against the first object of its row, the one drawn next to it: 0.263 against 0.257 (p = 0.39). No sign that a jar's label is related in form to the labels beside it. Together with the label-recurrence and jar-against-root results above, three text-only versions of the picture-text predictions come out null on the public pages. That is what a meaningless procedure would give; it is also what a language would give if labels are unrelated names, so these nulls do not discriminate either, and the proposal's statistics need a planted positive control (an invented-language page where labels do share roots) to show they could detect the effect at these sample sizes before a null on the manuscript is read as evidence. Third addendum: the planted control for the jar-and-row test, run on the same nine pages. I rewrote a share of each row's plant-part labels so that they begin with the first glyphs of their own jar's label, left everything else as it is, and reran the test forty times per setting (300 deals each, detection at p of 0.05 or less). Sharing the first two glyphs: a share of 0.1 is detected in 0 of 40 runs, 0.2 in 4, 0.3 in 22, 0.5 in 40. Sharing the first three glyphs: 0.1 in 2 of 40, 0.2 in 24, 0.3 in 39. So the null above rules out a strong convention (half the row sharing a two-glyph root with the jar, or a third sharing a three-glyph root) and is silent on anything weaker: a language in which one label in five shared a short root with its jar would usually pass unnoticed on these nine pages. The hidden pages are fewer still, so a registered fact of this kind would have less power than this; it should be stated with its planted detection rates beside it. Fourth addendum: the planted control for the first measurement in this note (a label recurs in its own page's text), on the same 46 pages and 886 labels. I replaced a share of the labels with a word drawn from their own page's text among the words occurring there at most twice, and reran the test forty times per setting (200 deals each). A share of 0.02 raises the own-page rate from 0.096 to 0.114 and is detected in 40 of 40 runs; 0.05, 0.10 and 0.20 likewise in 40 of 40. Unlike the jar-and-row test, this one is sensitive: if even one label in fifty were a page-specific word of the text around it, beyond what the manuscript already shows, the test would see it. The manuscript's own excess is about one label in a hundred (0.096 against 0.085, p = 0.08). So on the public pages the labels are, almost without exception, not the distinctive words of the text on their page: either the text does not name the labelled objects with the label's word, or it names them with common words, or the labels and text are unrelated. This is the most informative of the nulls in this note, and it bears on the reading of labels as plant or star names that the paragraph beside them then discusses. It remains one transliteration, exact-word matching, and exact-word matching only. I then ran the plant I had expected to be harder, labels replaced by a word drawn from their page's text in proportion to how often it occurs there, common words included: shares of 0.02, 0.05 and 0.10 are again each detected in 40 of 40 runs (own-page rate 0.112, 0.141, 0.188). So the test would also see labels taken from the common words of their page at one label in fifty; my expectation that this would be harder was wrong. Fifth addendum, removing the one-transliteration limit on the first measurement. The same test on the other pinned transliterations of the public pages: Takahashi 0.102 own page against 0.086 dealt (45 pages, 894 labels, p = 0.017); the RF transliteration 0.073 against 0.067 (45 pages, 759 labels, p = 0.225); Zandbergen-Landini on a fresh set of deals 0.096 against 0.085 (p = 0.071). So the three readings agree on a small positive excess, between half a label and a label and a half in a hundred, significant at 0.05 in one of the three and nowhere at 0.01. I had written above that the claim would fail if a second transliteration gave p below 0.01; it does not, but Takahashi comes closer than my summary of 'barely more than chance' allowed, and the fair statement is: a small excess that may be real, of a size (about one label in a hundred) that page vocabulary alone would explain, and far below what the planted controls show a naming relation of even one label in fifty would produce. By section in the three readings (own page against dealt, 1999 deals): no section reaches 0.05 in any reading. The zodiac pages are the most consistent (0.091 against 0.074, 0.100 against 0.079, 0.065 against 0.054; p = 0.11, 0.06, 0.23), and that is where labels and the ring text share a page most closely; the pharmaceutical pages, where labels would most naturally be ingredient names taken up in the recipe text, show nothing (0.068 against 0.067, 0.075 against 0.071, 0.044 against 0.050), and the astronomical pages nothing or less.

That is a null on a small sample (36 container labels), chosen features and one transliteration, not evidence of no meaning: names of containers and of plants need not differ in their first or last glyph. It does mean statistic (2) should be registered with the features fixed in advance and with the expectation, on this evidence, that it may well fail for the manuscript itself. Second addendum, the nearest thing the transliteration alone offers to the proposal's 'labels share roots with the text about the same object'. On the pharmaceutical pages each row opens with a jar and is followed by the plant parts drawn beside it; if a jar's label named a preparation and the parts' labels its ingredients, or the reverse, a jar's label might resemble the labels of its own row more than those of another row. Nine public pages have two or more such rows with clean readings (28 rows, 130 plant-part labels). Similarity is one minus edit distance over the longer length; null: the jars' labels dealt among the rows of their own page (3000 deals). Jar against all labels of its row: 0.244 against 0.253 under the null (p = 0.72). Jar against the first object of its row, the one drawn next to it: 0.263 against 0.257 (p = 0.39). No sign that a jar's label is related in form to the labels beside it. Together with the label-recurrence and jar-against-root results above, three text-only versions of the picture-text predictions come out null on the public pages. That is what a meaningless procedure would give; it is also what a language would give if labels are unrelated names, so these nulls do not discriminate either, and the proposal's statistics need a planted positive control (an invented-language page where labels do share roots) to show they could detect the effect at these sample sizes before a null on the manuscript is read as evidence. Third addendum: the planted control for the jar-and-row test, run on the same nine pages. I rewrote a share of each row's plant-part labels so that they begin with the first glyphs of their own jar's label, left everything else as it is, and reran the test forty times per setting (300 deals each, detection at p of 0.05 or less). Sharing the first two glyphs: a share of 0.1 is detected in 0 of 40 runs, 0.2 in 4, 0.3 in 22, 0.5 in 40. Sharing the first three glyphs: 0.1 in 2 of 40, 0.2 in 24, 0.3 in 39. So the null above rules out a strong convention (half the row sharing a two-glyph root with the jar, or a third sharing a three-glyph root) and is silent on anything weaker: a language in which one label in five shared a short root with its jar would usually pass unnoticed on these nine pages. The hidden pages are fewer still, so a registered fact of this kind would have less power than this; it should be stated with its planted detection rates beside it. Fourth addendum: the planted control for the first measurement in this note (a label recurs in its own page's text), on the same 46 pages and 886 labels. I replaced a share of the labels with a word drawn from their own page's text among the words occurring there at most twice, and reran the test forty times per setting (200 deals each). A share of 0.02 raises the own-page rate from 0.096 to 0.114 and is detected in 40 of 40 runs; 0.05, 0.10 and 0.20 likewise in 40 of 40. Unlike the jar-and-row test, this one is sensitive: if even one label in fifty were a page-specific word of the text around it, beyond what the manuscript already shows, the test would see it. The manuscript's own excess is about one label in a hundred (0.096 against 0.085, p = 0.08). So on the public pages the labels are, almost without exception, not the distinctive words of the text on their page: either the text does not name the labelled objects with the label's word, or it names them with common words, or the labels and text are unrelated. This is the most informative of the nulls in this note, and it bears on the reading of labels as plant or star names that the paragraph beside them then discusses. It remains one transliteration, exact-word matching, and exact-word matching only. I then ran the plant I had expected to be harder, labels replaced by a word drawn from their page's text in proportion to how often it occurs there, common words included: shares of 0.02, 0.05 and 0.10 are again each detected in 40 of 40 runs (own-page rate 0.112, 0.141, 0.188). So the test would also see labels taken from the common words of their page at one label in fifty; my expectation that this would be harder was wrong. Fifth addendum, removing the one-transliteration limit on the first measurement. The same test on the other pinned transliterations of the public pages: Takahashi 0.102 own page against 0.086 dealt (45 pages, 894 labels, p = 0.017); the RF transliteration 0.073 against 0.067 (45 pages, 759 labels, p = 0.225); Zandbergen-Landini on a fresh set of deals 0.096 against 0.085 (p = 0.071). So the three readings agree on a small positive excess, between half a label and a label and a half in a hundred, significant at 0.05 in one of the three and nowhere at 0.01. I had written above that the claim would fail if a second transliteration gave p below 0.01; it does not, but Takahashi comes closer than my summary of 'barely more than chance' allowed, and the fair statement is: a small excess that may be real, of a size (about one label in a hundred) that page vocabulary alone would explain, and far below what the planted controls show a naming relation of even one label in fifty would produce. By section in the three readings (own page against dealt, 1999 deals): no section reaches 0.05 in any reading. The zodiac pages are the most consistent (0.091 against 0.074, 0.100 against 0.079, 0.065 against 0.054; p = 0.11, 0.06, 0.23), and that is where labels and the ring text share a page most closely; the pharmaceutical pages, where labels would most naturally be ingredient names taken up in the recipe text, show nothing (0.068 against 0.067, 0.075 against 0.071, 0.044 against 0.050), and the astronomical pages nothing or less.

check: From data/raw/ZL3b-n.txt take, for each label line of a ring page, the first marker of the form <!hh:mm>; it is the clock position of the labelled figure. Pair a ring's figures with its label lines by nearest clock position, keeping the clockwise order. Re-key existing ring annotations by that rule (their authors can do it from their own recorded clock positions without looking at the scan again) and re-measure agreement between seats on label-matched objects. The correction above fails if, for any of the twelve rings, shifting my pairing by the stated number does not bring the mean distance between figure and marked position under half a figure's spacing. For the instructions: say in join.txt that ring labels are to be paired by the clock markers, which are layout notes and not words, so that using them does not break blindness.

detail.statement: In six blind picture annotations of zodiac wheels (f70v2, f72v1, f72v2, f72v3, f73r, f73v) I paired each ring's label lines with its figures clockwise from twelve o'clock and said in each statement that the starting point was an assumption. After submitting all of them I checked the assumption against the pinned Zandbergen-Landini file. The file settles it without anyone reading a word: every figure-label line on the zodiac pages carries a clock-position marker for its figure (299 marked label lines on 13 folios; the page notes say 'Clock position is that of nymph'). On those markers the direction I assumed is right, clockwise, and the starting point is wrong on eleven of my twelve rings. The first label of a ring sits between about a quarter to nine and half past eleven, never at twelve. Ring by ring (figures in the ring, clock position of the first label, how many of my pairings fall within half a figure's spacing of the marked position, and the shift k, meaning that the figure I numbered j, counting clockwise from twelve o'clock, should carry the label line I gave to figure j minus k, wrapping round the ring): f70v2 outer: 19 figures, first label at 9 o'clock, 0 of 19 of my pairings right, shift by 14; f70v2 inner: 10 figures, first label at 10 o'clock, 0 of 10 of my pairings right, shift by 8; f72v1 outer: 20 figures, first label at 8.75 o'clock, 0 of 20 of my pairings right, shift by 14; f72v1 inner: 10 figures, first label at 8.75 o'clock, 0 of 10 of my pairings right, shift by 7; f72v2 outer: 18 figures, first label at 10 o'clock, 0 of 18 of my pairings right, shift by 16; f72v2 inner: 12 figures, first label at 10.5 o'clock, 0 of 12 of my pairings right, shift by 10; f72v3 outer: 18 figures, first label at 10 o'clock, 0 of 18 of my pairings right, shift by 15; f72v3 inner: 12 figures, first label at 10.5 o'clock, 0 of 12 of my pairings right, shift by 10; f73r outer: 16 figures, first label at 11 o'clock, 0 of 16 of my pairings right, shift by 14; f73r inner: 10 figures, first label at 11.5 o'clock, 9 of 10 of my pairings right, shift by 0; f73v outer: 16 figures, first label at 10 o'clock, 0 of 16 of my pairings right, shift by 13; f73v inner: 10 figures, first label at 9.5 o'clock, 0 of 10 of my pairings right, shift by 8. After the shift the mean distance between my figure positions and the marked positions is 0.15 to 0.46 of an hour, so the counts and the clockwise order agree and only the start was off. So on eleven rings every one of my figure-to-label pairings is wrong by a constant rotation; only the inner ring of f73r (nine of ten) and the four figures on top of f73r and f73v, which I paired left to right and which the markers place from about eleven to one o'clock in that order, stand as submitted. What is not affected: the drawings as described, the ring counts, and the assignment of label groups to rings. The markers also confirm two things I had inferred: the group sizes per ring (for example 12, 11 and 7 on f72r3 from the outside in), and which wheel is which on the two-wheel verso canvas (the page notes give the animal wheel as f72v3 and the clothed-figure wheel as f72v2, as I had them). Where features were recorded figure by figure and so travel with the pairing (the blue caps and tub patterns of the f70v2 outer ring, the crown on f72v1, the postures of the f72r3 inner ring in my unsubmitted draft), the corrected label is the submitted one shifted by the number above. The same check should be made on every other seat's ring annotations before any picture-text test uses them: two seats can agree with each other on a pairing and both be rotated. One more of my submitted folios is touched, with weaker evidence: f67r2 has no clock markers, but its page notes number the twelve sectors from the one between nine and ten o'clock, clockwise, and say the sector text starts at ten o'clock. I paired the twelve red outer labels and the twelve moon labels from twelve o'clock, so those pairings are probably rotated by about three places as well; the notes do not say where the moon labels start, so I checked that ring on the scan (canvas 1006194, region 3450,850,800,500), reading the words now that the blind annotation is in: the red moon at twelve o'clock has the word of f67r2.54 under it, the yellow moon at one o'clock the word of f67r2.55, and the red moon at two o'clock the word of f67r2.56. So the moon labels run clockwise from the moon at ten o'clock, and my submitted pairing of that ring is off by two places (the moon I gave line n carries line n plus two, wrapping from 63 to 52). With that pairing and the colour order on which three seats agree, the red moons carry lines 52, 54, 56, 59, 60 and 62 and the yellow moons 53, 55, 57, 58, 61 and 63. Their labels do not divide by colour in form: labels of the same colour share their first two or last two glyphs in 0.13 of pairs, labels of different colours in 0.19 (p = 0.89 against random halves), and first glyphs are split evenly. Twelve labels cannot show much either way. The red outer labels of the sectors I did not check on the scan; they stay probably rotated, by the page notes. For f99r the same file settles the two places I had flagged as ambiguous, again without any reading of words: each label line there carries an object number from an older catalogue of the drawings, with a letter where several labels belong to one object. By those numbers the twelve, seven and seven detached objects I counted in rows 1 to 3 are right, the two-line label in row 1 is one object's (f99r.6 and f99r.7), and the spare label in each of rows 2 and 3 belongs with its neighbour as I had it (f99r.25 with f99r.26 on the sixth object of row 2, f99r.33 with f99r.34 on the first object of row 3). So my f99r pairing stands as submitted, and the three seats who paired every object there differ only in which line of such a pair they named. My other submitted folios (f66r, f68r1, f75v, f99r) have no ring pairing; the page notes agree with how I read the label groups on f66r and f75v and say nothing on the order of the star labels on f68r1. For that page I compared the first seven label lines with the words beside the uppermost stars on the scan, as far as I can read them at 1700 pixels: the transcription takes the stars in loose rows, left to right within a row (the two stars beside the sun, then the five of the next row from the left edge to the right), whereas I numbered strictly by height. My pairing is therefore right for the first three stars and wrong inside the second row (my stars 4 to 7), and very likely wrong inside the lower rows too; I then carried the check through at higher resolution (five tiles of canvas 1006196 at about 1700 pixels each), matching each star's word to the transliteration by eye. Result, as label line for each star in my submitted numbering 1 to 29: 8, 9, 10, 13, 14, 11, 12, 17, 18, 15, 16 for the first eleven (so the transcription does run in rows, but the right-hand pair of a row comes after the left-hand ones only loosely), and for the bottom of the page line 31 for the dark-dotted star at the left edge, 32 for the star whose label stands on its left, 33 and 35 for the two ring-centred stars, 34 for the one between them and 36 for the lowest star. The middle of the page I could match with less confidence: lines 19 to 22 go to the four stars of the fourth row from the left edge to the large star, 27, 28, 29 and 30 to the row below, and lines 23 to 26 to the four remaining stars (the one at the left edge of the third row, the two at the right of the fourth row, and the one at the left edge of the fifth) in an order I could not settle. With that pairing the eight ring-centred stars carry lines 14, 15, 17, 18, 30, 33, 35 and one of 24 to 26, and the two dark-dotted stars lines 20 and 31. Their labels do not stand apart from the other stars' labels: the nine with a certain reading share their first two or last two glyphs in 0.31 of pairs against 0.27 for nine labels drawn at random from the page (p = 0.33), and mean length, final y and pedestalled gallows are alike in both groups. So the centre mark, which three seats recorded the same way, predicts nothing visible in the label on this page; twenty-eight labels cannot show a small effect. My submitted f68r1 pairing is wrong for most stars and should be replaced by this one, with lines 23 to 26 marked uncertain. A first use of the rule, on the one ring feature all four seats on the record wrote down for f70v2: which outer figures wear a blue cap. Read in each seat's own clockwise order the four sequences are the same pattern (one capped figure, one bare, five capped, the other twelve bare); two seats began at twelve o'clock and two at the top left, two figures earlier, and once each sequence is laid on the marked clock positions all four agree on all nineteen figures. By the alignment with the least total clock distance the capped figures are the ones labelled by lines f70v2.8 and f70v2.10 to f70v2.14; the seats' clock estimates are coarse, so a slip of one figure was possible, and I checked it on the scan (canvas 1006200, region 1900,500,1500,1500), this time reading the words, which is allowed now that the blind annotation is in: the first capped figure has the word of f70v2.8 beside it, the bare figure after it the word of f70v2.9, and the next three capped figures the words of f70v2.10, 11 and 12, each word standing by its own figure's star. So the first reading is the right one, and the shift of fourteen figures given above for this ring is confirmed on the scan for these five figures. So with a closed feature and the clock rule, independent seats agree completely where the record's score for the same four annotations is 0.41 to 0.75. And a first, very small look at the second statistic of P-L4-013 (figures that share a feature have labels that share glyph groups): the six capped figures' labels share their first two or last two glyphs in 0.13 of pairs, against 0.40 for six labels drawn at random from the ring, and this is the lowest of the nineteen values obtained by sliding the same one-gap-five pattern round the ring. On this one ring the feature predicts nothing about the labels, if anything the reverse; six figures on one page cannot carry more than that. Having read the page notes for this check, I have now seen the transcription's descriptions of f70v1, f71r, f71v, f72r1 and f72r2 and should not be given those folios as blind picture steps.

Ring by ring (figures in the ring, clock position of the first label, how many of my pairings fall within half a figure's spacing of the marked position, and the shift k, meaning that the figure I numbered j, counting clockwise from twelve o'clock, should carry the label line I gave to figure j minus k, wrapping round the ring): f70v2 outer: 19 figures, first label at 9 o'clock, 0 of 19 of my pairings right, shift by 14; f70v2 inner: 10 figures, first label at 10 o'clock, 0 of 10 of my pairings right, shift by 8; f72v1 outer: 20 figures, first label at 8.75 o'clock, 0 of 20 of my pairings right, shift by 14; f72v1 inner: 10 figures, first label at 8.75 o'clock, 0 of 10 of my pairings right, shift by 7; f72v2 outer: 18 figures, first label at 10 o'clock, 0 of 18 of my pairings right, shift by 16; f72v2 inner: 12 figures, first label at 10.5 o'clock, 0 of 12 of my pairings right, shift by 10; f72v3 outer: 18 figures, first label at 10 o'clock, 0 of 18 of my pairings right, shift by 15; f72v3 inner: 12 figures, first label at 10.5 o'clock, 0 of 12 of my pairings right, shift by 10; f73r outer: 16 figures, first label at 11 o'clock, 0 of 16 of my pairings right, shift by 14; f73r inner: 10 figures, first label at 11.5 o'clock, 9 of 10 of my pairings right, shift by 0; f73v outer: 16 figures, first label at 10 o'clock, 0 of 16 of my pairings right, shift by 13; f73v inner: 10 figures, first label at 9.5 o'clock, 0 of 10 of my pairings right, shift by 8. After the shift the mean distance between my figure positions and the marked positions is 0.15 to 0.46 of an hour, so the counts and the clockwise order agree and only the start was off. So on eleven rings every one of my figure-to-label pairings is wrong by a constant rotation; only the inner ring of f73r (nine of ten) and the four figures on top of f73r and f73v, which I paired left to right and which the markers place from about eleven to one o'clock in that order, stand as submitted. What is not affected: the drawings as described, the ring counts, and the assignment of label groups to rings. The markers also confirm two things I had inferred: the group sizes per ring (for example 12, 11 and 7 on f72r3 from the outside in), and which wheel is which on the two-wheel verso canvas (the page notes give the animal wheel as f72v3 and the clothed-figure wheel as f72v2, as I had them). Where features were recorded figure by figure and so travel with the pairing (the blue caps and tub patterns of the f70v2 outer ring, the crown on f72v1, the postures of the f72r3 inner ring in my unsubmitted draft), the corrected label is the submitted one shifted by the number above. The same check should be made on every other seat's ring annotations before any picture-text test uses them: two seats can agree with each other on a pairing and both be rotated. One more of my submitted folios is touched, with weaker evidence: f67r2 has no clock markers, but its page notes number the twelve sectors from the one between nine and ten o'clock, clockwise, and say the sector text starts at ten o'clock. I paired the twelve red outer labels and the twelve moon labels from twelve o'clock, so those pairings are probably rotated by about three places as well; the notes do not say where the moon labels start, so I checked that ring on the scan (canvas 1006194, region 3450,850,800,500), reading the words now that the blind annotation is in: the red moon at twelve o'clock has the word of f67r2.54 under it, the yellow moon at one o'clock the word of f67r2.55, and the red moon at two o'clock the word of f67r2.56. So the moon labels run clockwise from the moon at ten o'clock, and my submitted pairing of that ring is off by two places (the moon I gave line n carries line n plus two, wrapping from 63 to 52). With that pairing and the colour order on which three seats agree, the red moons carry lines 52, 54, 56, 59, 60 and 62 and the yellow moons 53, 55, 57, 58, 61 and 63. Their labels do not divide by colour in form: labels of the same colour share their first two or last two glyphs in 0.13 of pairs, labels of different colours in 0.19 (p = 0.89 against random halves), and first glyphs are split evenly. Twelve labels cannot show much either way. The red outer labels of the sectors I did not check on the scan; they stay probably rotated, by the page notes. For f99r the same file settles the two places I had flagged as ambiguous, again without any reading of words: each label line there carries an object number from an older catalogue of the drawings, with a letter where several labels belong to one object. By those numbers the twelve, seven and seven detached objects I counted in rows 1 to 3 are right, the two-line label in row 1 is one object's (f99r.6 and f99r.7), and the spare label in each of rows 2 and 3 belongs with its neighbour as I had it (f99r.25 with f99r.26 on the sixth object of row 2, f99r.33 with f99r.34 on the first object of row 3). For that page I compared the first seven label lines with the words beside the uppermost stars on the scan, as far as I can read them at 1700 pixels: the transcription takes the stars in loose rows, left to right within a row (the two stars beside the sun, then the five of the next row from the left edge to the right), whereas I numbered strictly by height. My pairing is therefore right for the first three stars and wrong inside the second row (my stars 4 to 7), and very likely wrong inside the lower rows too; I then carried the check through at higher resolution (five tiles of canvas 1006196 at about 1700 pixels each), matching each star's word to the transliteration by eye. Result, as label line for each star in my submitted numbering 1 to 29: 8, 9, 10, 13, 14, 11, 12, 17, 18, 15, 16 for the first eleven (so the transcription does run in rows, but the right-hand pair of a row comes after the left-hand ones only loosely), and for the bottom of the page line 31 for the dark-dotted star at the left edge, 32 for the star whose label stands on its left, 33 and 35 for the two ring-centred stars, 34 for the one between them and 36 for the lowest star. The middle of the page I could match with less confidence: lines 19 to 22 go to the four stars of the fourth row from the left edge to the large star, 27, 28, 29 and 30 to the row below, and lines 23 to 26 to the four remaining stars (the one at the left edge of the third row, the two at the right of the fourth row, and the one at the left edge of the fifth) in an order I could not settle. With that pairing the eight ring-centred stars carry lines 14, 15, 17, 18, 30, 33, 35 and one of 24 to 26, and the two dark-dotted stars lines 20 and 31. Their labels do not stand apart from the other stars' labels: the nine with a certain reading share their first two or last two glyphs in 0.31 of pairs against 0.27 for nine labels drawn at random from the page (p = 0.33), and mean length, final y and pedestalled gallows are alike in both groups. So the centre mark, which three seats recorded the same way, predicts nothing visible in the label on this page; twenty-eight labels cannot show a small effect. My submitted f68r1 pairing is wrong for most stars and should be replaced by this one, with lines 23 to 26 marked uncertain. A first use of the rule, on the one ring feature all four seats on the record wrote down for f70v2: which outer figures wear a blue cap. Read in each seat's own clockwise order the four sequences are the same pattern (one capped figure, one bare, five capped, the other twelve bare); two seats began at twelve o'clock and two at the top left, two figures earlier, and once each sequence is laid on the marked clock positions all four agree on all nineteen figures. By the alignment with the least total clock distance the capped figures are the ones labelled by lines f70v2.8 and f70v2.10 to f70v2.14; the seats' clock estimates are coarse, so a slip of one figure was possible, and I checked it on the scan (canvas 1006200, region 1900,500,1500,1500), this time reading the words, which is allowed now that the blind annotation is in: the first capped figure has the word of f70v2.8 beside it, the bare figure after it the word of f70v2.9, and the next three capped figures the words of f70v2.10, 11 and 12, each word standing by its own figure's star. So the first reading is the right one, and the shift of fourteen figures given above for this ring is confirmed on the scan for these five figures. So with a closed feature and the clock rule, independent seats agree completely where the record's score for the same four annotations is 0.41 to 0.75. And a first, very small look at the second statistic of P-L4-013 (figures that share a feature have labels that share glyph groups): the six capped figures' labels share their first two or last two glyphs in 0.13 of pairs, against 0.40 for six labels drawn at random from the ring, and this is the lowest of the nineteen values obtained by sliding the same one-gap-five pattern round the ring. On this one ring the feature predicts nothing about the labels, if anything the reverse; six figures on one page cannot carry more than that. detail.statement: An extension of P-L4-010 with calibrated positions instead of index order. ZL3b records a clock position (<!hh:mm>) on each label line of the circular zodiac pages; I used those as each label's angle, so no rotation is fitted and no figure-to-word association is guessed. Pages: f70v1, f70v2, f71r, f71v, f72r1, f72r2, f72r3, f72v1, f72v2, f72v3, f73r, f73v. Rings are the label runs between circular text lines, counted from the outside (ring k on one page is compared with ring k on another); label lines before the first circular text (figures outside the circle on f73r/f73v) are excluded; words with uncertainty marks are dropped, and a label is all its remaining words joined. For every pair of pages and every shared ring, each label is compared with the label nearest its angle on the other page, if within 15 degrees: 1,303 comparisons. Observed: 0 exact label matches and 9 exact-or-one-edit matches (eva-basic glyphs). Null: labels shuffled within each ring of each page, positions kept, 999 permutations: mean 1.72 exact and 12.44 near; p = 1.0 (exact) and 0.89 (near), i.e. matches are if anything fewer than chance. With a 30-degree window (1,344 comparisons, 299 permutations): 0 and 9 observed, null means 1.78 and 12.71, p = 1.0 and 0.91. Power check: planting one shared word at 0 degrees and another at 180 degrees in the outer ring of every page gives 96 exact matches against a null mean of 11.2, p = 0.0033 (the minimum with 299 permutations). So a roster repeated at fixed clock positions, even for only two positions, would have been seen; none is. This agrees with the index-based result in P-L4-010 and is free of its rotation search. Rotating rosters: the same comparison, but for every pair of pages and ring the second page is rotated in 15-degree steps (24 offsets) in both directions and the offset with the most near matches is kept; the null applies the same maximisation to labels shuffled within rings (999 permutations). Observed: 17 exact and 78 near matches in 1,302 comparisons; null means 15.04 and 77.84; p = 0.196 (exact) and 0.543 (near). Power check for this version: planting the same two words at 0 and 180 degrees shifted by 30 degrees more on each successive page (a roster that rotates with the sign) gives 146 exact matches against a null mean of 85.5, p = 0.005 (the minimum with 199 permutations). So neither a fixed nor a rotating roster shared across signs is present at even two positions. Not tested: rosters in a different order on each page (no fixed sequence), which no position test can see.

detail.statement: An independent rerun of P-L4-007's check with my own code. Differences from the original, fixed before running: I used only the figure-label loci (unit Lz) of the twelve zodiac pages, 299 labels (15 on f70v1, f71r, f71v, f72r1; 29 on f72r2; 30 on the rest, f70v2 including its one centre label) where the original used 350; glyph strings with word breaks removed; for each of the 66 page pairs the largest number of agreements over every cyclic offset of the longer page against the shorter, summed; 1,000 shuffles. Two nulls: labels shuffled over the whole page, and labels shuffled only inside their own ring (the groups the transcription marks). Same position, no offset, ZL3b: 1 agreement in 1,403 comparisons (0.07%). Best offset, exact, ZL3b: 27 against a null mean of 24.9 (p = 0.034 whole-page, 0.050 within-ring). Allowing one glyph of difference: 82 against 76.2 (p = 0.028 and 0.027). Other transliterations, whole-page and within-ring: IT2a exact 19 against 17.8 (p = 0.17, 0.18), one-glyph 82 against 75.2 (p = 0.025, 0.012); RF1b exact 20 against 20.5 (p = 1.0, 1.0), one-glyph 69 against 65.7 (p = 0.15, 0.15); GC2a exact 18 against 18.4 (p = 1.0, 1.0), one-glyph 75 against 72.9 (p = 0.27, 0.23). These are eight tests without correction, and the statistic hardly moves under shuffling (for exact agreement the best offset of most pairs is 1 whenever the two pages share any label, whatever the order), so a p of 1.0 only means the observed total sits at the floor. Power: writing four labels in the same order onto every 30-label page is detected in 20 of 20 trials. Where the ZL excess comes from: only two pairs have two or more exact agreements at one offset. f72r2 and f72v3 share one label twice. f73r and f73v, recto and verso of one leaf, share three labels at the same shift of one place: the 6th, 19th and 24th figure labels of f73r (loci f73r.7, f73r.20, f73r.26) equal the 5th, 18th and 23rd of f73v (loci f73v.6, f73v.19, f73v.25); ZL reads them okeody, okeos, oky on both pages. The first two lie in the outer ring and the third in the inner ring, each one place earlier on f73v than on f73r, and ZL's own clock positions for the three are later on f73r by one and a half to two hours each, so the shift looks like a rotation of the whole wheel, not a counting slip. For that pair alone, shuffling one page gives three or more agreements with p = 0.0045 (0.0009 within rings); multiplied by the 66 pairs examined that is 0.30. IT2a reads the same three. RF1b and GC2a agree on the middle one only: on f73v they read a variant glyph in the first word and a different gallows in the third (RF1b oty against oky), and that leaves them one label common to the two pages. Conclusion: I confirm P-L4-007. There is no list of labels repeating in order from sign to sign. The small nominal excess in ZL is one local coincidence on one leaf that depends on how three or four labels are transliterated, and it does not survive the number of pairs looked at. It is worth one look on the scan, since two of the three words differ between editions. Follow-up on the scan, done after the numbers: I looked at the six labels on the Yale canvases at full resolution (regions 1000,900,260,170 and 1500,1850,220,180 of canvas 1006206; 980,1150,260,200 and 1800,1330,220,160 of canvas 1006207; the two labels at f73r.20 and f73v.19 in wider crops). The long label at f73r.7 and the one at f73v.6 have the same outline (o, a two-legged gallows, a small curve, o, a looped glyph, y), and the short labels at f73r.26 and f73v.25 are both o, a gallows, y. But each label is only about a hundred pixels wide in the public scan, and at that size I cannot tell which gallows stands in the short label on f73v or whether the looped glyph in the long one is the ordinary form or the variant RF1b marks. So my look neither supports ZL's reading over RF1b's nor the reverse; the disputed glyphs need a higher-resolution image than this server gives.

Two nulls: labels shuffled over the whole page, and labels shuffled only inside their own ring (the groups the transcription marks). Same position, no offset, ZL3b: 1 agreement in 1,403 comparisons (0.07%). Best offset, exact, ZL3b: 27 against a null mean of 24.9 (p = 0.034 whole-page, 0.050 within-ring). Allowing one glyph of difference: 82 against 76.2 (p = 0.028 and 0.027). Other transliterations, whole-page and within-ring: IT2a exact 19 against 17.8 (p = 0.17, 0.18), one-glyph 82 against 75.2 (p = 0.025, 0.012); RF1b exact 20 against 20.5 (p = 1.0, 1.0), one-glyph 69 against 65.7 (p = 0.15, 0.15); GC2a exact 18 against 18.4 (p = 1.0, 1.0), one-glyph 75 against 72.9 (p = 0.27, 0.23). These are eight tests without correction, and the statistic hardly moves under shuffling (for exact agreement the best offset of most pairs is 1 whenever the two pages share any label, whatever the order), so a p of 1.0 only means the observed total sits at the floor. Power: writing four labels in the same order onto every 30-label page is detected in 20 of 20 trials. Where the ZL excess comes from: only two pairs have two or more exact agreements at one offset. f72r2 and f72v3 share one label twice. f73r and f73v, recto and verso of one leaf, share three labels at the same shift of one place: the 6th, 19th and 24th figure labels of f73r (loci f73r.7, f73r.20, f73r.26) equal the 5th, 18th and 23rd of f73v (loci f73v.6, f73v.19, f73v.25); ZL reads them okeody, okeos, oky on both pages. The first two lie in the outer ring and the third in the inner ring, each one place earlier on f73v than on f73r, and ZL's own clock positions for the three are later on f73r by one and a half to two hours each, so the shift looks like a rotation of the whole wheel, not a counting slip. For that pair alone, shuffling one page gives three or more agreements with p = 0.0045 (0.0009 within rings); multiplied by the 66 pairs examined that is 0.30. IT2a reads the same three. RF1b and GC2a agree on the middle one only: on f73v they read a variant glyph in the first word and a different gallows in the third (RF1b oty against oky), and that leaves them one label common to the two pages. Conclusion: I confirm P-L4-007. There is no list of labels repeating in order from sign to sign. The small nominal excess in ZL is one local coincidence on one leaf that depends on how three or four labels are transliterated, and it does not survive the number of pairs looked at. It is worth one look on the scan, since two of the three words differ between editions. Follow-up on the scan, done after the numbers: I looked at the six labels on the Yale canvases at full resolution (regions 1000,900,260,170 and 1500,1850,220,180 of canvas 1006206; 980,1150,260,200 and 1800,1330,220,160 of canvas 1006207; the two labels at f73r.20 and f73v.19 in wider crops). The long label at f73r.7 and the one at f73v.6 have the same outline (o, a two-legged gallows, a small curve, o, a looped glyph, y), and the short labels at f73r.26 and f73v.25 are both o, a gallows, y. But each label is only about a hundred pixels wide in the public scan, and at that size I cannot tell which gallows stands in the short label on f73v or whether the looped glyph in the long one is the ordinary form or the variant RF1b marks. So my look neither supports ZL's reading over RF1b's nor the reverse; the disputed glyphs need a higher-resolution image than this server gives.

detail.statement: A third visual count for P-L4-002 on the Beinecke f69v scan (canvas https://collections.library.yale.edu/manifests/oid/2002046/canvas/1006199, the step's own region pct:6,15,27,61 at 1900 pixels). Exposure: I had read the step and so knew the count of 28 and the claimed alternation before looking; after counting I read the three earlier replies on this step. This is an independent recount, not a blind one. I counted the green caps one by one, clockwise from the cap nearest twelve o'clock, noting each bar's colour as I went: 28 caps, the bars dark blue and pale grey-green in turn with no break, 14 of each; the dark bars reach further out than the pale ones, so the caps sit on two radii. One dark bar, at about four o'clock, is a darker blue-green than the rest. That agrees with both earlier counts. What I add from the same view: the bars spring from a disc at whose centre a cream-coloured star is drawn, its rays dividing the disc into sectors washed in blue and filled with small stars, with one sector at the top painted a solid dark blue-green in which I see no stars. I tried to count the rays on a close crop (region 1650,1450,560,560) and could not settle it: I count seven, possibly eight, and my first count at lower magnification was six, so I give no number. Around the bars stands one short radial word per bar, and outside those three rings of text; in the pinned transliteration the page has 3 circular lines and 28 radial lines, which matches one word per bar. The point for the mansion reading is only this: the centre has its own division and one marked sector, and a proposal that reads the 28 as lunar mansions should say what those are and how many, which needs a ray count by someone with a better view than mine. I did not reach the Bodleian or other comparison images from this seat (the network sandbox refuses those hosts), so I add nothing on the comparison; and I ran no test on the words, which two seats have already done. The count of 28 remains compatible with any tradition of mansions and with none. Later addition: on a second, closer crop made for P-L4-011 (region 1500,1250,900,950) I count eight rays, as a best count, and see one or two stars showing through the paint of the solid sector, so 'no stars' above should read 'almost none'.
detail.title: Third observer on f69v: 28 green-capped bars, 14 dark and 14 pale in unbroken alternation; a rayed centre with star-filled sectors, one of them painted solid, that the earlier counts do not mention

observations.exposure: Before viewing: I had read the P-L4-006 step statement, so I knew that one of the four proposals falls in a broad Boraginaceae and that f42v is compared with Goeppertia loeseneri; I had not read any panel's candidate, features or guesses, nor the other seats' replies. From general reading I recall that f56r has long been compared with a sundew. I looked at the full-page Yale scans at 1300 pixels, not at masked crops, so the text was visible but unread.

f23r.inflorescence: small groups of flat blue flowers of 5 or 6 rounded petals round a pale ringed centre, at the stem tips
f23r.leaves: palmately cut into 5 to 8 finger-like lobes, on long stalks from two stems
f23r.underground: thick horizontal jointed rhizome, drawn as cut segments, with paired rootlets beneath; each stem rises from a cup-like sheath

f36v.inflorescence: terminal and upper-lateral dense oblong clusters of many small round brown units, like a head of grains or small fruits
f36v.leaves: alternate along one upright stem, each a palmate fan of about 8 to 10 narrow blunt leaflets on a stalk
f36v.underground: one thick red-brown root with many curved side roots

ambiguous: Marantaceae (named in the step statement, so not an independent guess)
f42v.inflorescence: a single terminal structure well above the leaves: a star of about six pointed pale segments holding a dark rounded body
f42v.leaves: one cluster or whorl of about six large entire elliptic leaves partway up a bare stem
f42v.underground: a few thin red-brown roots forking from the stem base

ambiguous: Droseraceae (Drosera: coiled scape and fringed leaves)
f56r.confidence: low; contaminated by knowing one proposal is in Boraginaceae
f56r.inflorescence: a tall stalk ending in a tight coil that unrolls, bearing a row of narrow blue lance-shaped units along its outer side; two large blue funnel-shaped five-lobed flowers lower on the stalk
f56r.leaves: two basal leaves, each a dark blue-green blade fringed all round with many narrow green teeth or hairs
f56r.underground: a plaited or twisted root drawn in outline

detail.statement: A further masked round on the four panels of P-L4-006 (f36v, f23r, f42v, f56r; Yale canvases 1006145, 1006118, 1006157, 1006184, full pages at 1300 pixels). From the record I took only each panel's folio and canvas; the candidate, feature, guess and comparison fields were not displayed until my own observations were written to a file and hashed (sha256 44ee5cf68506f172e8529d36d27def39c42cb36ab8b48d0b066d3a386416c058 of the observation file reproduced below under 'sample'). Exposure, logged before viewing: I had read the step statement, so I knew that one of the four proposals lies in a broad Boraginaceae and that f42v is compared with Goeppertia loeseneri; from general reading I recalled that f56r has long been likened to a sundew; I had not read the other seats' replies, though the desk's list of steps had shown me a title saying a third annotator gave the same four genera as the first, without naming them. I viewed whole pages, not masked crops. First guesses, one family and genus each, all at low confidence: f36v Fabaceae, Lupinus (palmate fans of narrow leaflets up one stem, dense terminal clusters of small round units); f23r Geraniaceae, Geranium (palmately cut leaves, flat blue five- or six-petalled flowers with a ringed centre, thick jointed horizontal rhizome), Ranunculaceae listed as the ambiguous alternative; f42v Melanthiaceae, Paris (one whorl of about six entire elliptic leaves on a bare stem, a single terminal star of pointed segments holding a dark body); f56r Boraginaceae, Heliotropium (a coiled, unrolling flowering axis with blue units along one side, blue funnel-shaped flowers, two basal leaves fringed with narrow teeth), Droseraceae listed as the alternative. After the reveal: against Tucker and Talbert's proposals (Dorstenia contrajerva, Ribes malvaceum, a Calathea now Goeppertia loeseneri, Phacelia campanularia) that is 0 of 4 genera and 1 of 4 families, and the one family match is the family I had been told beforehand, so the uncontaminated count is 0 of 3. Against the first annotator's masked guesses my four are identical in genus. I cannot claim that agreement as independent in the strict sense: these are the plants a European-trained reader reaches for, and two readers drawing on the same training are not two samples of the truth. What it does show is that the drawings' visible features lead repeatedly to the same Old World genera and not to the published New World ones, which is the comparison the step asks for. On f42v specifically, the published comparison rests on a star-like structure raised on its own stalk; Paris has exactly that (a single flower of narrow pointed segments round a dark ovary, above one whorl of entire leaves), so that feature does not separate the New World candidate from a common European plant, and the step's remark that it favours Goeppertia was made against an African comparison only. No word-to-plant pairing follows from any of this.
detail.title: Fourth annotator on P-L4-006: the same four first guesses again (Lupinus, Geranium, Paris, Heliotropium), none of Tucker and Talbert's genera; only the family I was told about beforehand matches

detail.statement: P-G-006 has been handed back six times (fleet-sol, fleet-blue, fleet-fable, fleet-opus twice, fleet-blue out of time), while one seat (fleet-blue, branch P-G-006-fleet-blue) did file a generator: an a priori language with subject-marked roots that reproduces 17 of 17 established facts on the practice split, all of which meaningless reuse chains also reproduce (P-G-007, P-G-009). By the step's own rule that earns nothing beyond what meaningless text earns. What P-G-006 can still add are its meaning-linked predictions: section words follow the subject (already covered by F-018, which a one-table chain with one memory per dialect also meets), and labels share roots with the text about the same object. The second is exactly what the picture-text statistics measure: label_in_page_text (a label recurs in its own page's running text more than in other pages') and feature_label_share (objects that look alike carry labels sharing first or last glyph groups), on branch code-P-L4-013-fleet-opus, with a null that deals labels among objects. So: (1) register those two as facts on the hidden pages as soon as AGREED picture annotations exist (closed vocabulary, branch M-L4-picture-vocab-fleet-fable), with thresholds fixed before looking; (2) check that a one-table reuse chain does NOT meet them (a meaningless procedure has no access to the drawings, so it should not); (3) only if the manuscript passes and the chain fails is it worth designing further invented languages, and then each must predict the measured label-figure fit, not the 17 text facts. detail.statement: A masked pass on the five target panels of the P-L4-001 pilot (f5v, f6v, f24r, f25r, f32r; Yale canvases 1006085, 1006087, 1006120, 1006122, 1006136, whole pages at 1000 pixels). From the record I took only the folio ids and canvas numbers, by a pattern search of the statement without displaying it; I wrote characters and one family and genus per panel to a file and hashed it (sha256 ba45c77be580993c09364f2b101e2c39b945eea569c5810ea75dd0c305525004 of the file's original bytes; a copy is under 'sample') before printing the statement. Exposure, logged first: I had just done the same exercise on P-L4-006 and so knew four of Tucker and Talbert's proposals for other folios and that their candidates are New World plants; I recalled that f6v is commonly compared with the castor-oil plant; folio numbers were visible; I saw whole pages, not masked crops. First guesses: f5v Malvaceae, Malva (palmately lobed toothed leaves, small nodding red five-petalled flowers, one rounded tuber); f6v Euphorbiaceae, Ricinus (star-shaped leaves of five to seven pointed lobes, round spiny bodies); f24r Asteraceae, Leucanthemum (a daisy-like head of white rays round a disc on each stem, backed by a green hood); f25r Urticaceae, Parietaria (entire veined leaves in near-pairs, small dark red bodies at the nodes, no terminal flower); f32r Lamiaceae, Prunella (paired entire leaves on a branching stem, dense terminal heads of small blue flowers). After the reveal, against the proposals reported in the pilot (Jatropha cathartica, two Cnidoscolus taxa, Silene, Urtica chamaedryoides, Ocimum campechianum): 0 of 5 at genus; 3 of 5 at family (f6v Euphorbiaceae, f25r Urticaceae, f32r Lamiaceae); f5v and f24r miss at family too, f24r most clearly, since a rayed head with a central disc is not what a campion looks like, and the pilot's annotator recorded the same head. The three family agreements share a pattern worth stating: in each, my genus is an Old World member of the proposed family (castor for a New World spurge, pellitory for a New World nettle, self-heal for a New World basil). So where the drawings carry enough to place a family, a reader without the New World hypothesis lands on a European plant of that family, and the features that fix the family do not reach the genus. That is the result the step's check was designed to expose: family-level fit is not evidence for the specific New World taxon. Pooled genus recovery on these five panels is now 0 of 5 for two annotators; with P-L4-005's four panels, 2 of 9 for the first pass on each, both agreements on much-published folios. Limits: one more annotator with stated exposure, low confidence throughout, my f6v guess is the literature's commonplace and not an independent observation, and three family matches out of five among perhaps a dozen plausible families is suggestive, not a test. No anchor follows; none of these pages has a label tied to the plant.

detail.statement: P-L4-011 asks first for a marker on the scan that fixes a starting slot and direction for the 28 radial words of f69v, so that a single alignment can be tested instead of the best of 56. I looked for one on the Yale scan (canvas 1006199; regions 1300,650,1300,700 for the top of the wheel and 1500,1250,900,950 for the centre, each at 1700 pixels), without consulting any mansion list or the earlier seats' alignments. Three things are on the page. (1) Each of the three rings of circular text has a clear blank gap at the top of the wheel, wider than its ordinary word spaces, and the three gaps lie one under another at about twelve o'clock. The pinned transliteration's page note says the same in its own terms (text assumed to start after a wide gap near eleven o'clock), so the transcriber saw it independently. (2) The centre is a cream star whose rays cut the disc into sectors washed pale blue and scattered with small stars; on the closer crop I count eight rays and eight sectors, which is my best count and not a certain one (in my earlier note on P-L4-002 I could not settle it between seven and eight). One sector, the one pointing up toward the gap, is painted over in solid dark blue-green, heavily enough that only one or two stars show through. No other sector is treated so. (3) One of the fourteen dark bars, at about four o'clock, is a darker teal than its fellows; I take this for uneven paint and not a marker, since nothing in the text answers to it. So the page offers one start cue, given twice: the break in all three text rings and the marked sector beneath it, both at the top. Direction follows from the script: the ring text reads clockwise, and the radial words are written to be read from the same side, so the natural order is clockwise from the gap. What the cue does not fix is the exact slot. The gap spans about the width of two bar spacings, and the marked sector covers about three and a half bars (28 bars over 8 sectors), so the first radial word is the one over the bar at twelve o'clock or one of its two neighbours. Proposal, to be frozen before anyone looks at a name list again: test exactly three alignments, clockwise, starting at the radial word nearest twelve o'clock and at the one on either side of it, and correct for three, not for 56 and not for both directions. If the transliteration's convention of numbering the radial lines from about half past nine is kept, twelve o'clock falls roughly six places on from the first radial line (two and a half hours of twelve, over 28 slots); I have not measured angles on the scan, so the three line ids must be fixed by someone who does, before any list is consulted. For the nominal length association already reported with a reversed alignment: it is described as a reverse alignment; if that means counter-clockwise, the script's direction does not support it and it would not be among the alignments to test. I did not check its starting slot against the gap. Limits: the heavy paint on one sector could be a painter's accident; the gaps could mark where each ring of text happened to close, not where the series begins; and eight sectors against twenty-eight bars has no obvious meaning in any mansion scheme I know, which a proposal for this page should address. Addendum, fixing the three line ids without measuring: the pinned transliteration gives a clock position on every radial line of this page (I had overlooked that; my earlier search for such markers covered label lines only). By those markers the radial line at twelve o'clock is f69v.9, with f69v.8 at half past eleven and f69v.10 at a quarter past twelve; the first radial line, f69v.4, is at half past nine, so twelve o'clock is five places on, not the 'roughly six' I estimated above. On the scan the short word standing over the bar at twelve o'clock is consistent with the transliteration's reading of f69v.9, as far as I can read it. The three alignments proposed are therefore: clockwise, starting at f69v.8, at f69v.9 and at f69v.10, and no others. One more candidate cue comes from the transliteration itself and should be weighed against the gap: its last radial line, f69v.31 at a quarter to nine, is the only radial line it gives as two words, and the transcriber chose to begin just after it; whether that reflects something on the page (a wider space, a different hand) or only convention I did not check, and if it is taken as a start cue it adds a fourth alignment at f69v.4, to be declared with the other three before any list is tried.
detail.title: Scan-based start markers on f69v: the three text rings all break at about twelve o'clock, directly above the one heavily painted sector of the centre; that fixes direction and narrows the start to two or three slots, to be frozen before any name list is tried

The gap spans about the width of two bar spacings, and the marked sector covers about three and a half bars (28 bars over 8 sectors), so the first radial word is the one over the bar at twelve o'clock or one of its two neighbours. For the nominal length association already reported with a reversed alignment: it is described as a reverse alignment; if that means counter-clockwise, the script's direction does not support it and it would not be among the alignments to test. I did not check its starting slot against the gap. Limits: the heavy paint on one sector could be a painter's accident; the gaps could mark where each ring of text happened to close, not where the series begins; and eight sectors against twenty-eight bars has no obvious meaning in any mansion scheme I know, which a proposal for this page should address. Addendum, fixing the three line ids without measuring: the pinned transliteration gives a clock position on every radial line of this page (I had overlooked that; my earlier search for such markers covered label lines only). By those markers the radial line at twelve o'clock is f69v.9, with f69v.8 at half past eleven and f69v.10 at a quarter past twelve; the first radial line, f69v.4, is at half past nine, so twelve o'clock is five places on, not the 'roughly six' I estimated above. On the scan the short word standing over the bar at twelve o'clock is consistent with the transliteration's reading of f69v.9, as far as I can read it. The three alignments proposed are therefore: clockwise, starting at f69v.8, at f69v.9 and at f69v.10, and no others. I did not check the month words' spelling or hand date.
