detail.statement: P-L4-008 asks, besides a masked rating round that needs comparison plates I cannot reach from this seat, for two things to be settled on the Voynich drawing itself: whether two oak-like leaves genuinely sit below the crown, and how the roots end. I looked at f35v on the Yale scan (canvas 1006143, full size 2853 by 3769; regions pct:50,5,48,60 for the upper plant and pct:20,68,78,30 for the root, at 1500 and 1700 pixels). I had not seen the step's rubric or its comparison plates; I had seen the page before, for a second look at anchor N-005, and knew that it has been compared with ivy and with oak. Leaves below the crown: yes, two, unmistakably separate from the crown. One stands at the left about halfway down the stem, one at the right a little higher; each is a single flat blade on its own curved stalk, with five to seven rounded lobes a side divided by open rounded sinuses, painted the same dark green as the crown. Their stalks leave the thin pale side stems, not the main stem. The crown itself is drawn with the same lobed outline repeated many times and overlapping, so the two lower leaves read as the crown's leaf shown once in isolation. Other things in the same view that a rubric should have a line for: a sheaf of fine parallel lines running from the main stem up into the base of the crown; about fifteen clusters of round blue-green bodies, three to eight to a cluster, each cluster hanging from a thin looped stalk off the side stems, with two clusters partly painted red-brown low on the left; and two pale side stems that leave the base, bow outward and cross: I see one crossing low on the plant, where the two side stems pass over each other and the main stem, and a second higher up, where the left side stem arches over the main stem to the right. I count that as two crossings; the upper one is a side stem over the main stem, not the two side stems over each other, which a rubric line about a 'doubled crossing' should make explicit. Roots: the root is complete on the scan; nothing is cut off by the image. It is red-brown, with one long arm running left along the foot of the page and ending in three or four thin upturned hooks, a row of short downward fingers along its underside, and on the right two or three short thick arms that curl back on themselves. The lowest fingers end at or within a hair of the lower edge of the leaf, so whether a few tips were lost when the leaf was trimmed cannot be told from the scan; the outline shows no finger that is plainly severed. So on the two criteria the step says no comparator met: a double crossing of stems is there in the sense just described, and the root is strongly lopsided and hooked as described. I add no score for any comparator and no opinion on ivy or oak; on this page the fruit clusters and the twining stems point one way and the leaf shape another, which is the step's own conclusion.
detail.title: The two scan questions P-L4-008 leaves open on f35v: two separate lobed leaves do sit below the crown, and the root is not clipped by a crop but drawn down to the page edge, long and hooked on the left, short and curled on the right

detail.check: From data/raw/ZL3b-n.txt take every zodiac figure label (unit Lz) with its first clock marker; group by page and by the label block it stands in; keep groups of seven or more; pair labels across pages by nearest clock position and count exact and one-glyph agreements against the second ring turned by a random angle. detail.statement: The earlier tests of whether the zodiac figure labels repeat from sign to sign (P-L4-007, P-L4-010) had to search over rotations, because the order of the labels in a ring was taken from the transcription's line order. The pinned Zandbergen-Landini file gives more than order: every figure label on the twelve zodiac pages carries the clock position of its figure. That allows a test with a single alignment fixed in advance by the page itself: if the figures stood for a fixed series tied to position in the wheel (days or degrees counted from a common point), the label at a given clock position on one sign should recur at the same clock position on another. Method, public pages only, one transliteration: the 21 rings and rows of figure labels on the twelve zodiac pages that hold seven or more labels (ring sizes 19 and 10; 10 on each of four pages; 15 and 9; 12, 11 and 7; 18 and 12 twice; 20 and 10; 16 and 10 twice; the five-label inner rings and the short top rows are left out); for every pair of rings on different pages and every label of the first, the label of the second whose clock position is nearest; first word of the label only, uncertain readings taken at their first alternative. Null: the second ring turned by a random angle, 400 times. Result: 2 exact agreements in 2415 comparisons against a null mean of 4.1 (p = 0.94); within one glyph, 37 against 33.7 (p = 0.27). So with the alignment fixed by the page and no freedom to rotate, labels at the same place in the wheel do not agree across signs any more than labels at random places do, which removes the one loophole the rotation-searching tests left (that their correction for searching hid a true alignment). It agrees with both earlier results. Limits: I pooled every pair of rings, so outer rings are also compared with inner ones, which a roster split by ring would not predict to match and which dilutes any effect confined to same-ring pairs; clock positions in the file are given to the nearest quarter or half hour, coarser than the spacing of figures in the larger rings, so nearest-position pairing is off by a figure fairly often and an exact positional roster could be blurred by that; rings differ in size, so the same clock position is not the same ordinal; one transliteration. A same-ring-only run and a run by ordinal from a common starting clock position are the obvious next variants and should be declared before they are run. Addendum: the same-ring-only variant, run after it was declared above. Rings were classed by size within their page, the largest as outer (twelve rings, one per sign) and the rest as inner (nine rings); only outer with outer and inner with inner were compared (the two inner rings of f72r3 are thereby also compared with each other, a small impurity). Result: 0 exact agreements in 1239 comparisons against 2.0 under random turning; within one glyph 15 against 16.0 (p = 0.65). Planted control on the same data: I gave one clock position, chosen at random, the same word on every outer ring and reran the test thirty times (100 turnings each); it was detected at p of 0.05 or less in 30 of 30 runs, and likewise with two and with three shared positions. So this test would see a single position in the wheel that carried the same label on every sign, and the manuscript has none. What it cannot exclude is a roster whose words change from sign to sign by more than one glyph, or one tied to ordinal position in rings of different sizes; the by-ordinal variant I did not run, because it is in substance the same-position, no-offset comparison already on the record in P-L4-007 (0.18% of positions agreeing, no more than at arbitrary offsets), which takes labels in the transcription's ring order. Second addendum, removing the one-transliteration limit on the same-ring variant: with the clock positions taken from Zandbergen-Landini and the words from each of the three pinned transliterations in turn, by line id (first word of each label), exact agreements at the same clock position across signs are 0 of 1239 for Zandbergen-Landini (2.0 expected under random turning), 1 of 1239 for Takahashi (1.6 expected, p = 0.84) and 1 of 1239 for the RF reading (1.2 expected, p = 0.71). No reading shows a positional roster.

So with the alignment fixed by the page and no freedom to rotate, labels at the same place in the wheel do not agree across signs any more than labels at random places do, which removes the one loophole the rotation-searching tests left (that their correction for searching hid a true alignment). It agrees with both earlier results. Limits: I pooled every pair of rings, so outer rings are also compared with inner ones, which a roster split by ring would not predict to match and which dilutes any effect confined to same-ring pairs; clock positions in the file are given to the nearest quarter or half hour, coarser than the spacing of figures in the larger rings, so nearest-position pairing is off by a figure fairly often and an exact positional roster could be blurred by that; rings differ in size, so the same clock position is not the same ordinal; one transliteration. A same-ring-only run and a run by ordinal from a common starting clock position are the obvious next variants and should be declared before they are run. Addendum: the same-ring-only variant, run after it was declared above. Rings were classed by size within their page, the largest as outer (twelve rings, one per sign) and the rest as inner (nine rings); only outer with outer and inner with inner were compared (the two inner rings of f72r3 are thereby also compared with each other, a small impurity). Result: 0 exact agreements in 1239 comparisons against 2.0 under random turning; within one glyph 15 against 16.0 (p = 0.65). Planted control on the same data: I gave one clock position, chosen at random, the same word on every outer ring and reran the test thirty times (100 turnings each); it was detected at p of 0.05 or less in 30 of 30 runs, and likewise with two and with three shared positions. No reading shows a positional roster.

detail.statement: Checked on the record (registry/items.jsonl on origin/main): the three proxies K-016-open-2 asks for are already corpora: Catalan C-002 (Maspons i Labros, Lo rondallayre, 1875), Galician C-042 (Lopez Ferreiro, O Castelo de Pambre, 1895), Old Occitan C-050 (Mahn, Die Werke der Troubadours, vol. 1). So the family Cheshire's proposal leans on is tested at the grid's measured power in all three and fails. Only the Old Occitan corpus is a medieval text; the Catalan and Galician ones are nineteenth-century prose, so a period mismatch remains for those two. The open work is therefore: (1) the medieval Galician-Portuguese corpus already proposed as P-J-003 (the Cantigas, verse-only); (2) a period Catalan text under an open licence (e.g. Llull or a chancery text); then the substitution and verbose cells for both. corpus.json.notes: License: printed 1846; the archive.org item https://archive.org/details/diewerkedertroub01mahnuoft (contributor Robarts - University of Toronto) is marked possible-copyright-status NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT. Why this file: the grid already has Catalan (two texts), Galician (1895) and Portuguese (modern Bible), so of the three proxies the step names only Occitan was missing, and it is the one closest in period to the manuscript; this edition is almost entirely Old Occitan verse and prose. Size: 771,281 bytes of OCR; vs/refcorpus.normalize(..., 'old_occitan') gives 589,721 characters. Contamination, measured: lines with two or more common German function words make up about 4.6% of the file (Mahn's German preface and occasional headings); French-like lines about 0.1%. Most frequent words after cleaning are e, que, qu, de, en, no, per, ni, es, non, ieu, lo, vos, ab, mas, as expected for Old Occitan. OCR quality: the Occitan verse reads cleanly on inspection (e.g. the vida of Arnaut de Maruelh); apostrophes and elisions (qu', d', s') become separate one-letter words after normalization. Named language old_occitan, not occitan, so that a later modern Occitan or Provencal text (Mistral, Goudouli) is not pooled with it.

detail.statement: The question left open by Gaskell and Bowern has two halves: can a long session of human-produced pseudotext show the manuscript's clustering of vocabulary by page and by section, or, failing new human samples, can a frozen model motivated by what their volunteers did. The second half already has an answer on this record, and I set it out here so that the question is not worked twice; the evidence is my own earlier work, so this is a pointer and a statement of limits, not an independent result. The model: a glyph chain over the line with ONE table fitted on all public training pages, no drift, no window, nothing fitted by position; its only memory is reuse at the start of a word, with probability 0.20 one of the last 15 words with one glyph changed, and with probability 0.45 a word that stands at least twice among the last 300 words, written again whole. That is copying and varying what was just written, which is the strategy self-citation proposals describe and, as I recall but have not re-checked in the paper, among those the volunteers reported. Written as a whole book (4,500 ordinary and 740 paragraph-opening lines) laid onto every page and measured on the public evaluation pages, it met all 17 facts then established on 3 of 3 seeds (P-G-017), and those include the three the question is about, jointly and in one text: words recur within their page more than chance (F-009), pages close together share more words than pages far apart (F-011: 0.060, 0.043, 0.058 against the manuscript's 0.074), and which word is written depends on the section (F-018). So local clustering and drift across sections arise together from a stationary procedure with a memory of a few hundred words; no section-specific table is needed, because a memory that turns over more slowly than a section is long makes sections differ by itself. What it did not reproduce with one table is the contrast between the two Currier languages (F-020); that needed two tables with separate memories (P-G-018), which is a statement about two stocks of habits, not about meaning. Limits, which are large. All of this is on the public practice split and under my proposed whole-book layout; the hidden-page verdicts on record are for the individual fact attacks, not for the whole-book text. The settings were chosen by me after seeing failures at neighbouring settings (whole-word reuse at 0.25 held F-011 on one seed of two, at 0.35 from 300 words it failed), so the model is frozen now but was not frozen before the comparison, and the margin on F-011 is thin. And it is a procedure, not people: nothing here shows that a human writer sustains such a memory over two hundred pages, which is what the first half of the question asks. That half needs new long handwritten samples and cannot be done by an agent; the useful specification for whoever collects them is the one the model suggests, namely that the session be long enough for the writer's stock of familiar words to turn over several times (several thousand words at least), and that page and section breaks be imposed on the writer's text afterwards at the manuscript's sizes, not chosen by the writer. Addendum, a re-scoring and not a fresh run: I scored the three whole-book texts of P-G-017 again, as they stand on my disk, with the whole-book cut that is now in the main code (the earlier figures came from my own branch of it), on the practice split. All three texts meet all three facts. Page vocabulary (F-009): 0.338, 0.331, 0.325 against the manuscript's 0.311. Neighbouring pages (F-011): 0.060, 0.043, 0.058 against 0.074. Section vocabulary (F-018): 0.865, 0.868, 0.935 bits against 1.183. So the joint result survives the change of code path, and it also shows where the procedure falls short of the manuscript while still passing: its section effect is about three quarters of the manuscript's and its neighbour effect two thirds to four fifths, so the manuscript clusters more strongly by section and by neighbourhood than this stationary memory alone produces. These are the same three texts, not new seeds; the check's fresh-seed run is still owed.

check: Recompute from the pinned ZL3b file: labels of unit Lz on the twelve zodiac pages that carry a clock comment, word breaks removed; cross-page pairs within 15 degrees; within-ring shuffle. A separate seat should test the low-side observation as a registered prediction before it is given any weight, with the window fixed in advance, for example on Takahashi's transliteration placed by the same positions.

detail.check: Recompute from the pinned ZL3b file: labels of unit Lz on the twelve zodiac pages that carry a clock comment, word breaks removed; cross-page pairs within 15 degrees; within-ring shuffle. A separate seat should test the low-side observation as a registered prediction before it is given any weight, with the window fixed in advance, for example on Takahashi's transliteration placed by the same positions.
detail.statement: P-L4-010 compares labels at equal positions in the transcription's list. This extension uses where each label stands on the page instead. The ZL transcription records a clock position for 298 figure labels on the twelve zodiac pages. I took every pair of labels on two different pages whose recorded positions lie within 15 degrees of each other, in any ring (4,902 pairs), and counted how many pairs are the same word, and how many are the same or one glyph apart. No rotation is fitted: the hypothesis tested is a roster tied to fixed places round the wheel. Null: the labels of each ring of each page shuffled among that ring's positions, 1,000 shuffles. The design was fixed before the run and run once; the lower-tail figures below were computed afterwards, when the result turned out to lie on the low side. Result, upper tail: ZL3b 0 identical pairs against a null mean of 5.1 (p = 1.0), 44 within one glyph against 47.4 (p = 0.74); IT2a 1 against 4.0 (p = 0.99) and 42 against 43.8 (p = 0.65); RF1b 1 against 4.3 (p = 0.99) and 29 against 37.1 (p = 0.94), IT2a and RF1b labels placed by ZL's positions for the same loci. Power: writing one word at 3 o'clock in the outer ring of every page is detected in 40 of 40 trials in each transliteration. So there is no roster of words tied to places round the wheel, which agrees with P-L4-010 and P-L4-007 by a route that does not depend on list order or starting figure. The low side: identical labels at matching positions are fewer than chance, 0 where about 5 are expected (lower-tail p = 0.005 in ZL3b, 0.08 in IT2a, 0.05 in RF1b, 3,000 shuffles). This was not predicted and I do not claim it; it would mean that when a word is used again on another page it tends to stand elsewhere on the wheel. Limits: positions are ZL's half-hour clock readings, not measurements; the 15 degree window was my choice and I tried no other; pages with 15 labels and pages with 30 are pooled.
detail.title: Extension of P-L4-010 by position on the page: zodiac figure labels standing at the same clock position on different pages agree no more often than shuffled labels, and in ZL they never agree at all

detail.check: recompute H1/H2 for the four encodings on vs.facts.ref_words('latin', 60000) with the stated constructions; per-source normalisation = H2 x (output length / source length)
detail.statement: Computed on 60,000 words of the pinned Latin reference text (vs.facts.ref_words('latin')), lower-cased, words joined by spaces. H1 = single-symbol entropy, H2 = conditional entropy of a symbol given the previous one (Bennett's second-order), both in bits. Encodings: (a) a random letter substitution; (b) a reversible verbose code mapping each letter to a fixed distinct pair drawn from 12 new symbols (space kept), length x1.84; (c) padding: a fixed null symbol after every letter, same length x1.84. Results, per output character / per source character (H2 x length ratio): source H2 3.358 / 3.358; substitution 3.358 / 3.358; verbose H1 3.495, H2 2.528 / 4.660; padding H1 3.139, H2 2.097 / 3.866. So (1) normalised by the length of the original source the fall does not persist: per source character the second-order entropy rises under both expansions, because a one-symbol context covers half a source letter; (2) against a matched padding control the verbose fall is not unusual: padding, which adds no information and encodes nothing, lowers per-character H2 further (2.10) than the verbose code (2.53). A low per-glyph H2 in the manuscript therefore cannot by itself point to a verbose cipher over a meaningless or a padded text; any claim needs the per-source-unit comparison and a padding control at the same expansion. Replication across four reference languages and three random codebooks each (H2 per output character / per source character): latin    source 3.36 | verbose seeds (per char/per source) 2.53/4.66 2.47/4.56 2.50/4.61 | padding 2.10/3.87; italian  source 3.12 | verbose seeds (per char/per source) 2.44/4.41 2.47/4.47 2.47/4.47 | padding 2.08/3.76; german   source 3.06 | verbose seeds (per char/per source) 2.50/4.53 2.45/4.44 2.42/4.39 | padding 2.07/3.76; english  source 3.29 | verbose seeds (per char/per source) 2.58/4.67 2.59/4.68 2.53/4.57 | padding 2.16/3.91. Every codebook in every language shows the same pattern: per-character H2 falls by about 0.6-0.8 bits, per-source-character H2 rises by about 1.2-1.4 bits, and padding lowers per-character H2 about 0.4 bits more than the verbose code. This is stable enough to register as a fact about the measure, not about the manuscript.

A wheel with a dark green four-legged animal at the centre, long-snouted, its tail curled up in a loop, a yellow star tethered above it and a word in a different script beneath. Around it are an inner and an outer ring of nude female figures standing with their feet toward the centre, without tubs, each holding a yellow star on a line and each with a short label; four more such figures stand in a row on top of the wheel, outside the outer text ring. The label groups in the transcription have 4, 16 and 10 lines; I matched them to the four figures on top (left to right), the outer ring and the inner ring. The four on top are a clear count; my own counts of the two rings agree with sixteen and ten to within one. Ring labels were paired clockwise from twelve o'clock, an assumption about starting point and direction, so each ring's pairing may be rotated. Per-figure features are recorded individually for the four top figures and are generic for the rings.

detail.statement: Annotated blind from the Beinecke scan only: canvas 1006196 ('68r', a foldout of three panels); f68r1 is the leftmost panel (canvas x about 280-2530), whose structure fits the line ids (paragraph lines at the top, 29 star labels f68r1.8-.36, one circular text f68r1.37). Drawn: 29 eight-pointed (some seven-pointed) stars with a tan/yellow wash scattered over the panel, each with one short word beside it (to its right, except one with the word to its left); seven have a small open circle at the centre and two a dark dot; one at the upper left is drawn faintly in grey. A sun-like circle with a frontal face and braided hair, ringed by about 24 small curved rays, sits under the top paragraph with words inside the circle; a crescent with a blue inner ring and a face sits at the bottom inside a ring of text. A long thin arc runs down the right side. A pale blue-green radiating shape behind the middle stars looks like show-through from the other side of the leaf and is not annotated. No star label line id is assigned to a star: the line ids carry no position and the blind rule forbids reading the words. detail.statement: Measured on the record at the time of writing: 21 blind picture annotations of 6 folios (f66r, f67r2, f70v2, f72r3, f75v, f99r) by five seats, 27 pairs of seats on the same folio, scored with the record's own picture_agreement. Agreement ranges from 0.20 to 0.75 with a median of 0.45; no pair reaches the 0.80 that makes a folio AGREED. The loss is not in what the seats saw. Matched objects agree on kind in every pair (median 1.00). On the features both seats happened to name, the median agreement is 0.25, and a matched object shares only about three feature names with its partner. Feature by feature, over all pairs: closed-answer features agree (sex 1.00, cheeks 1.00, facing 1.00, ring 0.81, points 0.80, clothing 0.75), free-wording features do not (posture 0.04, position 0.03, shape 0.03, star 0.00, container_pattern 0.05, colour 0.30, container 0.39). Two seats who both write that a figure stands in a tub score zero on posture unless they chose the same sentence. Label pairing is the second leak: the median share of object matches made through a shared label line is 0.20 (range 0 to 1), because several seats left ring figures unpaired while others paired them clockwise from an assumed start; unpaired objects are then matched by kind in list order, which compares unrelated figures. Consequence: as scored, the picture data will stay DRAFT however many seats annotate, and the picture-text tests that wait on agreed data cannot start. This is a statement about the scoring and the instructions, not about any seat's annotation. I am one of the five seats (eleven of my own folios are in or on their way to the record), so this is not an outside audit; the numbers are reproducible from the registry. detail.statement: Annotated from the Beinecke scan alone (the left-hand panel of the three-panel '68r' canvas, with one crop). Under a few lines of text there is a sun at the top, a round face ringed by flame-like rays with three short words inside its circle; a moon at the bottom, a face inside a blue and yellow crescent with a ring of text around it; and between them twenty-nine scattered stars, each with a short label beside it (to its right, except one near the lower left whose label is on its left). Eight stars have a small ring at the centre, two a dark dot, four are drawn in outline with little or no yellow, and one near the middle is larger than the rest. The transcription has twenty-nine star-unit label lines (f68r1.8 to f68r1.36), which matches my count of stars. Their order is not known to me: I numbered the stars from top to bottom (left to right where two are level) and paired the label lines in that order, which is an assumption made from the line ids alone, so the star-to-label pairing may be wrong for any star and should not be relied on without a check against the label positions. The sun and moon are not paired with a label line.

Around it an inner ring of about 10 and an outer ring of about 16 nude women, drawn radially with feet toward the centre, each tied to an eight-pointed ochre star; above the outer ring at the top stand 4 more nude women with stars, outside the circular text. Upper left, just above the outer ring, a dark blot and two open C-shaped strokes; two green patches in the lower left look like stains or offset. The transcription has 4 label lines before the first circular line (f73v.1-4), then blocks of 16 (6-21) and 10 (23-32), matching the 4 top figures, the outer ring and the inner ring. Limits of this annotation: the ring figures are faint and overlap, and in the time I had I did not resolve them one by one, so each ring is recorded as one group with its approximate count and label block; the 4 top figures are recorded individually, left to right. No label is attached to a single figure, because which line goes with which figure cannot be fixed from line ids without reading the words.

detail.statement: Blind annotators may not read label words, and ZL label line ids carry no position, so on circular and star pages they can say which ring a label is in (the counts match the figures exactly: f70v2 19+10, f72r3 12+11+7, f72v1 20+10, f72v2 and f72v3 18+12, f68r1 29 stars) but not which figure it sits beside; most annotations on the record therefore leave 'label' null or guess an order, and the picture-text statistics (P-L4-013, branch code-P-L4-013-fleet-opus) would have almost no labelled objects. The step: for each of f70v2, f72r3, f72v1, f72v2, f72v3, f73r, f73v and f68r1, a seat that has NOT annotated that folio opens the scan and the ZL transcription and records, for every label line id (unit L), where the label sits: for rings, ring (outer/middle/inner) and clock angle in degrees from the top, clockwise, measured at the label's first glyph; for f68r1, x and y as fractions of the panel. It also records which canvas and which circle it used (f72v2/f72v3 share a canvas and an identical line structure; record which circle carries which ids, which also settles the panel order the annotators had to assume). Output: one JSON file of {locus: {ring, angle_deg} or {x_frac, y_frac}} per folio, submitted as data. The join to picture objects (nearest object in the same ring by angle) is then mechanical and can be added to vs/dsl.py in the same code PR as P-L4-013. Reading the words is allowed for this step because it records positions only, never meanings; the person doing it must not also annotate the drawings of that folio.

sources: Beinecke MS 408, IIIF canvas https://collections.library.yale.edu/manifests/oid/2002046/canvas/1006196 (label '68r', the three-panel foldout; f68r3 is the right-hand wheel); the cluster at full size x=4850-6150, y=1100-1800: https://collections.library.yale.edu/iiif/2/1006196/4850,1100,1300,700/1300,/0/default.jpg

Zandbergen-Landini transliteration ZL 3b (pinned data/raw/ZL3b-n.txt), f68r3 page comment: 'Moon face in centre, 8 segments around it, four containing labeled stars, one of which probably the Pleiades'; star labels f68r3.10 dchol,day, f68r3.11 doaro, f68r3.12 oalcheol (locus type La, not Ls)

Stephen Bax (2014), A proposed partial decoding of the Voynich script, https://stephenbax.net/wp-content/uploads/2014/01/Voynich-a-provisional-partial-decoding-BAX.pdf : proposes that a word beside the seven stars on f68r reads as Taurus. I could NOT open this PDF from my environment (network refused), so I have not verified which EVA word he means.

Voynich Ninja thread 2102 (2017), summarized transcript of Bax's 2014 talk, https://www.voynich.ninja/printthread.php?tid=2102 : Bax says 'these seven stars might mean the Seven Sisters, the Pleiades'; the illustrating image is named 'DoarusComment.png'; the forum summary notes that the Pleiades/Taurus identification 'has been made by a number of people, including darkstar1 (January 2001)'
anchor.json.statement: UNCERTAIN; HERE IS WHY. What I checked on the scan myself (canvas 1006196, cropped at full resolution): in the upper-left segment of the f68r3 wheel there is one tight cluster of exactly seven small stars, drawn much smaller and closer together than every other star on the page, with a curved line (a tail) running from the cluster down toward the central moon face. Three Voynich words are near it: doaro immediately to the RIGHT of the cluster, on its baseline, nearer to it than to any other star; oalcheol written ALONG the tail line (ZL gives it a different locus type, La); and dchol,day written directly UNDER the single large star to the left, so it belongs to that star. So if any label names the cluster, doaro is the best candidate on the scan, with oalcheol second. The identification of a tight seven-star cluster in an astronomical diagram as the Pleiades (the Seven Sisters, in Taurus) is conventional and has been made repeatedly (ZL page comment 'probably the Pleiades'; darkstar1 2001 per the forum; Bax 2014), but it is an inference from the drawing, not from any writing on the page. The pairing of doaro with a NAME is weaker still: the only published name proposal I know of is Bax's 'Taurus', and I could confirm only indirectly (the image name 'DoarusComment' in a forum transcript) that it concerns this word; I could not read his paper. Names listed: the Latin names of the cluster (Pliades, Pleiades, Vergiliae) and Taurus, because a label beside the Pleiades could name either the cluster or its constellation, and I do not know which. Recommendation to second-lookers: agree only if you can read Bax's paper and confirm the word is doaro, or find a second independent published source pairing this label with the Pleiades or Taurus; otherwise dissent with that reason.

detail.statement: Blind annotation from the Beinecke scan alone (canvas '72v (part)' with two wheels; I describe the RIGHT-hand wheel, the one with a robed figure at the centre; a reduced view of the wheel and a full-resolution crop of its inner part). Identification of the panel is an inference, not a reading: f72v2 and f72v3 have the same label groups (18 and 12), so counts cannot separate them. I rely on the fold: on the recto canvas the panels run r1, r2, r3 away from the spine, so on the verso the back of r3 lies furthest left, and the wheel with the scales (identified as f72v1 by its inner count of 10) is the back of r1; the right-hand wheel of this canvas is then the back of r2. If that is wrong this annotation belongs to f72v3. Centre: a clothed figure in a blue-striped robe and blue hat holding a star. Two rings of nude standing figures without tubs, each with a star and a short label: 12 inner (counted on the scan), 18 outer (from the label group, not securely counted). Labels assigned from line ids and unit codes only, words not read; clockwise from the figure at the top by my assumption, so ids may be rotated by a constant within a ring. Ring figures carry generic features only.

detail.statement: P-L4-013 counts only folios whose picture annotations are AGREED. I measured where that stands on the record at commit d28440e, using vs/registry.py's own picture_agreement on the 21 merged annotations (V-001 to V-021) of six folios, three or four seats each; five of the 21 are mine, and I read the others only after submitting my own. Result: no folio is AGREED. Best pairwise agreement per folio: f70v2 0.747, f75v 0.653, f67r2 0.614, f72r3 0.495, f66r 0.474, f99r 0.398; three folios stand as DISAGREE and three as DRAFT. Where the loss comes from, summed over all 596 matched object pairs: the kind agrees in 537 (90%). Features with a closed set of values agree almost always: cheeks 60/60, sex 40/40, facing 12/12, crescent_colour 12/12, ring 219/270, clothing 113/151. Features written as free phrases almost never match as strings although the seats describe the same thing: star 0/177 (one seat writes 'yes', one 'true', one 'attached'), posture 10/246 ('half figure standing in a tub' against 'upper body rising from an upright tub'), position 7/205, shape 4/116 ('disc with crescent' against 'round face inside a crescent'), note 0/13. Colour agrees in only 100/338 partly for the same reason ('uncoloured' against 'ink only, red dots on cheeks') and partly from real differences (on f99r one seat's 'orange' is another's 'red' or 'tan'). The five seats used 144 distinct feature keys, 105 of them used by one seat only, so most recorded features are never compared at all. Second cause: object matching. Only 209 of the 596 pairs were matched by label locus; seven of the 21 annotations give a label to at most one object, so their objects are paired by kind in list order, which pairs unrelated figures whenever two seats walk a ring from different starting points or in different directions (f72r3 ring feature: 5/30 and 6/30 in two pairs for that reason). What simple repairs buy, recomputed on the same data: leaving 'position' and 'note' out of the comparison lifts only f70v2 over the line (best pair 0.856); the other best pairs become f75v 0.731, f67r2 0.643, f99r 0.558, f66r 0.600, f72r3 0.528. Counting two values as equal when half their words overlap gives f99r 0.779, f75v 0.750, f66r 0.667 and leaves the rest unchanged. So neither repair alone makes the picture data usable; a shared vocabulary and a shared walking order are needed. I have not looked at whether any label words agree with pictures; this note concerns only the picture data. My own annotations share the fault: I wrote free phrases under 'form', 'position' and 'note' and assumed a ring starting point without a stated convention. Addition on the walking order, found afterwards: the ZL transcription itself records where each zodiac figure label stands. 299 of its label lines, all on the twelve zodiac pages plus one on f57v, carry a clock-position comment, and on every zodiac page each ring's first label is placed between about 8:45 and 11:30, never at 12 o'clock. So my own wheel annotations, which number ring figures clockwise from the figure nearest 12 o'clock and give the n-th figure the n-th label line, are rotated against the transcription by roughly one to three figures per ring (f70v2, f72r3, and the pending f72v1, f72v2, f72v3, f73r, f73v); any other seat that assumed a 12 o'clock start has the same offset. Their label assignments on those rings should not be used as they stand. The repair is cheap: have annotators record each ring figure's clock position on the upright page, and match figures to label lines by ring and nearest clock position from the transcription's comments instead of by list order. Measured on one page: for f70v2 I took the positions of the 29 ring figures that I had noted from the scan when annotating (centre of the wheel at about 2008,1757 on canvas 1006200) and turned them into angles clockwise from the top. Each figure then falls within 17 degrees of exactly one label line's recorded clock position (23 of the 29 within 6 degrees, the worst three 12, 13 and 17), and the pairing is one to one. Against that, my merged annotation V-006 is rotated by three places in the outer ring and one in the inner: the figure I called outer-1 (my label f70v2.2) stands at f70v2.5, outer-2 at f70v2.6, and so on to outer-16 at f70v2.20, then outer-17, 18, 19 at f70v2.2, 3, 4; inner-1 to inner-9 stand at f70v2.23 to f70v2.31 and inner-10 at f70v2.22. Read V-006's ring labels with that correction. Its statement also says eight consecutive outer figures wear blue head coverings; its own object list records six (outer-4 and outer-6 to outer-10, that is label lines f70v2.8 and f70v2.10 to f70v2.14 after correction). The agreement of the angles with the transcription's clock positions, to a few degrees over 29 figures, shows the matching by clock position works on the public scans, as the code proposed on branch code-P-L4-013-fleet-opus assumes. The same matching applied to the one ring figure with a distinctive feature on my other merged wheel, f72r3 (V-011): the crowned figure of the inner ring stands at about 99 degrees clockwise from the top (figure at about 7470,1540 and wheel centre at about 7001,1464 on canvas 1006203), 9 degrees from the clock position recorded for label line f72r3.30 and 54 from the next nearest; V-011 gives it f72r3.29, so the crown belongs with f72r3.30. On the pending f72v1 annotation the crowned outer figure stands at about 10 degrees, between the positions recorded for f72v1.7 and f72v1.9, and the comment on f72v1.8 (01:45, out of sequence between 11:30 and 01:00) looks like a slip, so I leave that one undecided.

title: Before picture-text statistics can run: none of the first six annotated folios is AGREED, and most of the measured disagreement is wording, not what the seats saw; a fixed vocabulary is needed first

check: On the public pages: for every page with at least three label words and thirty other words, the share of label words (three or more glyphs, certain) found in the page's own non-label text, against label sets dealt among pages of the same section; then the same own-page against other-page comparison for a held-out paragraph line. The claim fails if the label ratio clearly exceeds the ordinary-word ratio once words are matched for length and frequency more finely than five bins, or if a second transliteration gives a label effect at p below 0.01.

detail.check: On the public pages: for every page with at least three label words and thirty other words, the share of label words (three or more glyphs, certain) found in the page's own non-label text, against label sets dealt among pages of the same section; then the same own-page against other-page comparison for a held-out paragraph line. The claim fails if the label ratio clearly exceeds the ordinary-word ratio once words are matched for length and frequency more finely than five bins, or if a second transliteration gives a label effect at p below 0.01.
detail.statement: The third statistic proposed in P-L4-013 (a label word recurs in its own page's running text more than in other pages') needs no picture annotation, so I measured it now on the public practice pages only (226 pages; nothing from the hidden pages). Selection: the 46 public pages with at least three label words and at least thirty words of other text (15 pharmaceutical, 12 zodiac, 10 biological, 5 astronomical, 3 cosmological, 1 text), 886 label words of three or more glyphs with no uncertain reading. Statistic: the share of label words that occur somewhere in the non-label text of their own page. Null: the same share after the label sets are dealt to other pages of the same section, 999 deals. Result, exact word: 0.096 on the own page against a null mean of 0.085 (95th percentile 0.097), p = 0.079. Allowing one glyph of difference: 0.366 against 0.335 (95th percentile 0.361), p = 0.030 on 199 deals. By section, exact word, no section is significant on its own: astronomical 0.036 against 0.042, biological 0.200 against 0.190, cosmological 0.174 against 0.108, pharmaceutical 0.068 against 0.066, zodiac 0.091 against 0.074 (p from 0.11 to 0.75). So there is at most a weak page effect for labels, a ratio of about 1.13 to 1. The comparison that matters: ordinary words show a page effect at least as strong as labels do. Holding out the last paragraph line of every public page with six or more paragraph lines (925 words), 0.351 of its words occur in the rest of their own page, against 0.267 in the rest of another page of the same section, a ratio of about 1.32 to 1. Matched for frequency (five bins of how often a word occurs in the public running text, ordinary words reweighted to the labels' mix; the other-page rate here is the average over all other pages of the section, so the label figures differ slightly from the deal above), the ratios are 1.21 for labels (0.096 against 0.080) and 1.35 for ordinary words (0.144 against 0.107). The transliteration's own locus types separate labels written on a container from labels beside a detached plant part, and twelve public pharmaceutical pages carry both (36 container labels, 141 plant-part labels, labels with an uncertain reading left out). Fourth addendum: the planted control for the first measurement in this note (a label recurs in its own page's text), on the same 46 pages and 886 labels. I replaced a share of the labels with a word drawn from their own page's text among the words occurring there at most twice, and reran the test forty times per setting (200 deals each). A share of 0.02 raises the own-page rate from 0.096 to 0.114 and is detected in 40 of 40 runs; 0.05, 0.10 and 0.20 likewise in 40 of 40. Unlike the jar-and-row test, this one is sensitive: if even one label in fifty were a page-specific word of the text around it, beyond what the manuscript already shows, the test would see it. The manuscript's own excess is about one label in a hundred (0.096 against 0.085, p = 0.08). So on the public pages the labels are, almost without exception, not the distinctive words of the text on their page: either the text does not name the labelled objects with the label's word, or it names them with common words, or the labels and text are unrelated. This is the most informative of the nulls in this note, and it bears on the reading of labels as plant or star names that the paragraph beside them then discusses. It remains one transliteration, exact-word matching, and exact-word matching only. I then ran the plant I had expected to be harder, labels replaced by a word drawn from their page's text in proportion to how often it occurs there, common words included: shares of 0.02, 0.05 and 0.10 are again each detected in 40 of 40 runs (own-page rate 0.112, 0.141, 0.188). So the test would also see labels taken from the common words of their page at one label in fifty; my expectation that this would be harder was wrong. Fifth addendum, removing the one-transliteration limit on the first measurement. The same test on the other pinned transliterations of the public pages: Takahashi 0.102 own page against 0.086 dealt (45 pages, 894 labels, p = 0.017); the RF transliteration 0.073 against 0.067 (45 pages, 759 labels, p = 0.225); Zandbergen-Landini on a fresh set of deals 0.096 against 0.085 (p = 0.071). So the three readings agree on a small positive excess, between half a label and a label and a half in a hundred, significant at 0.05 in one of the three and nowhere at 0.01. I had written above that the claim would fail if a second transliteration gave p below 0.01; it does not, but Takahashi comes closer than my summary of 'barely more than chance' allowed, and the fair statement is: a small excess that may be real, of a size (about one label in a hundred) that page vocabulary alone would explain, and far below what the planted controls show a naming relation of even one label in fifty would produce. By section in the three readings (own page against dealt, 1999 deals): no section reaches 0.05 in any reading. The zodiac pages are the most consistent (0.091 against 0.074, 0.100 against 0.079, 0.065 against 0.054; p = 0.11, 0.06, 0.23), and that is where labels and the ring text share a page most closely; the pharmaceutical pages, where labels would most naturally be ingredient names taken up in the recipe text, show nothing (0.068 against 0.067, 0.075 against 0.071, 0.044 against 0.050), and the astronomical pages nothing or less. Last addendum, the jar-and-row test on the other two pinned transliterations of the public pages: Takahashi 0.262 for a jar against its own row and 0.250 dealt (8 pages, 25 rows, 111 labels, p = 0.24); the RF reading 0.227 against 0.245 (7 pages, 20 rows, 79 labels, p = 0.89); Zandbergen-Landini on fresh deals 0.244 against 0.253 (p = 0.72). The sign of the difference is not even consistent between readings, so the null holds in all three. And the jar-against-plant-part comparison of label form on the other two readings, which qualifies what I wrote above about that test. Two of its differences recur in all three transliterations with the same sign and about the same size: labels written on jars are longer (6.9 against 6.1 glyphs in Zandbergen-Landini, 6.8 against 6.1 in Takahashi, 6.8 against 6.2 in RF; p = 0.07, 0.10, 0.18) and seldom end in l or r (0.08 against 0.23, 0.09 against 0.24, 0.07 against 0.23; p = 0.06, 0.09, 0.09). The three readings are of the same ink, so they are not three independent tests and their p values must not be combined; what the agreement shows is that the difference is not a transcriber's artefact. It is still a difference found by looking at eight features on a few dozen jar labels, and none of the p values passes 0.05. I therefore withdraw 'a label's form does not tell a jar from a root' as too strong: the fair statement is that jar labels may be somewhat longer and may avoid a final l or r, and that this is exactly the kind of claim that should be frozen now, as two one-sided predictions with these two features and no others, and scored once on the hidden pages. If it held there it would be the first picture-linked regularity in the labels on this record; I make no claim that it will.

detail.statement: Two results and the state of the picture route. (1) P-L4-010, position-calibrated: using the clock position ZL3b records on each zodiac label, labels at the same clock angle in the same ring on different signs agree no more than labels shuffled within their rings, whether positions are taken as fixed (0 exact, 9 near matches in 1,303 comparisons; p 1.0 and 0.89) or each page pair may rotate and reverse (17 exact, 78 near; p 0.20 and 0.54). Planted rosters of only two positions, fixed or rotating with the sign, are detected at the permutation floor (p 0.003, 0.005). So the zodiac labels are not a repeated ordered list of names; whatever they are, each sign's labels are its own. (2) P-L4-002: all four transliterations give f69v exactly 28 radial lines, numbered clockwise from 09:30; the sequence is frozen for a masked, pre-registered comparison with mansion lists. State of the picture route: every labelled zodiac and star folio has three or more blind annotations; none is AGREED because features are free text (kind agreement 0.90, feature agreement 0.35). The code that turns this into a test is written: the picture-text statistics with a shuffle-labels null, and a join of ring figures to their label lines by ZL3b clock angle (22-29 of 26-30 figures per folio on fleet-opus's annotations), branch code-P-L4-013-fleet-opus; the closed feature vocabulary is on branch M-L4-picture-vocab-fleet-fable. Next, in order: review and merge those two branches; re-annotate the zodiac folios with the vocabulary; then register label_in_page_text and feature_label_share as facts on the hidden pages. These ask the remaining question the text statistics cannot: does a label fit the figure it stands beside?

statement: One procedure, fitted on the public training pages only, written as a whole book and sent with cut book: 4,500 ordinary lines and 740 paragraph-opening lines, laid onto every page of the manuscript in order. (1) A glyph chain over the whole line, with the word space and the line end as ordinary symbols; each glyph is drawn given the four symbols before it, or, 6 times in 10, given only the two before it; it starts afresh at each line, from one start mark for a line that opens a paragraph and another for any other line. (2) Three tables, fitted on the public pages labelled Currier A, Currier B and unlabelled. At each point of the book the writer uses the table of the public page that lies at that point (by share of lines written), as a scribe would whose exemplar or habit changes from sheet to sheet. (3) Each table keeps its own memory. At the start of any word but the first of a line: with probability 0.20 the writer takes one of the last 15 words written under that table (on a paragraph-opening line, only words already on that line) and changes one glyph to another that the chain allows between its neighbours; with probability 0.45 (ordinary lines only) it writes again, whole, a word standing at least twice among the last 300 words written under that table. In both cases it prefers a word whose first glyph the chain allows after what was just written. No rule names a glyph or a word; the only labels used are those of public pages. Lines holding a four-word run of the manuscript are redrawn. Fairness: the procedure cannot know a hidden page's language; on the practice split the public page lying at the same point of the book has the evaluation page's label for 29 of 34 pages. Local result, practice split, three seeds, none selected: every established fact holds on 3 of 3; same-language minus different-language page similarity 0.127, 0.080, 0.110 (manuscript 0.122); labels dealt among whole pages, p at or below 0.01 on 2 of 3; labels rotated along the page order, at or below 0.05 on 0 of 3. So this text, seed 1, reproduces the level and the deal null and is expected NOT to pass the rotation: it is sent as the strongest attempt I have, to put on the record whether the fact stands against it. If it stands, it does so by the rotation null alone, which has no margin at this sample size.

check: Use disjoint public training and evaluation works, verify inversion exactly, and report all orders 0–8 for identity, fixed substitution, constant letter padding, deterministic two-symbol padding, matched random two-symbol padding, and constant word suffix. Include an inverse-aware reference and both denominators.

detail.check: Use disjoint public training and evaluation works, verify inversion exactly, and report all orders 0–8 for identity, fixed substitution, constant letter padding, deterministic two-symbol padding, matched random two-symbol padding, and constant word suffix. Include an inverse-aware reference and both denominators.
detail.findings: The addB analogue expands source length by 1.82–1.86. For Latin, Italian, Spanish and English respectively, order-8 identity rates are 3.785, 3.969, 3.677 and 3.386 bits per source symbol. At the same order, constant B padding yields 2.163, 2.368, 2.177 and 1.964 bits per output symbol, or 4.021, 4.342, 3.965 and 3.580 per source symbol. Fixed substitution preserves every measured rate. Matched random padding also reduces the order-8 per-output rate, while costing 5.442, 5.537, 5.365 and 5.151 per source symbol. At order 4 constant padding can improve even the source-normalized estimate (Italian 3.165 vs 3.516, Spanish 3.165 vs 3.219). At the best order within 0–8, constant padding costs more per source symbol in all four pairs. Those minima describe this evaluated grid only.
detail.interpretation: A fixed injective transformation preserves joint Shannon entropy of the whole source block. An inverse-aware encoding can model the original text and reconstruct deterministic pads for zero extra bits. Independent random pads cost the coin cross-entropy in addition to the source code. A finite-context model uses a different effective source context after insertion, so normalization alone need not make its estimates equal. This tests the denominator and transformation controls on public texts. The companion paper uses its own resampling protocol and entropy statistics.
detail.methods: Use the first 100 normalized blocks of each training work and the first 30 of each evaluation work from the pinned reference corpus. Compare Augustine/Erasmus, Dante/Villani, Lucanor/Buen Amor and Chaucer/Paston. Reset context at the existing block boundaries. Keep spaces, use fixed lowercase-ASCII support and reserve uppercase pad symbols. Use order 0–8 character models with recursive Dirichlet backoff of strength 2 and a 0.5 base pseudocount. For the two-symbol controls, choose B or D via parity of the preceding source letter index or independently via a coin estimated from those deterministic training pads. Fix independent train/test random seeds 40801/40802. The constant word suffix is a separate comparator. No manuscript data enter the test.
detail.reproduction: Save embedded python as measure.py and run PYTHONPATH=. python3 /path/to/measure.py from the project checkout with the pinned reference corpus available. It writes rates-frozen.json next to the script.
detail.source: Bowern and Gaskell, Character Entropy in Historical Texts: Beyond Language, CEUR Workshop Proceedings 3313 (2022), §2 and Table 1, https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-3313/paper6.pdf. Related open-source catalogue https://github.com/Ayan-Bandyopadhyay/voynich-swarm/pull/423.
detail.statement: For reversible transformations used as pseudotext controls, report held-apart model code lengths on the original symbol scale alongside per-output entropy summaries. Preserve token boundaries and include padding controls so an apparent drop can be traced to deterministic redundancy, stochastic expansion, or the finite-order model.

detail.statement: A second visual pass for P-L4-002 on the Beinecke f69v scan (canvas https://collections.library.yale.edu/manifests/oid/2002046/canvas/1006199, region 1300,1080,1250,1250 at full resolution). Exposure: I had read the step statement, so I knew the earlier count of 28 and the claimed 14/14 alternation before looking; this is an independent recount, not a blind one. I read no glyph values and no words of the transcription; from it I took only line ids and unit codes. What I see: 28 bars radiate from a central disc, each ending in a green oval cap. Going clockwise from the bar nearest 12 o'clock I coded each bar as dark blue or pale grey-green: D P D P D P D P D P D P D P D P D P D P D P D P D P D P, that is 14 dark and 14 pale with no break in the alternation anywhere round the circle. The dark bars are also the longer ones (their caps sit further out) and the pale bars the shorter, without exception, so length and colour are one feature, not two. The eleventh bar clockwise (about 4 o'clock) is a darker, greener blue than the other dark bars; I cannot tell paint variation from intent. The central disc is cut by pale yellow curved arms into wedges, about six or seven (I could not fix the number), filled with blue wash and small stars in unequal numbers, one wedge at the top solid blue-green with almost no stars. Outside the bars stand short radial words, one beyond each bar as far as I can see; the transcription has exactly 28 lines of the radial unit (f69v.4 to f69v.31), matching the bar count, and three circular text lines (f69v.1 to 3). Faint blue lines continue outward from some bars into the text rings, roughly eight of them, unevenly spaced. Consequence for the test the step asks for: apart from the count, the only ordered visual feature of the 28 loci is a two-state alternation. Under any rotation and either direction a tradition's list can be laid on it in only two distinguishable ways (which parity is dark), so the picture can at most test a prediction of the form 'odd-numbered mansions differ from even-numbered ones in some named property'; it cannot rank Middle Persian, Arabic and Latin lists against each other. Any tradition-specific evidence has to come from the 28 radial labels, compared in order, and the eleventh bar is the only candidate for a visual origin mark, a weak one. Not done: the masked comparison with Bodleian MS Bodl. Or. 133. The Bodleian image server is blocked for this seat, so I did not see those scans and code nothing about them. Before learning that, and before looking at any image, I fixed this feature list for whoever can reach both: number of equal radial divisions; whether divisions alternate in two tones; whether each division carries its own written name; number of concentric bands of writing; centre motif; dot or star groups of varying count and whether they sit in the divisions or in the centre; divisions as rays from the centre or as cells of a ring; visible grouping of divisions into larger named sets; figurative drawings in the divisions. My f69v codes: 28; yes; yes (28 radial words); 3; disc with curved arms and star-filled wedges; yes, in the centre only; rays; none visible; none. Addition, a text check that follows from the above: if the two-state alternation of the bars meant something about the 28 items, the 28 radial labels might alternate too. I fixed three statistics before running anything and ran them once: the difference in mean label length (glyphs) between labels at odd and even positions; and, for the first glyph and for the last glyph, the number of positions whose glyph equals the one two places on minus the number equal to the one next to it, round the circle. Null: the same 28 labels in shuffled order, 20,000 shuffles. Position parity does not depend on where the transcription starts or which way it runs, so no alignment had to be chosen. ZL3b loci f69v.4 to 31: length difference 0.07 glyphs (p = 1.00), first-glyph excess -1 (p = 0.71), last-glyph excess -5 (p = 0.99). IT2a gives the same and RF1b the same except a last-glyph excess of -4 (p = 0.97); GC2a gives 0.36 (p = 0.39), -1 (p = 0.71), -3 (p = 0.93). Power: adding one glyph to every label on one parity of a shuffled ring is detected at p < 0.05 in 157 of 200 trials, so the length test would have seen a one-glyph alternation about four times in five; the first-glyph test is weak because 20 of the 28 labels begin with the same glyph. So the labels show no period-two pattern to go with the bars: on this evidence the dark and pale bars do not mark two classes of label.
detail.title: Second observer on f69v: 28 bars strictly alternating dark and pale, which the 28 radial labels do not echo; the drawing alone cannot separate one mansion list from another, and the Bodleian comparison was not reachable from this seat

The eleventh bar clockwise (about 4 o'clock) is a darker, greener blue than the other dark bars; I cannot tell paint variation from intent. The central disc is cut by pale yellow curved arms into wedges, about six or seven (I could not fix the number), filled with blue wash and small stars in unequal numbers, one wedge at the top solid blue-green with almost no stars. Outside the bars stand short radial words, one beyond each bar as far as I can see; the transcription has exactly 28 lines of the radial unit (f69v.4 to f69v.31), matching the bar count, and three circular text lines (f69v.1 to 3). Faint blue lines continue outward from some bars into the text rings, roughly eight of them, unevenly spaced. Consequence for the test the step asks for: apart from the count, the only ordered visual feature of the 28 loci is a two-state alternation. Under any rotation and either direction a tradition's list can be laid on it in only two distinguishable ways (which parity is dark), so the picture can at most test a prediction of the form 'odd-numbered mansions differ from even-numbered ones in some named property'; it cannot rank Middle Persian, Arabic and Latin lists against each other. Any tradition-specific evidence has to come from the 28 radial labels, compared in order, and the eleventh bar is the only candidate for a visual origin mark, a weak one. Not done: the masked comparison with Bodleian MS Bodl. Or. 133. The Bodleian image server is blocked for this seat, so I did not see those scans and code nothing about them. Before learning that, and before looking at any image, I fixed this feature list for whoever can reach both: number of equal radial divisions; whether divisions alternate in two tones; whether each division carries its own written name; number of concentric bands of writing; centre motif; dot or star groups of varying count and whether they sit in the divisions or in the centre; divisions as rays from the centre or as cells of a ring; visible grouping of divisions into larger named sets; figurative drawings in the divisions. My f69v codes: 28; yes; yes (28 radial words); 3; disc with curved arms and star-filled wedges; yes, in the centre only; rays; none visible; none. Addition, a text check that follows from the above: if the two-state alternation of the bars meant something about the 28 items, the 28 radial labels might alternate too. I fixed three statistics before running anything and ran them once: the difference in mean label length (glyphs) between labels at odd and even positions; and, for the first glyph and for the last glyph, the number of positions whose glyph equals the one two places on minus the number equal to the one next to it, round the circle. Null: the same 28 labels in shuffled order, 20,000 shuffles. Position parity does not depend on where the transcription starts or which way it runs, so no alignment had to be chosen. ZL3b loci f69v.4 to 31: length difference 0.07 glyphs (p = 1.00), first-glyph excess -1 (p = 0.71), last-glyph excess -5 (p = 0.99). IT2a gives the same and RF1b the same except a last-glyph excess of -4 (p = 0.97); GC2a gives 0.36 (p = 0.39), -1 (p = 0.71), -3 (p = 0.93). Power: adding one glyph to every label on one parity of a shuffled ring is detected at p < 0.05 in 157 of 200 trials, so the length test would have seen a one-glyph alternation about four times in five; the first-glyph test is weak because 20 of the 28 labels begin with the same glyph. So the labels show no period-two pattern to go with the bars: on this evidence the dark and pale bars do not mark two classes of label.

statement: A word table and one copying rule, fitted on the public training pages only; no glyph, word or position is named. Line lengths are drawn from the public paragraph line lengths (5 to 14 words). Each word is drawn independently from the public word list by frequency, except that with probability 0.025 the writer instead looks at the line directly above, picks one of its words of four or more glyphs at random, and writes a word from the public word list that differs from it by exactly one glyph (one inserted, dropped or replaced); if the list holds no such word it draws by frequency as usual. Lines holding a four-word run of the manuscript are redrawn. This is Timm's self-citation reduced to its smallest form, and it does write the target pattern in directly (a copy from the line above with one glyph changed), so by the red team's own rule it should count as a weak refutation if a second look says so: what it shows is how little copying the fact needs, not that the copying arises from something else. Fitting, all on the practice split: the measured excess grows about in proportion to the copying rate. At 0.04 three seeds gave 0.029, 0.053, 0.052 (two over the fact's upper bound of 0.045); at 0.08 and 0.12 one seed each gave 0.088 and 0.117 (over); at 0.025 four seeds gave 0.021, 0.040, 0.022 (pass) and 0.008 (under the floor of 0.012). This text is seed 1 at 0.025, the first seed drawn, not the best of the four. The spread between seeds is as wide as the fact's window, so a miss on the hidden pages would be sampling noise as easily as a failure of the procedure; the fact's own notes report the same spread for the manuscript.

detail.check: Publish the condition grid and seed list before measuring held-apart samples. Match line and page sizes. Compare all controls jointly on repetition and excess section association under each null. Report whether a joint match survives an order-preserving comparison, and report any dependence on hand, token support, page length or the number of surviving practice pages.
detail.limitations: Whole-page label exchange changes section token totals and breaks the contiguous runs of section labels. Its IID control alone averages about 0.161 bits of apparent excess in both editions, so judge source-control contrasts under the same layout and show token and cyclic comparisons as well. Cyclic label shifts preserve the sequence of section labels but can also change token totals, and the nominal p is coarse. The practice subset is sparse and may confound section, total token counts, Currier variety and hand. Runs reuse a manuscript-trained unigram and measure copy alone. The outcomes do not establish how long human sessions behave and do not rule out mutation or other drift schedules.
detail.methods: Use exactly the 615 certain eligible P-line loci shared by both public practice editions, arranged in original face order across 31 surviving pages. Reuse the observed slot counts in each edition. For each token, draw from pooled public-training unigram frequencies or copy a uniformly selected recent token with probability 0.33. Evaluate FIFO windows 0 (iid), 30, 180 and 720, and 180 with a reset every five retained pages regardless of actual section. Freeze the grid and seeds 201–216, with no fitting of per-section parameters. For local clustering, divide the within-page exact token-pair collision probability by the whole-sample collision probability. For across-section association use mutual information between token identity and IVTFF illustration section. Use 39 global token shuffles with fixed page and section sizes, 39 whole-page label permutations, and the complete 31-position cyclic orbit of section labels. Paired edition outcomes share the same underlying physical manuscript.
detail.reproduction: Save the embedded Python as measure.py. Run from the project checkout with PYTHONPATH=. python3 /path/to/measure.py. The script uses the pinned public corpus and writes /tmp/fleet-sol-long-session.json.
detail.results_summary: Observed 5,185 ZL and 5,106 IT practice tokens. Within-page collision ratios are 1.919 and 1.940. The 30-token window can reach those values (4/16 ZL, 5/16 IT), and longer windows did not in this grid. Observed excess section mutual information over the whole-page label shuffles is 0.306/0.315 bits in ZL/IT, versus maximum 0.262/0.269 in the full tested control grid. The observed whole-page-label p is 0.025 in each edition but cyclic rank is 3/31 for each. Relative to global token shuffles, the source excess is 0.252/0.261 bits, while every 30-token control has a larger excess (ZL 0.274–0.337, IT 0.293–0.344). Thus some simple copy runs match both target levels versus token shuffle alone. Comparisons preserving page vocabulary and preserving order give weaker support for a joint match.
detail.source: Daniel E. Gaskell and Claire L. Bowern, Gibberish after all? Voynichese is statistically similar to human-produced samples of meaningless text, 2022, §4, https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-3313/paper4.pdf . The illustrative pitshol/pitsholh report and discussion of copying from the current section motivate finite memory and periodic breaks. Copying exact tokens is a simplified model of those strategies.

experiment.json.summary: In matched public practice runs, 30-token copying matched or exceeded local page clustering in 4/16 ZL and 5/16 IT controls. No tested copy condition matched the observed excess section association over whole-page label permutations. A token shuffle instead gave the opposite ordering for 30-token copy.

step.json.check: Publish the condition grid and seed list before measuring held-apart samples. Match line and page sizes. Compare all controls jointly on repetition and excess section association under each null. Report whether a joint match survives an order-preserving comparison, and report any dependence on hand, token support, page length or the number of surviving practice pages.
step.json.limitations: Whole-page label exchange changes section token totals and breaks the contiguous runs of section labels. Its IID control alone averages about 0.161 bits of apparent excess in both editions, so judge source-control contrasts under the same layout and show token and cyclic comparisons as well. Cyclic label shifts preserve the sequence of section labels but can also change token totals, and the nominal p is coarse. The practice subset is sparse and may confound section, total token counts, Currier variety and hand. Runs reuse a manuscript-trained unigram and measure copy alone. The outcomes do not establish how long human sessions behave and do not rule out mutation or other drift schedules.
step.json.methods: Use exactly the 615 certain eligible P-line loci shared by both public practice editions, arranged in original face order across 31 surviving pages. Reuse the observed slot counts in each edition. For each token, draw from pooled public-training unigram frequencies or copy a uniformly selected recent token with probability 0.33. Evaluate FIFO windows 0 (iid), 30, 180 and 720, and 180 with a reset every five retained pages regardless of actual section. Freeze the grid and seeds 201–216, with no fitting of per-section parameters. For local clustering, divide the within-page exact token-pair collision probability by the whole-sample collision probability. For across-section association use mutual information between token identity and IVTFF illustration section. Use 39 global token shuffles with fixed page and section sizes, 39 whole-page label permutations, and the complete 31-position cyclic orbit of section labels. Paired edition outcomes share the same underlying physical manuscript.
step.json.reproduction: Save the embedded Python as measure.py. Run from the project checkout with PYTHONPATH=. python3 /path/to/measure.py. The script uses the pinned public corpus and writes /tmp/fleet-sol-long-session.json.
step.json.results_summary: Observed 5,185 ZL and 5,106 IT practice tokens. Within-page collision ratios are 1.919 and 1.940. The 30-token window can reach those values (4/16 ZL, 5/16 IT), and longer windows did not in this grid. Observed excess section mutual information over the whole-page label shuffles is 0.306/0.315 bits in ZL/IT, versus maximum 0.262/0.269 in the full tested control grid. The observed whole-page-label p is 0.025 in each edition but cyclic rank is 3/31 for each. Relative to global token shuffles, the source excess is 0.252/0.261 bits, while every 30-token control has a larger excess (ZL 0.274–0.337, IT 0.293–0.344). Thus some simple copy runs match both target levels versus token shuffle alone. Comparisons preserving page vocabulary and preserving order give weaker support for a joint match.

statement: One procedure, fitted on the public training pages only. A writer keeps two stocks of familiar words. Stock A is the word list of the public training pages carrying Currier's label A, stock B the list of those carrying B, and a third, smaller list serves the pages Currier left unlabelled; each stock also carries an order-3 glyph chain over its own words, used only for words the stock has never had. The writer works through the book in order and, on each page, takes up the stock of that page: it reaches for a word of the stock, drawn from the stock's own frequency list; with probability 0.10 it instead writes a word the stock has never had, shaped by that stock's glyph chain; with probability 0.15 it alters one glyph of whatever it just chose; and with probability 0.25, before any of that, it re-writes a word it has already written at least twice among the last 300 words. It keeps the manuscript's line lengths and writes paragraph-opening lines like any other line. No rule names a shared word, one page being alike to another, or the statistic: the sharing between pages of one stock is what sampling from a finite list does by itself. DISCLOSURE, because it decides what this is worth: the procedure switches stock on the page's Currier label, public metadata pinned in the repo for all 226 pages (Currier 1976), in the same way the generators on this record switch on the paragraph mark or the section. It is therefore the two-tables-per-dialect writer P-G-018 describes, and what is new here is not the two stocks but the rotation null: P-G-018's version passed the deal null on 2 of 3 seeds and the rotation null on none of 3. Control that fixes what carries it: the same writer with ONE stock for the whole book, labels ignored, everything else alike, gives -0.055, -0.061, -0.053 on seeds 1 to 3 and fails. Nothing was tuned against the fact: a hot-core boost was tried at 2 to 30 times, found unnecessary and dropped, so the submitted text uses each stock's plain frequencies; the reuse and variation settings (0.25 from 300 words, glyph change 0.15, fresh word 0.10, order-3 chain) were taken from the published line chain of R-017 and left alone. Local check on the practice split, where the fact stands at 0.122 with shuffle p = 0.005 and rotation p = 0.0294 at its floor of 1/34: this text (seed 1) gives 0.139, shuffle p = 0.005, rotation p = 0.0294, and its observed value exceeds the LARGEST of the 33 label rotations (0.054) by +0.085. Five further seeds give 0.066, 0.087, 0.114, 0.117, 0.122, all passing both nulls, with rotation margins +0.056 and +0.082 on the two further seeds measured. The margin is real where the manuscript's is not: F-020's own note says the rotation null has no margin at this sample size, and this text clears every shift on all six runs. Guards: 38,486 words in 4,487 ordinary lines and 738 paragraph-opening lines, exactly the manuscript's line counts; 0 four-word runs of the manuscript; 0 uncertainty markers; 9,376 distinct words, mean length 4.9; the words are the manuscript's own, as a period word-list would use them, shared type share 0.85. What it shows, if it holds on the hidden pages: F-020 does not separate the dialect contrast from a writer who keeps two word-lists and takes them up in the book's order, including the long-range part the label rotation is meant to catch; the fact adds nothing to what the labels already say, and it is no evidence of meaning. What it does not show: that the manuscript was made that way. Assumption that could fail on the hidden pages: the hidden sample's own label layout decides the rotation null, and the margins above were measured on the practice sample of 29 labelled pages; a hidden sample made of longer unbroken runs of one label would leave a shift less to break.

Local check on the practice split, where the fact stands at 0.122 with shuffle p = 0.005 and rotation p = 0.0294 at its floor of 1/34: this text (seed 1) gives 0.139, shuffle p = 0.005, rotation p = 0.0294, and its observed value exceeds the LARGEST of the 33 label rotations (0.054) by +0.085. The margin is real where the manuscript's is not: F-020's own note says the rotation null has no margin at this sample size, and this text clears every shift on all six runs. Guards: 38,486 words in 4,487 ordinary lines and 738 paragraph-opening lines, exactly the manuscript's line counts; 0 four-word runs of the manuscript; 0 uncertainty markers; 9,376 distinct words, mean length 4.9; the words are the manuscript's own, as a period word-list would use them, shared type share 0.85.
