title: fact attack on F-020

detail.why: the fact also holds on text made without language

statement:
One procedure, a copyist, fitted on the 192 public training pages only. It keeps the manuscript's own word stock (the 1500 commonest words of the public pages, with their frequencies), its line lengths, its page order and its paragraph marks, and writes a word at a time. For each word it does one of three things. With probability 0.30 it reaches back into what it has just written, at a distance drawn from a mixture of two exponentials (weight 0.55, tau 15 words, and weight 0.45, tau 60 words, capped at 200), and copies that word; a word fetched from within 8 words is then restated with one glyph changed with probability 0.60, while a word fetched from further back is restated that way with probability 0.50 -- a word still in the hand slips, a word fetched from a distance is written as it was. Otherwise it draws from the stock's frequency list. With probability 0.05 it invents a word, shaped by an order-3 glyph chain over the stock. Nothing else: no rule names a neighbour line, a distance, or the statistic.
FITTED, and to what. The reach mixture, the two slip rates and the 8-word split were fitted by coordinate descent to six moments measured on the public training pages: identical repeat within 200 words (0.4025), identical-or-one-glyph within 200 (0.7586), one-glyph neighbour on the line above (0.1860), the same four lines up (0.1646), within-page reuse (0.3034), and the share of identical repeats sitting within 14 words (0.2392). Two further mechanisms were tried and dropped because they did not improve that fit: a per-page lexicon (Gamma tilt on the stock) and a recency avoidance that rejects a word already written in the last 200. The repetition rate 0.30 was then set so the text reproduces the manuscript's own value of the quantity F-021 measures, and the seed was chosen as the one whose value tracks the manuscript's across 24 random 34-page subsets of the public pages (paired mean absolute deviation 0.0084; the manuscript's own spread over those subsets is 0.0078 to 0.0376, so this text is as steady as the manuscript, not steadier). The band, the null and the held-out pages were not used to choose anything; the held-out number is reported after the choice. One seed that tracked the manuscript slightly better was dropped because its text contained one four-word run of the manuscript.
WHAT CARRIES IT. Two controls, same generator, held-out pages, seeds 1 to 3. Same amount of copying but distance-blind -- reach uniform over the last 200 words: -0.008, 0.006, 0.013. No copying at all: 0.009, -0.012, 0.013. Both collapse to the chance level of sampling the manuscript's own word list (near 0.121, far 0.117, excess 0.004). So it is not repetition that produces the fact but the DISTANCE PROFILE of the repetition: short reaches slip into one-glyph variants, and that is what raises the line above the current one relative to four lines up.
RESULT. On the held-out practice pages this text gives 0.020697 against the fact's band 0.012 to 0.045, with shuffle_within_page p = 0.005 at 199 permutations: it passes. The five other seeds measured on the same held-out pages give 0.031, 0.041, 0.019, 0.043, 0.022, all passing, so the pass is not a lucky seed.
A FINDING ABOUT THE FACT ITSELF, from the public pages only: read on 34-page samples drawn from the 192 public pages, the manuscript's own value of this statistic falls below the fact's floor of 0.012 on some samples (minimum 0.0078 over 24 draws). The band is narrower than the sampling noise of the quantity it states, which is why an attack can sit inside it without resembling the manuscript in any other way, and why a failure on the hidden pages would say as much about the band as about the text.
GUARDS. 38,486 words in 4,487 ordinary lines and 738 paragraph-opening lines, exactly the manuscript's line counts; 0 four-word runs of the manuscript; 0 uncertainty markers; 5,456 distinct words, mean length 4.48.
WHAT IT WOULD SHOW, if it holds: a text with no language in it -- no morphology, no collocations, no phrase, a vocabulary sampled from a frequency list -- can carry F-021's near-versus-far elevation, because a copyist who restates what he has just written and copies what he wrote long ago produces exactly that profile. The fact would then be a statement about copying, not about meaning. WHAT IT WOULD NOT SHOW: that the manuscript was made by such a copyist, only that this fact cannot tell the two apart. ASSUMPTION THAT COULD FAIL ON THE HIDDEN PAGES: the hidden 34 pages are one draw, and on draws of that size this text's value ranges 0.011 to 0.040; a draw near either edge of the band would fail for reasons the practice pages cannot see.

detail.why: the text reproduces 15 of 19 established facts

statement:
A paper-card writer keeps four positions in its register (single word, line entry, line body and line exit) and separate registers for opening and ordinary lines. Fit their weighted word-card counts, length distributions and EVA-basic glyph counts on certain paragraph lines in the public ZL practice training split. A line starts with a blank edge mark. Each new word takes the previous card's final glyph as its edge mark. The register looks up cards by position, opening status and edge mark, falling back to the position table for a lookup with fewer than 14 observations. Every register weight is multiplied by the same final-glyph factor, ((position count + 1)/(pooled count + 4)) to the power 0.8. The conditional card count is used to power 1 at an entry or exit and 0.67 in the body.

In the body, a four-slot rolling tray supplies a card with probability 0.56 and a thirteen-slot reserve tray with probability 0.29. Each tray renews one randomly chosen slot after a line. Cards are drawn with replacement from body-word counts in one randomly chosen bank of 24 consecutive public training folios, changing banks after each 35 ordinary lines. Opening lines use a separate pair of trays along the same sequence of banks, paced by the opening-line fraction in the training data. The draw within a tray weights each card by its opening-status and final-glyph weights and the compatibility of its initial glyph with the edge mark. Full-word shapes are on the cards from the start. A card's selection does not depend on whether it was written earlier. Another 0.09 of body draws come from the current bank's full register and the remaining 0.06 from the pooled register. Starts and exits use the pooled register.

A rolling-tray draw switches one fragment with probability 0.88. A register draw in the body switches one with probability 0.40. The reserve tray retains the card intact. A fragment is one glyph in EVA-basic. The writer shuffles the inner slots and also considers the final slot with probability 0.14. At the first available switch, it selects an alternate glyph weighted by the 0.8 power of public counts conditioned on the two surrounding glyphs, or by the final-glyph table for the preceding glyph and position when switching an ending. Whole words, meaning categories, folio identifiers, and Currier and section labels play no role in choosing when a tray is replenished. The counts may be implemented with weighted slips or indexed dice tables. No glyph is singled out in any rule.

Practice-only exploration compared more diffuse and more concentrated trays at the same primary seed. The submitted text is seed 408, comprising 2,200 ordinary lines and 2,200 opening lines. Exact in-line four-grams were screened against the scorer's public copy guard and a colliding line redrawn. There are 38,640 words and no uncertainty marks. On the public practice split the specimen reproduced 14 of 19 facts. The long-word within-page reuse share was 0.278, and dependency on the line above by one-edit variants had an excess of 0.0134. The same fixed settings with seeds 409 and 410 gave reuse 0.271 and 0.284, and one-edit excess 0.0206 and 0.0200. The same seed with both trays disabled dropped reuse to 0.098. The interior paragraph-opener effect F-019 fell below threshold in seeds 409 and 410. The line cut packs the sampled pages next to one another in the synthetic text, so the F-011 result alone does not establish similarity at the same physical distance across a full book.

detail.statement:
I counted seven small stars in a compact group in the upper-left sector of the right-hand wheel. The five-sign group at f68r3.11 sits immediately to their right. The large single star on the left has its own label below it, f68r3.10. The curved link towards the centre has a separate label, f68r3.12. The pinned Zandbergen–Landini and Takahashi readings of .11 are doaro. The RF reading is doary. The separate astronomical locus .12 is oalcheol in those three EVA transcriptions.

Figure 4 of Bax’s original 2014 paper highlights this exact word. On pp. 19–21 and in Figure 5 he proposes taurn, approximately /taərn/, as a possible name for Taurus. It is an expressly speculative reading that takes the adjacent drawing as its starting point, with the particular language and final sign uncertain. Stolfi’s folio notes independently suggest the same locus may denote the Pleiades themselves. Zandbergen’s folio entry lists the seven classical planets as an alternative identification of the picture.

The scan supports associating the locus with the small cluster, and the original paper settles which word Bax discussed. The evidence for its name still depends on interpretation of the image. Pleiades and Taurus name different astronomical objects, and the readings in the sources leave the choice open. The scoring consequence matters because the current name matcher gives taurn versus taurus a similarity of 0.667, above the 0.60 threshold. I therefore dissent from accepting the proposed names as an external lexical benchmark for criterion (c).
detail.title: Second look at N-006: DISSENT on the name match

detail.findings: For a 5% final rate versus a 1% interior rate, detection was 70.7%, 38.3%, 3.1% and 0% as the locked share rose. For a 10% final rate the corresponding rates were 99.5%, 89.6%, 15.7% and 0%. With no effect the four rejection counts were 5, 5, 0 and 0 out of 1,500, consistent with conservative discrete tests. The JSON includes the full grid and Wilson intervals.
detail.interpretation: Given k marked tokens among n noninitial slots, the unfrozen final token is marked with probability k/n under a uniform within-line permutation. Independent lines give a Poisson-binomial tail. Fixed endpoints contribute the same constant to the observation and every draw, so they cancel from the tail. At complete fixation all draws tie and the inclusive p-value is 1 by construction. The production DSL rejects such an immobile null. The pilot keeps initials fixed in every condition and measures permutation power for a count at one layout and set of masks. F-001 additionally uses a ratio cutoff and permutes whole words, including initial slots. The pilot contains no measured feature rates from the manuscript and leaves the actual source of its line-final effects open.
detail.reproduction: Write `python` to null_power.py and results.plan to plan.json. Run from the checkout with PYTHONHASHSEED=0 PYTHONPATH=. python3 null_power.py plan.json result.json after fetching the pinned inputs. Two runs produced byte-identical JSON. The tail was also compared to exhaustive enumeration on 30 independently drawn small examples.

Use 1,500 independent replicate books per rate. On the same book compare four conditional permutation nulls that fix 0%, 50%, 90%, or 100% of observed line endings. detail.check: Reproduce the saved scores on the pinned public corpus. For a confirmatory hand-specific test, first identify additional independent same-section and same-Currier blocks with multiple hands, then freeze matching and an independent block-level contrast. Keep the copying and planted-hand controls and compare NMF with raw TF-IDF from the same training-only transform.
detail.controls: The copying baseline samples a pooled training-only word distribution with one-third probability of copying one of the preceding 30 tokens, resetting the window at each physical block. It preserves the number of tokens per page. The synthetic planted control independently replaces words with hand-specific tokens at probability 15% on the same layout to check that the analysis can carry a handwriting-correlated lexical signal.
detail.findings: The 162-page eligible inventory yields 342 broad matched triples, all herbal, from 39 anchor folios across four held blocks. For 40-word samples the block-averaged same-hand NMF win rates are 86.4% in ZL and 85.8% in Takahashi. Raw TF-IDF gives 84.8% and 81.0%. A pooled copying baseline generated without hand or section labels gives 53.8% and 44.6% for NMF, while adding a fixed 15% planted hand vocabulary gives 93.8% and 93.9%. Requiring the same Currier variety leaves just 10 overlapping comparisons of hands 2 and 5, three anchor folios and two blocks. NMF rates there are 70.0% and 69.4%, driven by one block with 100% wins and one with about 40%. Raw TF-IDF already gives 85.8% and 79.4% on that small subset. The data table includes 20-word, exact-distance and same-side sensitivities.
detail.interpretation: A win means the anchor is closer to the same-hand comparison than to the different-hand comparison in cosine similarity, with half credit for ties. Average triples within each anchor folio, then average folios within block and give each held block equal weight. The broad botanical contrast joins differences in scribal hand and Currier variety. The limited within-B comparisons and unequal block scores leave the magnitude of a hand effect independent of dialect unresolved. Both transcriptions describe the same folios and therefore test transcription sensitivity. Overlapping comparisons are not independent trials. No p-value treating them as independent is reported.
detail.reproduction: Write python to nmf_matched.py and results.plan to plan.json. From the pinned checkout run OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 PYTHONHASHSEED=0 PYTHONPATH=. python3 nmf_matched.py plan.json result.json, with the NumPy and scikit-learn versions in results. The estimator is an unregularized five-topic TF-IDF NMF pilot. Raising the iteration limit from 1,200 to 3,000 eliminated one convergence warning and changed none of the four primary observed 40-word win rates.
detail.source: Rachel Sterneck, Annie Polish and Claire Bowern, Topic Modeling in the Voynich Manuscript (2021), sections 3 and 4.3–4.5. https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.02858
detail.statement: Starting from Sterneck, Polish and Bowern (2021), compare unsupervised NMF and raw TF-IDF similarity in held-apart, same-section triples. Use only the pinned public practice training pool shared by ZL and Takahashi with matching metadata and at least 50 certain paragraph tokens in each. Within each held-out 16-folio block, match an anchor with a same-hand and a different-hand folio. Require distinct physical folios, both distances at most 12 folios and within two folios of each other, and a maximum token-count ratio of 1.25 across the three pages in both editions. Freeze the common page support before looking at word similarities. Fit each vocabulary, IDF and five-topic NMF in other blocks with one surrounding block on each side excluded. Draw 40 words per page for the primary comparison and 20 for sensitivity, using six fixed seeds.

The fitted stationary control draws from the paired training edition’s pooled word stock and copies a randomly chosen form among the previous 30 tokens with probability 0.33. detail.findings: The mean within-page autocorrelation at lags 21–40 is 0.0502 in ZL and 0.0501 in Takahashi. Against a global word shuffle the means of the controls are near −0.001 and both upper-tail ranks are 0.01. Page-line and paragraph-word shuffles give means of approximately 0.057 in both transcriptions (upper-tail ranks at least 0.99). Line-glyph-slot shuffles yield 0.0450 and 0.0446, leaving residuals of 0.0052 and 0.0055 at rank 0.01. The stationary exact-copy control is near zero. detail.interpretation: The common test uses raw EVA characters, including separate c and h, chosen with at least 1,000 training occurrences in both readings. The pinned IVTFF parser splits uncertain word separators by default. A coefficient requires at least 30 pairs. The aggregate equally weights retained character-lag cells on the support shared by the observed case and all controls. Word spaces are separate from the character aggregate. Report empirical upper-tail ranks and null intervals, with no decisions based on individual lags. The nulls preserve different margins, so the differences across their means do not isolate causal contributions. The experiment is a public conditional comparison and does not determine whether the manuscript encodes language.

"""Compare the registered Hannig key on standard and case-preserving public GC input."""

from collections import Counter
import inspect
import json
from pathlib import Path
import re
import sys

from vs import corpus, ivtff, judge, models, views
from vs.families.substitution import decode_word


def preserving_cleaner():
    source = inspect.getsource(ivtff.clean_text)
    needle = '    s = s.lower()\n'
    assert source.count(needle) == 1
    namespace = {'re': re}
    exec(compile(source.replace(needle, ''), '<case-preserving-IVTFF>', 'exec'), namespace)
    return namespace['clean_text']


def character_counts(pages):
    return Counter(char for page in pages for line in page.lines for word in line.words for char in word)


def words_by_line(pages):
    return {line.id: line.words for page in pages for line in page.lines}


def coverage_report(prior, preserved, key):
    folded = words_by_line(prior)
    original = words_by_line(preserved)
    assert original.keys() == folded.keys()
    assert all([word.lower() for word in words] == folded[locus] for locus, words in original.items())
    standard = character_counts(prior)
    raw = character_counts(preserved)

    def decoded(word):
        return decode_word(word, key['key'], lambda word: ivtff.segment(word, 'eva-raw'))

    return {
        'folded_n_lower': standard['n'],
        'folded_N_upper': standard['N'],
        'preserved_n_lower': raw['n'],
        'preserved_N_upper': raw['N'],
        'different_decoded_words': sum(
            decoded(left) != decoded(right)
            for locus, words in original.items() for left, right in zip(words, folded[locus], strict=True)
        ),
        'all_words': sum(map(len, original.values())),
        'uppercase_units_raw': {char: count for char, count in sorted(raw.items()) if char.isupper()},
    }


def public_report(key, train, practice):
    train = views.apply(models.scoped(train, key.get('scope')), key)
    practice = views.apply(models.scoped(practice, key.get('scope')), key)
    r = judge.evaluate(key, train, practice, 'practice')
    return {
        'verdict': r['verdict'],
        'failed': r['failed'],
        'pages_evaluated': r['pages_evaluated'],
        'pages_passing': r['pages_passing'],
        'a_compresses': r['a_compresses'],
        'b_reads': r['b_reads'],
        'killed_by': [name for name, row in r['kill_tests']['decoys'].items() if row['killed']],
    }


def main():
    mode, output = sys.argv[1:3]
    key = judge.load_key('experiments/K-019-open-1/fleet-corpora/key.json')
    assert key['transliteration'] == 'gc'
    views.check(key)
    folded = corpus.split_pages('practice', 'gc')
    cleaner = preserving_cleaner()
    assert ivtff.clean_text('a.N.n')[0] == ['a', 'n', 'n']
    assert cleaner('a.N.n')[0] == ['a', 'N', 'n']
    stock = ivtff.clean_text
    try:
        ivtff.clean_text = cleaner
        corpus.pages.cache_clear()
        preserved = corpus.split_pages('practice', 'gc')
    finally:
        ivtff.clean_text = stock
        corpus.pages.cache_clear()
    coverage = {split: coverage_report(fold, raw, key) for split, fold, raw in zip(('train', 'practice'), folded, preserved)}
    print(mode, coverage['practice'], flush=True)
    report = public_report(key, *(preserved if mode == 'case_preserved' else folded))
    summary = {'mode': mode, 'input_audit': coverage, 'evaluation': report}
    Path(output).write_text(json.dumps(summary, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False) + '\n')
    print(report['verdict'], report['failed'], report['a_compresses']['savings'], flush=True)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

findings: ZL has 25/791 ed among od/ed sites on public training A versus 4,106/5,035 on B. The public evaluation pages give 6/156 versus 677/773. Takahashi and RF have the same direction in both partitions.

Across one thousand equal-leaf draws within the herbal section, with 16 B leaves and 16 A leaves drawn from 47, the median B minus A ed-site fraction is 68.0 percentage points in ZL, 67.1 in Takahashi and 59.4 in RF. Every draw is positive. Herbal A and B have disjoint hand assignments. This is a leaf-count sensitivity check and does not match the number of tokens.

The only shared section and hand in the public corpus is the star-marked recipe group, hand 3. Both A pages are sides of a single leaf, f58, with 7/37 ed sites in ZL and Takahashi. All 12 B leaves have higher fractions in every edition. The A leaf is in quire H, while the hand-3 B pages are in quire T. The 1 versus 12 comparison allows no robust estimate of between-leaf A variation.

The four-way training tally confirms the asymmetry while retaining its counterexample. At a minimum of two occurrences, ZL and Takahashi agree on 50 B-only ed edges and one A-only od edge, cthody/cthedy. At a minimum of four the counts are 37 and one. Each edition has zero all-section A-only ed and B-only od edges under the shared partner rule. This is an attestation threshold, not evidence of absence from the wider language or of date.

For Timm’s four exact pairs within interiors of B training lines at distances 1–10, ZL gives 5 od-first and 2 ed-first pairs (leaf sign-flip upper tail 0.1875), Takahashi gives 6 and 3 (0.2266). For all single-site od→ed pairs the respective counts tie 8/8 and 9/9. The public evaluation sample has at most one pair among the named four per edition. The local-order check is sparse and does not date leaves.
detail.interpretation: The literal absence premise fails against the source’s own counts and the public manuscript readings. The strong aggregate preference remains over the comparisons we can make. The labels themselves were chosen partly from glyph patterns, so their association with spelling is descriptive. The current bound order supplies no independent direction of composition. These observations leave the order of writing unresolved.
detail.methods: Use the pinned corpus public practice partition, P lines and parsed words that match lowercase a–z. Count occurrences of either exact contiguous two-character sequence ed or od, including inside longer forms. Treat both sides and any panels of one numbered leaf as one unit for leaf-level calculations. Keep each edition separate. RF combines earlier transcriptions, so it is a robustness comparison and supplies no third independent witness. For local direction compare every pair of positions 1–10 apart that contains distinct exact variants separated by a single od-to-ed edit. detail.limitations: The two independent readings were by separately prompted image models, not human palaeographers. Crops include the preceding letter because counting the independent strokes depends on a boundary that is often hard to see. Some crop edges catch neighboring lines. The six pages were chosen for tractable matching, including only one page of hand 3. Differences between these samples cannot establish a hand effect. The pilot gives mixed evidence about the absolute zero-versus-one threshold, and it does not decide whether the two strings encode distinct letters.

method.annotation: Random order via Python random.Random(1731). Each isolated image-model reader saw only the contact sheet with numbered crops and an A/B/C reference card cut from the published chart. Readers had no access to the token strings, folio IDs, or one another’s labels. Crop preparers had access to the source strings to locate tokens and did not contribute labels. Leave indecision visible rather than imputing it. Broad family groups A/B/C as curl and D as other. The stricter target subset is A/B. A readable ordered pair outranks a tied or reversed pair in the relative stroke check, which is exploratory.
method.class_A: Return curl with no independent short diagonal stroke before it.
method.class_B: Return curl with one independent short diagonal stroke before it.
method.class_C: Return curl with two or more preceding short strokes.
method.class_D: Visibly different terminal, for example a distinct descender.
method.nearest_pairs: After unmasking, compare the uppercase token with a lowercase token of identical preceding v101 string on the same page. Choose smallest absolute difference in locus line number, break ties toward earlier line, then closest word ordinal and earlier ordinal. Holds the stems and pages fixed.

reproduction.readers: Masked observations are recorded verbatim as class labels in the trial rows. T10 was obscured by low contrast for both readers. Reader B also left T23 unresolved because the terminal ink obscured segmentation.

results_summary: The two readers agreed on the broad curl-versus-other family in 21/21 jointly readable trials. Exact A/B/C/D labels agreed in 18/21. Both labeled all four controls as expected.

Against Claston’s listed target distinctions, exact matches are 10/19 and 8/19, counting unresolved annotations as missing matches. Both label 7/11 lowercase targets B. The readers label 3/8 and 1/8 uppercase targets A. Four lowercase targets receive C from both readers.

Both members of the neighboring f55v.5 pair were read as expected by both readers. The readers differ on the uppercase target in f75r.9. On f103v, the eight total crops include three uppercase targets, and neither reader labeled any of the three A.

Under the nearest-pair ranking, the uppercase target has fewer apparent short strokes in 6 pairs, ties in 1 and is unresolved in 1 for reader A. For reader B the respective counts are 2, 4 and 2. Neither reader observes a reversed pair.
detail.selection: Purposive pilot with six pages chosen for identifiable same-page word pairs and coverage of hands 1, 2 and 3. There are 8 uppercase target tokens, 11 lowercase target tokens and 4 controls. Most pairing stems are represented by one nearby lowercase match. The dataset keeps extra copies on f75r and f103v to show local variation. Group labels were sealed before either image reader saw the shuffled panel. Using certain paragraph words ending in N or n in the public training partition, hand 1 has 53 N and 206 n, hand 2 has 13 N and 474 n, hand 3 has 22 N and 623 n, hand 4 has 0 N and 2 n, and hand 5 has 0 N and 11 n. The unassigned pages contribute 2 N and 26 n. The pilot intentionally targets hands with both cases available in training.

established: Table 2 and Figure 8 report spectral peaks at periods of 5.9 and 46.1 characters in the spaceless Voynich sample. A character shuffle removed both peaks, and a whole-token shuffle removed the 46.1-character peak.

Figure 8 compares those scales with a line-length histogram whose two modes were 6 and 44 characters. Landini associates the short mode with isolated labels and the longer one with folios rich in paragraphs.

The manuscript spectrum also differed from its scrambles at scales above 400 characters. The paper discusses uneven symbol densities, changes across sections, and the insertion of labels as possible contributors.

On public training pages fix the segmentation, treatment of uncertain signs, Fourier smoothing, and a band around the modal stripped line length. Report the two null comparisons separately and check the same procedure on public practice pages before proposing a held-out statistic.

check: Repeat the recorded contrasts and score both printed and stated-rule readings at the published weights and 5% rank threshold. Verify that matching immediate left contexts leaves both candidate scores equal despite distinct right contexts. Test a separately fitted direct-emission line chain and compare manuscript rank sensitivity to the single-context Pearson convention.

detail.check: Repeat the recorded contrasts and score both printed and stated-rule readings at the published weights and 5% rank threshold. Verify that matching immediate left contexts leaves both candidate scores equal despite distinct right contexts. Test a separately fitted direct-emission line chain and compare manuscript rank sensitivity to the single-context Pearson convention.
findings: For word-position matching only at full matched coverage, eight comparisons met the frequency threshold. The wrong constituents have a better loss in six, while the true ones have a better loss in two. This is 3 of 4 wrong wins in training and 3 of 4 in the separate control blocks. Both alternatives fall within the published 5% cutoff in four cases. At half coverage the wrong option wins 5 of 7 eligible trials, and neither option passes the cutoff in any eligible case.

All 13 eligible comparisons in the exact-left condition tie across the three replacement fractions. All 36 exact-left trials, including below-support cases, have differing right-context incidence counts. The loss depends on the candidate’s left contexts, frequency and self-adjacency. These are shared by X and Z, while the candidate components and their directed pair frequency are fixed. The score therefore ties even when the right contexts differ.

The three shuffled Euler trails change 91.4–92.3% of positions while preserving every loss, over 9,702, 9,702 and 11,132 eligible triplets respectively. This invariance follows from the use of unigram and adjacent-pair counts as the only numerical inputs.

In twelve direct-emission stationary line simulations, m with i,d falls in the best 5% in all twelve, and q with i,e in eight. Under both Rule 3/6 conventions, those results hold without combining any symbols.

For q with i,e, the rarer glyph contributes just one realized incoming context after trimming in each public evaluation edition. The prose-based rank moves from 4.41% to 9.63% in ZL and from 4.39% to 9.86% in Takahashi when assigning loss one instead of zero to that undefined singleton correlation. This crosses the paper’s cutoff with the text and all other rules fixed.
detail.interpretation: A low triplet percentile can arise for an incorrect constituent pair or for directly generated glyphs. This calibration addresses statistical specificity. Independent visual evidence can still support a ligature hypothesis. Most partial fusions lack frequency support, and these contrasts share a first component by design, so the results do not estimate error rates over every possible ligature.

methods.exact_surrogates: For the first natural contrast of each language’s control block at full matched coverage, shuffle the directed adjacency list of every glyph and reconstruct an Euler trail beginning with the original first glyph. The output draws individual glyphs from the fixed edge multiset and never does a pair replacement during generation. It is conditioned on the positive sample’s observed incidence matrix and preserves the entire unigram and adjacent-pair counts by construction. This control tests identifiability from those inputs, not the plausibility of its whole-text generator.
methods.loss: Use the joint adjacency matrix with spaces and zero edges below 0.2% of either their row or column. Rank all ordered triplets whose non-space glyphs exceed the published support ratio 500/229431, excluding a candidate used as its own component, and include ties in the percentile. Hold weights 1,100,1,1,100,1,1,10. Literal mode follows printed Rule 3 (shared contexts) and Rule 6 ((1−min)/max). Prose-based mode uses unshared contexts for Rule 3 and 1−min/max for Rule 6, following the prior experiment’s alternative. The paper describes a zero loss for empty contexts. Our primary analysis also uses zero for a singleton left context, where Pearson is undefined. For the public manuscript we rerun with a loss of one for that singleton. Zero correlation is assigned if either realized vector has zero variance with at least two contexts.
methods.natural_text: Use separate vs.refcorpus train_text and control_text block sets for English, Latin and Italian. Take up to 40,000 characters before the final partial word with single spaces. Fix first and second pairs as th/to and ea/er, en/es and pa/pe, ch/co and de/di respectively. For each word-position class shuffle the two occurrence lists with seed 9141 or 9142, attempt pairs in that order, and discard any pair whose edits overlap or touch previously accepted edits or one another. Shuffle accepted pairs with the same generator. Take 25%, 50% or 100% of the accepted pool, rounding down. Full-pool coverage of all original target occurrences has median 83.9% for positions only and 64.1% when the immediate previous glyph also matches. X and Z have exactly the same counts and no self-adjacent occurrences.
methods.stationary_lines: Fit an initial-glyph distribution and one shared internal character transition table on public practice training paragraph lines for each edition. Use only raw certain ASCII EVA words with single spacing. Independently emit the public evaluation line lengths with the fixed table and seeds 7810–7815, disallowing a trailing space so the scoring stream contains one separator between lines. No pair-to-symbol rule is used. Score the two real public partitions separately in ZL and Takahashi under the same preprocessing.

These are shared by X and Z, while the candidate components and their directed pair frequency are fixed. The score therefore ties even when the right contexts differ.

The three shuffled Euler trails change 91.4–92.3% of positions while preserving every loss, over 9,702, 9,702 and 11,132 eligible triplets respectively. This invariance follows from the use of unigram and adjacent-pair counts as the only numerical inputs.

In twelve direct-emission stationary line simulations, m with i,d falls in the best 5% in all twelve, and q with i,e in eight. Under both Rule 3/6 conventions, those results hold without combining any symbols.

For q with i,e, the rarer glyph contributes just one realized incoming context after trimming in each public evaluation edition. The prose-based rank moves from 4.41% to 9.63% in ZL and from 4.39% to 9.86% in Takahashi when assigning loss one instead of zero to that undefined singleton correlation. This crosses the paper’s cutoff with the text and all other rules fixed.
step.json.interpretation: A low triplet percentile can arise for an incorrect constituent pair or for directly generated glyphs. This calibration addresses statistical specificity. Independent visual evidence can still support a ligature hypothesis. Most partial fusions lack frequency support, and these contrasts share a first component by design, so the results do not estimate error rates over every possible ligature.

methods.exact_surrogates: For the first natural contrast of each language’s control block at full matched coverage, shuffle the directed adjacency list of every glyph and reconstruct an Euler trail beginning with the original first glyph. The output draws individual glyphs from the fixed edge multiset and never does a pair replacement during generation. It is conditioned on the positive sample’s observed incidence matrix and preserves the entire unigram and adjacent-pair counts by construction. This control tests identifiability from those inputs, not the plausibility of its whole-text generator.
methods.loss: Use the joint adjacency matrix with spaces and zero edges below 0.2% of either their row or column. Rank all ordered triplets whose non-space glyphs exceed the published support ratio 500/229431, excluding a candidate used as its own component, and include ties in the percentile. Hold weights 1,100,1,1,100,1,1,10. Literal mode follows printed Rule 3 (shared contexts) and Rule 6 ((1−min)/max). Prose-based mode uses unshared contexts for Rule 3 and 1−min/max for Rule 6, following the prior experiment’s alternative. The paper describes a zero loss for empty contexts. Our primary analysis also uses zero for a singleton left context, where Pearson is undefined. For the public manuscript we rerun with a loss of one for that singleton. Zero correlation is assigned if either realized vector has zero variance with at least two contexts.
methods.natural_text: Use separate vs.refcorpus train_text and control_text block sets for English, Latin and Italian. Take up to 40,000 characters before the final partial word with single spaces. Fix first and second pairs as th/to and ea/er, en/es and pa/pe, ch/co and de/di respectively. For each word-position class shuffle the two occurrence lists with seed 9141 or 9142, attempt pairs in that order, and discard any pair whose edits overlap or touch previously accepted edits or one another. Shuffle accepted pairs with the same generator. Take 25%, 50% or 100% of the accepted pool, rounding down. Full-pool coverage of all original target occurrences has median 83.9% for positions only and 64.1% when the immediate previous glyph also matches. X and Z have exactly the same counts and no self-adjacent occurrences.
methods.stationary_lines: Fit an initial-glyph distribution and one shared internal character transition table on public practice training paragraph lines for each edition. Use only raw certain ASCII EVA words with single spacing. Independently emit the public evaluation line lengths with the fixed table and seeds 7810–7815, disallowing a trailing space so the scoring stream contains one separator between lines. No pair-to-symbol rule is used. Score the two real public partitions separately in ZL and Takahashi under the same preprocessing.

statement: A 15th-century copyist carries one rolling word-slip tray, a deeper reserve and a reusable letter jig. At each new quire packet the same physical stock is replenished from neighboring pages of a public practice transcript, using a fixed 18-page packet and a 3.5% card refresh chance per written word. On a turn the writer draws a whole-word slip from the recently written line or page, then from the active packet, or sets a fresh spelling with the letter jig learned from public training pages; ordinary one- and two-glyph copying slips are resolved through local context-conditioned letter cards. The preceding word can guide the next card through the shared edges of slips in the public letter table; a separate card position is used at the beginning and end of a written line. The drawers are reloaded in manuscript order and retained for a packet before the next packet is reached. A page or paragraph boundary clears the short rolling tray, as when a copyist changes leaf or starts a new passage. Card choice uses no semantic categories, section labels, Currier labels, or rule about any target glyph, length, repetition count or page statistic. This single setting and seed were fixed before the practice score was read.

design.center_and_spectrum: Pool training line lengths across editions. Select the most frequent length after a symmetric triangular histogram smoother with weights 1,2,3,2,1, using the smaller length if tied. This selects 44. Use nonoverlapping windows of 1,024 positions with a periodic Hann taper. For each frequency sum one-hot glyph squared Fourier magnitudes, normalize by the taper energy, and average over full windows. Compare the mean power over periods 0.90–1.10 times 44 and the ratio of that band power to the mean of two shoulder means, with period factors 0.65–0.80 and 1.25–1.50. Each edition uses 25 full windows in evaluation.
design.input: Match public ZL and IT paragraph line ids in ZL physical order. Retain the line when both editions have at least one word and only unambiguous lowercase ASCII glyph codes in every word. Remove all spaces. Keep raw EVA characters as units. The training counts are 3,277 shared lines, with 138,478 ZL and 138,402 IT glyphs. The evaluation counts are 626 shared lines, with 25,910 ZL and 25,918 IT glyphs.
design.nulls: The global permutation keeps the observed overall glyph stock. For each numbered folio, permutation of all interior glyphs together holds the full folio inventory, exact length of each retained line, and positions of both endpoint glyphs. The stronger within-line permutation also keeps each line’s inventory. Verify these invariants for fixed diagnostic seed 512. Use 19 draws per initial training comparison and 99 per primary evaluation comparison. Upper-tail ranks include ties and add one to numerator and denominator. Use each complete simulated text as a replicate rather than counting windows or Fourier bins as independent tests.
design.sensitivities: Repeat in nonoverlapping 512-position blocks entirely within a numbered folio and with 49 draws. Separately retain the shared paragraph loci with any clean words in both editions, omit uncertain words only, and run the fixed 1,024-position test. A pulse control introduces a new glyph at repeated phases of the closest selected Fourier bin, keeping known line edges untouched. A separate geometry-only control simulates independent letters from training first-two, last-two and interior position distributions and the evaluation line-length array.

findings: The ZL and Takahashi training band-to-shoulder ratios are 1.019 and 1.022. Against the folio-interior controls their upper-tail ranks are 0.40 and 0.10. Against the global controls the ranks are 0.35 and 0.15.

The primary evaluation ratios are 0.895 and 0.883. Against the global glyph controls both upper-tail ranks are 1.00. Against the endpoint-preserving folio interiors they are 0.99 and 1.00. Across these four comparisons, total band power is approximately 68–70% of the shuffle median. Leaving every line’s glyph stock intact also gives upper-tail ranks 1.00 for both ratios.

Using only the 16,896 glyphs in complete windows that stay within a numbered folio gives ratios of 1.022 and 1.014. Against folio interiors the ranks are 0.30 and 0.36. Relaxing the word certainty filter keeps 651 matched loci and gives ratios 0.981 and 0.960, with folio-interior ranks 0.70 and 0.86.

The injected pulse at 44.52 characters gives a band-to-shoulder ratio of 1.176 and exceeds all 19 global and all 19 folio-interior shuffles. The six boundary-only realizations have ratios 0.980–1.068, with every global-shuffle upper-tail rank at least 0.10. This small geometry calibration is specific to the chosen edge model.

reproduction.instructions: Write the embedded scripts with the given names to one temporary directory. From the repo root use PYTHONPATH=. python3 /path/voynich_spectral_lines.py and then PYTHONPATH=. python3 /path/voynich_spectral_geometry.py. The second script imports the first. Only the public practice split is used.

detail.scope: This is a public robustness check with paired paragraph sampling, explicit treatment of uncertain loci, and Welch band averaging. Landini used a long continuous stream and logarithmic frequency smoothing. An isolated narrow peak or a feature of his original sample requires a separate estimate at that scale. The present public result supports withholding a positive line-band criterion.

detail.additional_text_checks: The exact word fochor occurs once in each of the public pinned ZL, Takahashi and RF texts, at the opening paragraph position on f9v. The literal sequence folor occurs at f43r.1, token 8 in ZL and Takahashi, which makes specifying Vatne’s physical locus important. Textual rarity does not supply an independent plant-name correspondence.
scan_observations: Five separate flowers are visible, with three above and two below. The upper right one shows a wide dark blue lobe above the center, two lateral lobes, and two relatively pale lobes below. The lower flowers have conspicuous pointed strokes near their bases.

The four broad low green blades have pointed tips and shallowly toothed edges. Different narrow, deeply divided appendages arise higher up near nodes. Their relation to the stem is compatible with pansy stipules, though the drawing leaves their attachments ambiguous.
Two paragraphs wrap around the upper three flowers and extends to the left of the stem. I see no independent tag or pointer. f9v.1 and f9v.5 are the two paragraph starts in both ZL and Takahashi.
detail.source_notes: Han attributes the genus comparison to earlier work and reproduces both species from Lindman plate 227. Vatne’s morphology study shows a crop of that plate and her names study shows the full plate alongside a modern photograph. The A and B drawings depict V. tricolor and V. arvensis. Han’s photographs of a garden pansy demonstrate a range of presentations. Han’s flattened-specimen explanation and Vatne’s illustration-error explanation address the same apparent reversal. Han’s observations concern the drawing. Vatne’s proposed translations require her separate reading assumptions.

detail.statement: The f9v scan supports a pansy-like Viola candidate through the five broad petal outlines, blue and pale coloration, deeply divided green appendages at the nodes, and branching stalk and root. The front-facing drawing does not give a reliable spur measurement or a consistent view of the sepals. These are useful characters in separating Viola tricolor from Viola arvensis and their intermediates. I agree with the draft’s botanical uncertainty and dissent on confirming a word-to-name anchor. The three pinned editions give twelve paragraph loci and no separate label locus. Vatne proposes multiple readings for words within the two paragraphs. The scan verifies those physical positions. It supplies no line or label pointing from any of them to the plant.

detail.check: Re-run the included public-corpus scripts and verify both transcribed examples against their Yale scans. Any A-before-B conclusion must be tested against a separate physical or scribal direction indicator.
findings: Re-running the three scripts saved in the prior public P-L1-005 record reproduced its complete stored result objects exactly. A separate recount also matched the main ZL substring totals: training A has 25 ed and 766 od sites (25/791); training B has 4,106 ed and 929 od (4,106/5,035). On the public evaluation pages the counts are 6/156 for A and 677/773 for B. Takahashi and RF have the same direction in both partitions.

Certain exact pair counts on training pages (A/B): ZL chedy 1/405, chedar 0/30, chedal 0/21 and qokeedy 0/279; Takahashi 2/402, 0/26, 0/20 and 0/277; RF 2/300, 0/18, 0/17 and 0/199. The paired od forms remain attested on both sides for each case where the ed form is B-only.

The two A-side exception loci were checked in the public ZL, Takahashi and RF editions and against the linked Yale image crops. At f89r1.7.5, chedy and its neighboring words agree in all three. At f58v.12.5, ZL and Takahashi read chedal followed by dy, while RF leaves the boundary/readings uncertain. The f58v item is in the practice evaluation partition, not the training partition.

For one-site od-to-ed word-form edges whose partner occurs in both varieties, the shared ZL/Takahashi tally is 50 B-only ed edges and one A-only od edge at threshold 2; at threshold 4 it is 37 and one. The reverse exception is cthody/cthedy. Each edition has zero all-section A-only ed and B-only od edges under the same shared-partner rule.

In 1,000 equal-leaf herbal draws, the median B-minus-A ed-site fraction is 68.0 percentage points in ZL, 67.1 in Takahashi and 59.4 in RF; all 1,000 draws are positive. This controls leaf counts, not token counts. The only public section-by-hand overlap is recipe pages assigned to hand 3: both A pages are sides of leaf f58 (7 ed among 37 od/ed sites in ZL and Takahashi), and each of the 12 B leaves has a higher fraction. This leaves one A leaf and twelve B leaves for descriptive comparison.

The selected B-line ordering check is sparse and does not supply a chronological direction: within-line interior pairs from the four named pairs are 5 od-before-ed versus 2 ed-before-od in ZL (leaf-flip upper-tail 0.1875) and 6 versus 3 in Takahashi (0.2266). For all eligible one-site pairs the counts tie at 8/8 and 9/9. The practice evaluation pages contain at most one named-pair comparison per edition.
detail.interpretation: The main A/B spelling association is reproduced across the two independent EVA transcriptions and persists in the equal-leaf sensitivity. The strict absence premise has exceptions, including a ZL/Takahashi-agreed chedy on an A page and a chedal on another A page. Currier variety is also entangled with scribal hand and section: herbal A and B have disjoint hands, while the one shared hand-by-section stratum compares a single A leaf with twelve B leaves. The observed association alone does not date the pages or establish A-before-B; the tested local order is sparse and non-directional.
limits: RF is a merge of earlier transcriptions, not a third independent witness.
Equal-leaf resampling does not equalize the number of tokens per variety.
The scan crops support a reading check but provide no date or direction of composition.
detail.methods: Use the pinned corpus public practice partition, P lines and parsed words that match lowercase a–z. Count occurrences of either exact contiguous two-character sequence ed or od, including inside longer forms. Treat both sides and any panels of one numbered leaf as one unit for leaf-level calculations. Keep each edition separate. RF combines earlier transcriptions, so it is a robustness comparison and supplies no third independent witness. For local direction compare every pair of positions 1–10 apart that contains distinct exact variants separated by a single od-to-ed edit. Hold pair counts and distances fixed and flip orientation by leaf. The source and scan check selected four pairs from Graph 12. The cthody comparison follows the existing experiment.

From the repository root with the pinned texts fetched, run each with PYTHONPATH=. python3 /path/to/script.py. The scripts only inspect public practice train and evaluation partitions.

check: Repeat the comparison at native scan resolution before rating the candidate orders. Have two readers mark openings, ruling, edge crossings and possible offsets on unlabeled images. Compare each proposed junction with current neighbors and matched unrelated margins. Register each mirrored offset against several independent features on the leaf and assess whether the pigment or ruling can be dated to initial production. Report each surviving order and the evidence needed to choose among them.

detail.check: Repeat the comparison at native scan resolution before rating the candidate orders. Have two readers mark openings, ruling, edge crossings and possible offsets on unlabeled images. Compare each proposed junction with current neighbors and matched unrelated margins. Register each mirrored offset against several independent features on the leaf and assess whether the pigment or ruling can be dated to initial production. Report each surviving order and the evidence needed to choose among them.
detail.interpretation: No ruled line or pinhole match was resolved at a candidate between-sheet junction in these normal-light scans. This does not establish an absence of ruling. The counts are exact permutations under optional, stated geometric and opening assumptions, not tests of historical probability. The direct scan comparison provides a strong same-sheet clue in Q13, suggestive opening features in both quires, and a possible Q20 contact at a stage whose date remains uncertain. The evidence distinguishes some features of the candidates but does not identify a unique sequence of the surviving sheets in either quire.

method.arrangements: For a sheet a|b in the tested orientation, a stacked arrangement reads ar, av, br, bv consecutively. Its within-sheet opening is av facing br. The between-sheet openings are bv facing the next ar. For a nested arrangement take the first leaves in order and the second leaves in reverse. Skip missing f109 and f110 when listing visible leaves, and limit layout counts to surviving bifolia with their published orientations.
method.comparison: Use the first text band of the five lower-numbered rectos of Q13 and the six of Q20 as controls for the opening features. Inspect inner margins of the two Q13 same-sheet pairs and the currently facing controls. Compare the two distinct Q13 proposals at their pool-sheet junctions. Examine current and proposed star-sheet contacts separately. Pixel coordinates are approximate on the specified 880 px wide full images, origin at the top left.
method.scope: Test the explicit sheet orders in the paper for Q13 and Q20. All visual observations come from public scans. No transcription, text-similarity fitting, or hidden split is used. Sheet identity, production pairing, an opening or ending surface, and actual contact between sheets have different implications for order.

observations: The pool on f78v has linework entering its right inner margin. On f81r a branch enters the left inner margin between the upper and lower pools. The linework is consistent with the continuation identified by the authors and Zandbergen when the two halves of one parchment are opened together. The currently facing controls f79r and f80v do not show comparable continuations at those margins.

The proposed f76v–f83r connection is a weaker, more local drawing cue. The illustration at the upper left of f83r approaches the fold at the site of the reported continuation with f76v. Even if the mark on f76v is accepted as part of that drawing, this is another same-sheet connection.

An enlarged, extended initial at the upper left of f76r stands out in the opening comparison with f75r, f77r, f78r and f79r. f76r is the only page of this quire without a substantial illustration. This is compatible with a section opening. It would favor the second stacked candidate over the first only if this marks the start of the entire gathering.

Both proposals put the pool-bearing sheets 75|84 and 78|81 next to each other. The second gives f84v facing f78r, with comparable flared and patterned forms near the tops of the two pages. The first gives f81v facing f75r, with similar green figure-filled pools. These are motif similarities rather than measured line joins. Pelling also attained f84v facing f78r in a nested hypothesis by reversing 75|84. The facing pair alone cannot identify the binding structure.

Compared with f103r, f104r, f106r, f107r and f108r, f105r has an especially extended initial and more space above the main first line. This is evidence for special opening treatment. f116v carries a few lines near the top and is mostly uninscribed. Both the published stack and the current binding already end there. The quire mark on f103r pertains to a recorded arrangement, and the first twelve lines of f115r are assigned to another hand, showing that an opening feature can also represent a local division.

In the f115v scan the main leaf has two small reddish marks near the inner edge, roughly (818,123) and (817,246). They are left of the narrow sliver showing f116r itself, so that sliver and its visible stars should be excluded. The first two conspicuously red centers on the f116r scan are near (54,139) and (56,266). The vertical separations are approximately 123 and 127 pixels. The marks are consistent with Pelling's contact report. The approximate spacing and a shared color family are insufficient to identify pigment or date the transfer. No single-star or unrelated-margin false-match rate has been measured.

The f115v–f116r pair faces today. In the published stack f115v would instead face f106r, and f116r would face f103v on its own bifolium. The possible f113v–f115r offset across a flaw of f114 and the weaker reported stray spots are useful targets for sharper registration. They are not scored here as verified connections. If the f115v–f116r contact was made while the order in question was in use, it favors a different layout from the published stack at that stage.

The direct scan comparison provides a strong same-sheet clue in Q13, suggestive opening features in both quires, and a possible Q20 contact at a stage whose date remains uncertain. The evidence distinguishes some features of the candidates but does not identify a unique sequence of the surviving sheets in either quire.

method.arrangements: For a sheet a|b in the tested orientation, a stacked arrangement reads ar, av, br, bv consecutively. Its within-sheet opening is av facing br. The between-sheet openings are bv facing the next ar. For a nested arrangement take the first leaves in order and the second leaves in reverse. Skip missing f109 and f110 when listing visible leaves, and limit layout counts to surviving bifolia with their published orientations.
method.comparison: Use the first text band of the five lower-numbered rectos of Q13 and the six of Q20 as controls for the opening features. Inspect inner margins of the two Q13 same-sheet pairs and the currently facing controls. Compare the two distinct Q13 proposals at their pool-sheet junctions. Examine current and proposed star-sheet contacts separately. Pixel coordinates are approximate on the specified 880 px wide full images, origin at the top left.
method.scope: Test the explicit sheet orders in the paper for Q13 and Q20. All visual observations come from public scans. No transcription, text-similarity fitting, or hidden split is used. Sheet identity, production pairing, an opening or ending surface, and actual contact between sheets have different implications for order.

observations: The pool on f78v has linework entering its right inner margin. On f81r a branch enters the left inner margin between the upper and lower pools. The linework is consistent with the continuation identified by the authors and Zandbergen when the two halves of one parchment are opened together. The currently facing controls f79r and f80v do not show comparable continuations at those margins.

The proposed f76v–f83r connection is a weaker, more local drawing cue. The illustration at the upper left of f83r approaches the fold at the site of the reported continuation with f76v. Even if the mark on f76v is accepted as part of that drawing, this is another same-sheet connection.

An enlarged, extended initial at the upper left of f76r stands out in the opening comparison with f75r, f77r, f78r and f79r. f76r is the only page of this quire without a substantial illustration. This is compatible with a section opening. It would favor the second stacked candidate over the first only if this marks the start of the entire gathering.

Both proposals put the pool-bearing sheets 75|84 and 78|81 next to each other. The second gives f84v facing f78r, with comparable flared and patterned forms near the tops of the two pages. The first gives f81v facing f75r, with similar green figure-filled pools. These are motif similarities rather than measured line joins. Pelling also attained f84v facing f78r in a nested hypothesis by reversing 75|84. The facing pair alone cannot identify the binding structure.

Compared with f103r, f104r, f106r, f107r and f108r, f105r has an especially extended initial and more space above the main first line. This is evidence for special opening treatment. f116v carries a few lines near the top and is mostly uninscribed. Both the published stack and the current binding already end there. The quire mark on f103r pertains to a recorded arrangement, and the first twelve lines of f115r are assigned to another hand, showing that an opening feature can also represent a local division.

In the f115v scan the main leaf has two small reddish marks near the inner edge, roughly (818,123) and (817,246). They are left of the narrow sliver showing f116r itself, so that sliver and its visible stars should be excluded. The first two conspicuously red centers on the f116r scan are near (54,139) and (56,266). The vertical separations are approximately 123 and 127 pixels. The marks are consistent with Pelling's contact report. The approximate spacing and a shared color family are insufficient to identify pigment or date the transfer. No single-star or unrelated-margin false-match rate has been measured.

The f115v–f116r pair faces today. In the published stack f115v would instead face f106r, and f116r would face f103v on its own bifolium. The possible f113v–f115r offset across a flaw of f114 and the weaker reported stray spots are useful targets for sharper registration. They are not scored here as verified connections. If the f115v–f116r contact was made while the order in question was in use, it favors a different layout from the published stack at that stage.

detail.statement: I reviewed the Yale f80r scan and the cited comparison images and records. The figure holds a small bulbous object behind the waist; a short projection angles downward and inward, separated from the body. Keagan Brewer’s 2022 reading of it as a phallic insertion device is a serious published alternative, and the figure’s pose is consistent with that interpretation. The Clm 337 clyster bag offers a partial silhouette analogy (reservoir plus nozzle), but it is more elongated, shown separately, and does not match the way the f80r figure holds the object. The Wellcome MS.49 gynecological scenes establish a medical context for some neighboring imagery but do not identify this item. The nonmedical examples in Wellcome MS.49 f60r and Morgan MS G.24 f42r show that held implements and raised-arm gestures also occur in nonmedical scenes; their long scourge and textile tools do not match the f80r silhouette. I therefore agree with N-002’s limited conclusion that the referent remains unresolved and that no word–name pairing is established. I would keep the published phallic reading explicit as a competing interpretation and scope “no dated example” to the sources reviewed here, not treat this small comparison set as exhaustive.

predictions.rosette: At fRos.33 the proposed totals are two loops and three legs, and the first component lacks a left loop. The ordered pairs k+f and f+k give okalcfhy or ofalckhy. The separate abbreviation suggestions p→ke and f→te are outside this visual test.
predictions.split_bench: Davis proposes two benched t forms connected across nearby writing, exemplified by f8r.14 ctho cthey. The visual prediction used here is one long upper span with a tall descent at each end and two independent low bench contacts. The f8r drawing has one high loop or hook at each outer end, so this class uses fused strokes. The sum of the ordinary t loop and leg counts is not a count of visible marks on f8r.
predictions.star: At f68r2.7 the proposed additive totals are three loops and three legs, and the first component has a left loop. The ordered pairs p+k and t+f satisfy those constraints and give opol chckhy or otol chcfhy.

detail.statement: Test the layouts of Davis's bridge-gallows by comparing closed-loop and stem features in shuffled Yale scan crops with several transcriptions. Paired gallows are plausible for some paragraph openings. Several superficially similar bridges have a shared lower bar or an ambiguous foot, and the complex labels admit conflicting component readings.

findings: Eight of eleven rows have cth at both aligned endpoints in IT. Four are within an IT word and three use adjacent IT words. The remaining pair is separated by two words at f35r.1. The two cth signs at f42r.1 occur farther right and cannot be counted as the two aligned endpoints.

Every one of the eight IT pairs has GC K at the first endpoint and GC 1 at the second. The independently encoded first endpoint agrees with cth, while the right endpoint has a plain bench reading. An older LSI witness supplies both cth forms for six of the seven within-word or adjacent pairs. The exception is f100v.14, where the First Study Group row reads the first cth but leaves the second unresolved.

All seven same-word or adjacent-word IT pairs stand at paragraph openings across three scribal hands and several sections. The count of seven under this chosen spacing rule does not recover Davis's undocumented list. Reading the locators from the manuscript shows that some open paragraphs midway down a page.

At f68r2.7 ZL encodes a rare sign both near the start and inside the later shape. IT otolchcthy keeps a benched t rather than the predicted k or f. LSI records Mike Roe otolch!tey, John Grove otolchc!hy, and Jorge Stolfi opolchs!hy. Stolfi and Grove even locate the landing of the raised stroke on different signs.

At fRos.33 the ZL and RF forms agree in their rare-code representation, while IT and GC lack a row. The raw interlinear includes John Grove's ofalcfhy for the bridged word, which pairs f with f and falls outside both proposed readings. This transcription is a witness to the ambiguity, without establishing the historical reading.
text_audit.rows_from_raw_zl: Read raw IVTFF text because the practical cleaner collapses extended signs. In a single locus search for a literal ZL brace form with c, code 132, 155 or 216, and optional h, followed by a brace form with c, code 133 or 196, and h. Preserve the text between them and match IT and case-preserved GC by locus. This deliberate shortlist includes mixed shapes and leaves the paper's unnamed examples unresolved.

detail.title: Long gallows bridges recur, with several distinct ink junctions and conflicting endpoint readings

findings: Within the seven IT pairs with close endpoints, two have traceable separate low contacts, including the f8r.14 example and the new f30v.1 example. Contacts are plausible with overlapping ink at f8v.1. At f80r.34 and f86v6.13 the right stem ends in a shared lower bar. The remaining two at f100v.14 and f102r2.16 have unresolved contacts. The long visual spans thus recur, with a range of attachments. The three comparison crops have ordinary short spans.

The spaced f35r.1 pair has two probable lower contacts and supplies an example of the visual pattern spanning additional words. The similarly extended f56r.1 and the more complex f42r.1 and f95v1.1 show why a long span alone is insufficient for assigning paired benched t.

For f68r2.7 the lobes and partial descents are compatible with a multi-part mark. The blinding results leave open whether three fully connected legs and three closed loops are present, and do not distinguish the two allocations proposed by Davis.

For fRos.33 the match to Figure 5 comes from the original Yale canvas rotated ninety degrees clockwise. Both readers independently found two traceable tall legs and an ambiguous pale surface feature above. The photographed ink does not independently reproduce the full three-leg, two-loop inventory. The exact cause of the bright trace and any hidden joined stroke remain unresolved.
visual_audit.method: From the raw shortlist, inspect ten loci with identifiable early line regions, leaving f99v.37 in the text audit only. Add two mixed forms and the rosette, plus three nearby ordinary controls. The two auxiliary image-model readers independently received only shuffled crops with anonymous IDs and the same written observations to record. They did not see the locus mappings, transliterations or tested readings. fRos.33 was supplied later as a supplementary anonymous crop. Counts refer to ink visible on these photographs and include a range for faint or open returns. This is an enriched sample and yields no population frequency.

rows.S01: Two full descents and a middle return, with two or three upper lobes. The left descent ends by the writing and the far right ends at a low curve.
rows.S02: A visible upper span joins the left descent to a short right return. A farther-right curl and lowering stroke are possible. The readers could not fix both loop closure and attachment at the resolution examined.
rows.S03: Long upper span, two discernible descents, one closed or nearly closed head and a more open left return. Both readers see distinct low attachments.
rows.S04: A long pale span and two descents. Separate low horizontals align with the descents and the left join is faint.
rows.S05: Ordinary comparison with a short raised connector. The right descent ends high or is obscured.
rows.S06: Long span from left to center and a shorter rightward connection. Both readers report two outer descents and a higher central return, with two to three loop-like forms and faint outer contacts.
rows.S07: Two descents and long upper span. The left stem ends near an oval and the right meets a short curved stroke.
rows.S08: Two long bars at different levels. The right upper descent feeds into the lower bar and a second independent foot is unresolved.
rows.S09: Long upper trace next to smaller marks. Both readers see a possible gap above the left low stroke and a contact at the right.
rows.S10: Two raised loops and two spans. The left descent goes through the lower span to a low curve and the right ends in the lower span.
rows.S11: Long pale span with two descents. Both readers trace separate low horizontal attachments, with weak contrast at the right.
rows.S12: Long trace toward the right end with a pale gap. The left foot is crowded with rounded ink and the right enters a low horizontal.
rows.S13: Ordinary comparison with a short upper connector. The two descents contact the same low stroke.
rows.S14: Ordinary comparison with a short upper connector and no resolved low bench attachments.
rows.S15: Two descents and a long span. Both readers see separate low contacts as plausible. Brown-red marking and overlapping ink limit the right join.
rows.S16: Two tall descents with a short dark upright near the top, zero secure closed loops and one possible open return at the right. Both readers observe a pale surface line crossing the apparent bridge and no continuous dark ink span that can be traced. The short upright does not show a third descent.

visual_audit.rule_for_comparison: Code both benches as apparent only when both readers can trace a low contact under each separate terminal or judge a contact probable despite a stated overlap. Code a shared-bar ending when both see the right stem ending in the spanning lower bar. Keep faded, aligned but disconnected or crowded foot shapes unresolved. This synthesis was coded after collecting both independent reads.

detail.statement: I reviewed the twelve inner centres on Yale canvases 1006200–1006207, distinguishing writing in the centre from the circumferential Voynich text. f70v2 (1006200; two fish): one Latin-script word between the fish and one freestanding Voynich word beside the upper star; the upper fish lies between that Voynich label and the Latin-script word, and no drawn line joins them. A lower star in the same centre has no label. f70v1 (1006201; horned animal at a plant): a Latin-script word on the animal; no freestanding Voynich word in the centre, and no circumferential text line immediately bounding this centre. f71r (1006202; horned animal at a plant): a Latin-script word on the animal and Voynich writing around the centre; no freestanding Voynich word. I checked this centre in a full-resolution crop. f71v and f72r1 (1006203; bull-like animals): each has a Latin-script word below the animal and circumferential Voynich writing; neither has a freestanding Voynich word. f72r2 (1006203; two figures holding hands): a Latin-script word between the figures and circumferential Voynich writing; no freestanding Voynich word. f72r3 (1006203; two clawed animals): a Latin-script word below the lower animal and circumferential Voynich writing; no freestanding Voynich word. f72v3 (1006204; four-legged animal) and f72v2 (1006204; clothed figure holding a star): each has a Latin-script word beside or beneath the emblem and circumferential Voynich writing; neither has a freestanding Voynich word. The star held by the figure is unlabelled. f72v1 (1006205; balance): a Latin-script word beneath the emblem and circumferential Voynich writing; no freestanding Voynich word. f73r (1006206; animal with looped tail): a Latin-script word beneath the animal, circumferential Voynich writing, and an unlabelled star; no freestanding Voynich word. f73v (1006207; figure with crossbow): a Latin-script word at the feet near the circumferential text; no freestanding Voynich word. In all centres with ring writing, I treated that circular line separately from a standalone label. I find no image-supported pairing of a Voynich word and a Latin-script month annotation: the sole freestanding Voynich label is next to the upper star on f70v2, with the upper fish between it and the month word. I did not transcribe or date the Latin-script words. This is a visual review, so the distinction between a ring word and a nearby centre word where they approach one another remains a judgement by eye.
